problems.title: [Iodatometric titration of ascorbic acid and its transformations in solution]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [Iodatometric titration of ascorbic acid and its transformations in solution]

Ascorbic acid ($\mathbf{AA}$) is an important vitamin and antioxidant. Its quantity in pharmaceuticals is determined by titration with potassium iodate in 0.5 M HCl medium in the presence of starch, during which dehydroascorbic acid $\ce{C6H6O6}$ ($\mathbf{DHA}$) and iodide ion are formed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-1-1-fig1.png

1. Write down the equations of titration reaction and reaction producing iodine that gives color to the indicator. Calculate the amount of $\mathbf{AA}$ in the sample (in mol), if $9.5\,\mathrm{mL}$ of 0.100 M $\ce{KIO3}$ solution was spent for its titration.

$\mathbf{DHA}$ is slowly converted into xylosone $\ce{C5H8O5}$ as a result of addition of a water molecule and decarboxylation. Xylosone rapidly (much more rapid than during the previous stage) is reduced by the second molecule of $\mathbf{AA}$ to yield xylose $\ce{C5H10O5}$ and another molecule of $\mathbf{DHA}$. Then xylose slowly cyclizes to give furfural $\ce{C5H4O2}$.

Having started a titration of $\mathbf{AA}$ (total amount: 1.00 mmol) with iodate as described in question 1, the analyst left the lab, and when he returned, he found no ascorbic acid in solution. At the same time, xylose and furfural were found in solution, their total amount being 0.55 mmol.

2. Write down the reactions of $\mathbf{DHA}$ and xylosone transformations during storage of the solution using chemical formulas (no structures).

3. What was the volume of 0.100 M iodate solution that the analyst had spent before he left the lab?

4. What other organic components, beside xylose and furfural, and in what quantities were present in solution by the time the analyst returned, if the system reached equilibrium?

5. What side reaction except for the mentioned ones could also lower the $\mathbf{AA}$ concentration in solution during its storage?

If titration of $\mathbf{AA}$ by iodate is performed in the medium of 5 M HCl, then iodate will be also reduced to iodide, but $7.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of 0.100 M iodate solution will be spent for 0.300 mmol of $\mathbf{AA}$.

6. What will be the product of oxidation of $\mathbf{AA}$ under these conditions? Write down the reaction of titration and the structure of this product if no other carbon-containing compounds are formed in the reaction.

problems.title: [A scheme of binary compounds of one class]
problems.problem:
Problem 2. [A scheme of binary compounds of one class]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-1-2-fig1.png

$\mathbf{X}$ (mass content of the heavy element 98.45%) is formed as a red-brown precipitate at mixing of a solution of a blue salt $\mathbf{A}$ (crystallohydrate) with a solution of a monobasic phosphorus containing acid $\mathbf{B}$. A white powder $\mathbf{Y}$ can be obtained by reacting of $\mathbf{L}$ with an iodide $\mathbf{C}$ or a flammable liquid $\mathbf{D}$ (molar mass $95.4\,\mathrm{g/mol}$). $\mathbf{Z}$ is readily produced by direct interacting of equimolar amounts of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$ under pressure. $\mathbf{E}$ presents in minerals such as olivine, dolomite and carnallite. $\mathbf{L}$ is prepared by the reduction of a steady nitride $\mathbf{G}$, containing 40.20% of nitrogen. $\mathbf{L}$ and its derivatives are widely used in preparatory chemistry as strong reduction agents. $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are rather unstable and decompose higher than $90\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ are metals with adjacent atomic numbers, $\mathbf{J}$ is an acid containing chlorine. $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $\mathbf{L}$ – binary compounds related to one class.

1. Define all the denoted compounds.

2. Write down all presented reactions.

3. Explain why $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$ are stable in water, $\mathbf{Z}$ decomposes in water slowly while $\mathbf{L}$ reacts with water easily with a high exothermic effect.

4. What does $\mathbf{Z}$ serve as in the alternative power engineering?

5. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{B}$ and explain why $\mathbf{B}$ is a monobasic acid?

problems.title: [Anhydrous nitrates from liquid N2O4 and N2O5]
problems.problem:
Problem 3. [Anhydrous nitrates from liquid N2O4 and N2O5]

Copper reacts with deluted $\ce{HNO3}$ to originate a colorless gas $\mathbf{X}$ (readily becomes brown in air) and the blue solution. On evaporating this solution one may crystallize a blue hydrate $\mathbf{A}$ containing 2.5 molecules $\ce{H2O}$ per formula unit. One cannot eliminate water from $\mathbf{A}$ to prepare an anhydrous salt $\mathbf{D}$ by means of thermal decomposition on air. The decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$ runs in accordance with the two-stage process (scheme I, $\mathbf{B}$ is a hydroxo salt, $\mathbf{C}$ is an oxide) with mass loss 48.4% in the first stage.

Scheme I. $\mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{t\,^\circ\mathrm{C}} \mathbf{B}$ (52.9% Cu, 5.8% N) $\xrightarrow{t\,^\circ\mathrm{C}} \mathbf{C}$ (79.9 % Cu)

To synthesize an anhydrous $\mathbf{D}$ the copper should be treated by liquid $\ce{N2O4}$ dissolved previously in ethyl acetate or acetonitrile. These solvents provide the dissociation of $\ce{N2O4}$ into ions coordinated by copper. The anhydrous $\mathbf{D}$ synthesis also runs in accordance with the two-stage process (scheme II, $\mathbf{Y}$ is a complex salt $\ce{CuN4O10}$).

Scheme II. $\mathrm{Cu} \xrightarrow{\ce{N2O4},\ \ce{CH3CN}} \mathbf{Y} \xrightarrow{t\,^\circ\mathrm{C}} \mathbf{D}$

To synthesize some other anhydrous nitrates (for example, zirconium nitrate $\mathbf{E}$) one can use $\ce{N2O5}$ undergoing a dissociation into ions in the presence of anhydrous $\ce{HNO3}$. The salt $\mathbf{Z}$ (see scheme III) is built up similarly to $\mathbf{Y}$.

Scheme III. $\ce{ZrCl4} \xrightarrow{\ce{N2O5},\ \ce{HNO3}} \mathbf{Z}$ (20.4% Zr, 18.8% N) $\xrightarrow{t\,^\circ\mathrm{C}} \mathbf{E}$

1. Write down the equations for the autoionization of $\ce{N2O4}$ and $\ce{N2O5}$ taken place in corresponded solutions.

2. Determine the $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ formulae and the ions forming $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ complex salts.

3. Write down the equations for the reactions described.

4. Draw the graphic formula for $\ce{N2O4}$ and $\ce{N2O5}$.

problems.title: [A thiophene derivative for organic transistors]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [A thiophene derivative for organic transistors]

Thiophene molecules are the efficient building blocks for production of organic transistors because they are structurally inflexible and relatively stable but can be easily functionalized. In 2011, it was synthesized derivative of thiophene which was shown to be efficient for preparation of organic transistors:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-1-4-fig1.png

1. Which aromatic compound – thiophene or benzene – is more reactive in the electrophilic substitution reactions?

2. Thiophene nitration produced a mixture of two mononitroderivatives in a ratio of ~100:1. Write down the structural formula of the main product.

3. Write down the structural formula of amine $\ce{RNH2}$ if it is known that its $^{13}$C NMR spectrum contains 3 signals (molecule has 3 types of carbon atoms).

4. Decipher scheme of synthesis accounting for fact that $^{1}$H NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{D}$ contains four signals with the relative intensities of 2:2:3:3.

problems.title: [Electrospray and electron-impact mass spectrometry]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Electrospray and electron-impact mass spectrometry]

Electrospray is a method for ionization of molecules in solutions. The main advantage is low fragmentation. A liquid passes through a thin capillary and leaves the needle tip in the form of small charged droplets. The droplets move under electric field, growing smaller in size due to vaporization of the solvent and spontaneous fragmentation into smaller parts. As a result, micro-droplets are generated, containing only one charged molecule (ion). After vaporization of the last portions of the solvent the ions are directed to a mass spectrometer to be analyzed by the mass-to-charge ratio ($m/z$).

Electrospray is used for determination of the molecular mass of proteins. The peaks of multiply protonated ions $[\mathbf{A} + n\mathrm{H}]^{n+}$, where $n$ – the number of protons, attached to the molecule $\mathbf{A}$, are registered by mass spectrometer. In the figure the mass spectrum of lysozyme $\mathbf{A}$ is shown. The charges of neighboring ions differ by one unit.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-1-5-fig1.png

1. In the mass spectrum choose any two peaks and from the values $m/z$ calculate the molecular mass M of $\mathbf{A}$. Express the mass in daltons ($1\,\mathrm{Da} = 1\,\mathrm{a.m.u.} = 1.66054\cdot10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$) and round it off to the nearest whole number. The proton mass $m_\mathrm{p} = 1.0073\,\mathrm{Da}$.

2. Find the charges ($z$) of all the ions, presented in the mass spectrum (whole numbers in elementary charges $e = 1.602\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$).

The stability of a charged droplet with respect to ruptures is conditioned by competition between electrostatic and cohesion (surface) energy. For a spherical droplet, $U_\mathrm{el} = q^2/8\pi\varepsilon_0 r$, where $q$ – charge of the droplet, $r$ – radius, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{J^{-1}\,C^2\,m^{-1}}$, $U_\mathrm{surf} = \sigma S$, where $S$ – area of the droplet surface, $\sigma$ – surface tension.

3. From energetic considerations derive the stability condition for a spherical droplet with respect to rupture into two parts of the same shape and volume (with charges $q/2$). Inequality, expressing the condition, should contain $q$, $r$ as the variables, and $\sigma$, $\varepsilon_0$ as the constants.

4. Determine the maximum charge $q$ (in elementary charges $e$), which can bear a water droplet with $r = 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{cm}$? Round off the answer to the whole number. Surface tension of water $\sigma = 7.28\cdot10^{-2}\,\mathrm{J\cdot m^{-2}}$.

Distinguished from electrospray, molecules under electron impact ionization undergo, as a rule, considerable fragmentation. Mass spectrum of fullerene derivative $\mathrm{C}_N(\mathrm{C}\mathbf{X}_3)_n$, obtained from its vapor, is shown in figure. The element $\mathbf{X}$ is halogen. All the peaks represent ions with the charge +1, but different numbers of $\mathrm{C}\mathbf{X}_3$-groups.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-1-5-fig2.png

5. a) How many carbon atoms ($N$) does the fullerene molecule, ($\mathrm{C}\mathbf{X}_3$-derivative of which was studied) contain? b) Determine the element $\mathbf{X}$; c) Determine the number of functional groups ($n$) in the studied compound.

problems.title: [Menthone and its stereoisomers]
problems.problem:
Problem 6. [Menthone and its stereoisomers]

Essential oils of some herbs are source of menthone ($\mathbf{I}$) which has a number of stereoisomers:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-1-6-fig1.png

1. Cycloalkanones are often synthesized by pyrolysis of calcium salts of the appropriate acids. In particular, this method was utilized to confirm structure of menthone by counter synthesis. Write down structural formula of acid pyrolysis of which calcium salt produces $\mathbf{I}$.

2. Write down IUPAC name for $\mathbf{I}$ and structural formulae of all its stereoisomers.

In (–)-menthone carbon atom, connected to $\ce{CH3}$ group, has $R$-configuration. In aqueous $\ce{CH3COOH}$ solution (–)-$\mathbf{I}$ undergoes epimerization at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ producing the equilibrium mixture of (–)-menthone and (+)-isomenthone [(+)-$\boldsymbol{iso}\mathbf{I}$]. This mixture has specific rotator power of $-3^\circ$. The transformation (–)-$\mathbf{I} \rightleftarrows$ (+)-$\boldsymbol{iso}\mathbf{I}$ proceeds via the intermediate formation of unstable compound $\mathbf{X}$ which is isomer of (–)-$\mathbf{I}$ and (+)-$\boldsymbol{iso}\mathbf{I}$. IR spectrum of $\mathbf{X}$ contains a broad band at $3500 - 3200\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

3. Calculate content of (%) (–)-$\mathbf{I}$ ($[\alpha]_\mathrm{D}^{20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}} = -30^\circ$) and (+)-$\boldsymbol{iso}\mathbf{I}$ ($[\alpha]_\mathrm{D}^{20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}} = +92^\circ$) as well as equilibrium constant $K$. Write down structural formula of $\mathbf{X}$.

4. Accounting for your answer on question 3, propose structural formulae of (–)-$\mathbf{I}$ and (+)-$\boldsymbol{iso}\mathbf{I}$, using cyclohexane conformations giving in the answer sheet.

problems.title: [Samarium–neodymium dating of the Moama meteorite]
problems.problem:
Problem 7. [Samarium–neodymium dating of the Moama meteorite]

Chemistry of isotopes has different useful applications in many fields of science and industry. For example, it is used for studies of reaction mechanisms and kinetics, for catalysis studies, diffusion, adsorption, etc. In geology, one of the applications of isotopes is determination of the age of rocks and other objects, such as meteorites.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-1-7-fig1.png

One of such methods, based on samarium and neodymium isotopes, was developed by Langmar in 1947. The $^{143}$Nd quantity increase due to $^{147}$Sm decay ($\tau_{1/2} = 1.06\cdot10^{11}$ years) from initial value $n_0(^{143}\mathrm{Nd})$ at the moment of object formation ($n$ – number of moles). The quantity of $^{144}$Nd does not change in time, permitting determination of the sample age, measuring the ratios $^{143}\mathrm{Nd}/^{144}\mathrm{Nd}$ and $^{147}\mathrm{Sm}/^{144}\mathrm{Nd}$ by mass spectrometry.

In 1940, in Australia, there was found a meteorite, named Moama. It is believed that the age of this meteorite is comparable to the age of Solar system. In 1978 two minerals were extracted from Moama – plagioclase and pyroxene, which were analyzed:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Mineral} & n(^{143}\mathrm{Nd}) / n(^{144}\mathrm{Nd}) & n(^{147}\mathrm{Sm}) / n(^{144}\mathrm{Nd}) \\ \hline \text{Plagioclase} & 0.510 & 0.111 \\ \text{Pyroxene} & 0.515 & 0.280 \end{array}$$

1. a) Write down the decay reaction for $^{147}$Sm; b) Determine the decay constant.

2. Determine the initial ratio $n_0(^{143}\mathrm{Nd}) / n_0(^{144}\mathrm{Nd})$ at the moment of meteorite formation using table data. Remember that $n_0(^{143}\mathrm{Nd}) / n(^{144}\mathrm{Nd})$ is the same for both minerals.

3. Calculate the age of Moama.

4. Is it possible, using Langmar’s method, to determine the age of rocks, which were formed in 3 – 5 millennium B.C.? Confirm the answer by a numerical example.

problems.title: [An alpha-emitting isotope X and the exhumation of Y. Arafat]
problems.problem:
Problem 8. [An alpha-emitting isotope X and the exhumation of Y. Arafat]

The President of the Palestinian National Authority, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Y. Arafat died suddenly under strange circumstances in November 2004. In 2012 the Y. Arafat’s body was exhumed as insisted by his widow, and the tissue samples were subjected to analysis. The results demonstrated the probability of Y. Arafat’s death because of the fatal poisoning with the substance containing an isotope of $\mathbf{X}$.

The numbers of α-particles emitted in a unit of time by 1.00 mg sample of ($T_{1/2} = 138.4$ days) and 4.55 g sample of $^{226}$Ra ($T_{1/2} = 1601$ year) are identical.

1. Write down the equation of radioactive decay of $^{226}$Ra isotope.

2. Calculate the molar mass of $\mathbf{X}$.

3. When the exhumation of Y. Arafat’s body (70 kg) would have become meaningless due to decreasing of the total α-radioactivity of the organism tissues up to 0.3 Bq/kg, if:

a) the minimal lethal dose of $\mathbf{X}$ is $1\,\mathrm{\mu g}$;

b) in norm, the α-activity ($A_\alpha$) of human body (70 kg) is 0.2 Bq/kg, this value staying unchanged for many years;

c) a non-radioactive isotope is formed from $\mathbf{X}$ in the process of its α-decay.

The ratio of the number of neutrons to protons ($N/Z$) in $\mathbf{X}$ equals 1.50.

4. Determine $\mathbf{X}$.

More than 90% of $\mathbf{X}$ is produced in Russia. The $^{209}$Bi isotope is used as the target in the one-step procedure for obtaining $\mathbf{X}$.

5. Write down the theoretically possible equations of nuclear reactions if the total mass of all the rest (but $\mathbf{X}$ and $^{209}$Bi) particles in the reaction does not exceed 1 a.m.u.

A sample of $\mathbf{X}$ of $1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ ($\rho_\mathbf{X} = 9.2\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) evolves significant energy per time unit (1210 W), which is comparable to that of an electric iron. This is behind the extreme toxicity of $\mathbf{X}$ for living things.

6. Calculate the initial kinetic energy (in MeV) of the α-particle formed in $\mathbf{X}$ decay supposed the kinetic energy completely transforms into the heat one ($1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$).

problems.title: [Acid dependence of the dissociation rate of the tris(bipyridyl)iron(II) complex]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Acid dependence of the dissociation rate of the tris(bipyridyl)iron(II) complex]

Baxendale and George showed, that the dissociation rate of $\mathrm{Fe(NH_4C_5{-}C_5H_4N)_3^{2+}}$ (tris-bipyridylferrum (II)) (after $\ce{Fe(bipy)3^{2+}}$) depends on the $\ce{H+}$ concentration:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} C(\mathrm{H^+}),\ \mathrm{mol}/L & 0 & 0.02 & 0.05 & 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.4 & 0.5 & 1.0 & 2.0 \\ \hline k_\mathrm{H}\cdot10^2 & 3.52 & 8.57 & 12.48 & 15.60 & 18.12 & 19.83 & 20.22 & 21.50 & 21.50 \end{array}$$

The resulting dependence they explained by protonation process, that preceded dissociation $\ce{Fe(bipy)3^{2+} + H+ <=> Fe(bipy)3H^{3+}}$, and considered, that $\ce{Fe(bipy)3^{2+}}$ dissociates slower than $\ce{Fe(bipy)3H^{3+}}$, and the speed limit is reached when only $\ce{Fe(bipy)3H^{3+}}$ is present in the solution. However this mechanism was disproved by the results of electron spectroscopy and another one was proposed. It included the break of one bond Fe–N ($k_1$, $k_{-1}$) followed by two streams: the first with break of the second bond Fe–N ($k_2$); the second – protonation of atom N ($k_3$) with subsequent break of the second bond Fe–N ($k_4$).

1. Draw the plot of dependence $k_\mathrm{H} = f(C(\mathrm{H^+}))$ and estimate the value of $C(\mathrm{H^+})$ corresponding to the start of achieving the speed limit.

2. Give the reason, why the spectra at $C(\mathrm{H^+}) = 0$ and $C(\mathrm{H^+}) = 2$ disproved the mechanism.

3. Write down the second mechanism with the help of structural formulae. Derivate kinetic equation and the equation for $k_\mathrm{H}$.

4. Give the value of the rate constant $k_1$, considering that at high $C(\mathrm{H^+})$ the limit rate is observed.

5. Find the ratio between the period of the first bond formation Fe–N and the period of breaking of the second bond Fe–N at $C(\mathrm{H^+}) = 0$.

6. Determine the structure of low-spin $\ce{Fe(bipy)3^{2+}}$ and high-spin $\ce{Fe(bipy)2^{2+}}$ by the CFT method and point the dissociation rate of what complex is higher.

problems.title: [Vacancies in a body-centered cubic metal]
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 2). [Vacancies in a body-centered cubic metal]

As there is no fish without bones, there are no materials without defects

The structures of real materials generally are not regular crystals as there are always different defects inside. These defects are formed in equilibrium, during material fabrication or use. The simplest defect is vacancy – absence of atoms in crystalline lattice.

Metal $\mathbf{A}$ is largely used in industry, it has body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice (see figure). If each 32$^\mathrm{th}$ elementary cell has one vacancy, this metal have the following parameters: $a_0 = 2.87$ Å, $\rho = 7.73\,\mathrm{g\cdot sm^{-3}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-2-2-fig1.png

1. a) How many atoms has one elementary bcc cell?

b) Determine the metal $\mathbf{A}$ by calculation of its molecular mass to one place decimals.

There are several characteristics of vacancies (v): concentration $c_\mathrm{v}$, formation Gibbs energy $\Delta_f G^0_\mathrm{v}$, diffusion coefficient $D$ ($\mathrm{sm^2\cdot sec^{-1}}$) and diffusion energy $E_\mathrm{D}$. Diffusion energy $E_\mathrm{D}$ is the sum of vacancy formation energy $\Delta_f U^0_\mathrm{v}$ and migration activation energy $E_\mathrm{A}$:

$$c_\mathrm{v} = \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta_f G^0_\mathrm{v}}{RT}\right), \qquad D = D_0\exp\left(-\frac{E_\mathrm{D}}{RT}\right) = D_0\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta_f U^0_\mathrm{v} + E_\mathrm{A}}{RT}\right).$$

Assume that vacancy formation enthalpy equals to formation energy.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-2-2-fig2.png

2. The change in which values should be neglected to be certain that $\Delta H \approx \Delta U$: a) temperature, b) pressure, c) volume, d) entropy?

3. Using the plot, determine $D_0$ and vacancy diffusion energy $E_\mathrm{D}$.

4. Neglecting vacancy formation entropy and taking into account that $\Delta_f U^0_\mathrm{v} = 3E_\mathrm{A}$, determine the vacancy concentration at 800K.

5. Is it possible that material with the defects concentration, pointed in question 1, is formed in equilibrium at 800K?

Diffusion coefficient is related to the vacancy jump frequency $\nu$ and jump distance $d$ by the equation: $D_0 = \nu k d^2/6$, where $k$ – the number of equivalent jumps (i.e. the number of nearest neighboring atoms).

6. Calculate jump frequency $\nu$ for a metal with bcc cell if $D_0 = 0.01\,\mathrm{sm^2\cdot sec^{-1}}$.

7. Vacancy formation energy is directly proportional to the number of neighbors ($k$). Calculate $\Delta_f U^0_\mathrm{v}$ on two surfaces, which are formed by cutting the metal by planes (200) and (110).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2014-2-2-fig3.png

problems.title: [Radiolysis of water, Fenton's reagent and the O–O bond energy]
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Radiolysis of water, Fenton's reagent and the O–O bond energy]

High-energy radiation can cause chemical reactions in substances. Radiolysis of water is one of the most important radiation-chemical processes. In particular, hydrogen gas is evolved. Release of $\ce{H2(g)}$ from aqueous solution of radium bromide was first observed by German scientist F. Giesel in 1902. Marie Curie compared this phenomenon with "electrolysis without electrodes".

In the first experiment water was subjected to γ-radiation from $^{60}$Co source, weighting 2 g. The half-life period of $^{60}$Co equals $\tau_{1/2} = 5.3$ years. Contribution of γ-decay to overall radiation constitutes 0.1% (there is also β-decay). The energy of one γ-quantum equals 1.332 MeV. The radiation-chemical yield of hydrogen $G = 0.047\,\mathrm{\mu mol\cdot J^{-1}}$. Assume that radiolysis occurs under the action of γ-rays only, and they are completely absorbed by the water. $1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.

In the second experiment hydrogen was produced by electrolysis with the current 8 A. Faraday constant $F = 96485\,\mathrm{C\cdot mol^{-1}}$. The duration of both processes was 1 hour.

1. a) Write down the equations of the processes at anode and cathode; b) Compare the volumes of hydrogen (at normal conditions), evolving in radiolysis and electrolysis of water.

If a diluted solution of $\ce{Fe(HSO4)2}$ is exposed to ionizing radiation one can get Fenton’s reagent – a mixture of hydrogen peroxide and a salt of Fe(II), which is used for water purification from organic pollutants of phenol series. Below are the reactions of oxidation of $p$-hydroxybenzoic acid (B):

$$\begin{array}{lcc} \ce{H2O2 + Fe^{2+} -> Fe^{3+} + OH- + OH^{\bullet}} & (k_1) & (1) \\ \ce{B + H2O2 -> B_{ox}} & (k_2) & (2) \\ \ce{B + OH^{\bullet} -> B_{ox}} & (k_3) & (3) \\ \ce{H2O2 + OH^{\bullet} -> HO2^{\bullet} + H2O} & (k_4) & (4) \\ \ce{OH^{\bullet} + Fe^{2+} -> Fe^{3+} + OH-} & (k_5) & (5) \end{array}$$

2. Using the stationary concentrations method, deduce the kinetic equation for oxidation of B.

Chloride ions can serve as inhibitors for Fenton’s reaction. In presence of $\ce{Cl-}$ the following reactions occur in the solution:

$$\ce{Cl- + HO^{\bullet} + H+(aq) -> Cl^{\bullet} + H2O}, \qquad \ce{Cl- + Cl^{\bullet} <=> Cl2^{-\bullet}}.$$

Ion $\ce{Cl2^{-\bullet}}$ practically does not react with organic molecules, disappearing mostly in the reaction with $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$, Electromotive force (e.m.f.) of this reaction is 1.528 V.

3. a) Write down the reaction of $\ce{Cl2^{-\bullet}}$ with $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$; b) Determine the equilibrium constant for this reaction at 298K. $E^0(\ce{Cl2^{-\bullet}}/\ce{Cl-}) = 2.3\,\mathrm{V}$, $E^0(\ce{Fe^{3+}}/\mathrm{Fe}) = -0.058\,\mathrm{V}$, $E^0(\ce{Fe^{2+}}/\mathrm{Fe}) = -0.473\,\mathrm{V}$.

$p$-Hydroxybenzoic acid can be oxidized catalytically to formic acid HCOOH:

$$\ce{C7H6O3(liq) + 11O(g) = 3HCOOH(liq) + 4CO2(g)}, \qquad \Delta_r H^0_{298} = -4994.69\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}.$$

Standard combustion enthalpy of formic acid: $\Delta_c H^0_{298}(\text{HCOOH, liq}) = -254.58\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$. Standard formation enthalpies of the compounds: $\Delta_f H^0_{298}(\ce{H2O}\text{, liq}) = -285.83\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta_f H^0_{298}(\ce{CO2}\text{, g}) = -393.51\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta_f H^0_{298}(\ce{C7H6O3}\text{, liq}) = -594.5\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

4. a) Write down the combustion reaction of HCOOH(liq); b) Calculate the enthalpy of the bond $\Delta H^0_{298}$(O–O) in $\ce{O2}$ molecule; c) Calculate the energy of this bond $\Delta U^0_{298}$(O–O); d) Calculate the bond energy at zero absolute temperature $\Delta U^0_0 = D^0_0$(O–O).

problems.title: [Minamata disease]
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem 1). [Minamata disease]

Minamata disease is caused by poisoning with a number of toxic compounds, in particular with substances $\mathbf{X}$ (colorless crystals, $t_\mathrm{melt} = 167\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and $\mathbf{Y}$ (colorless liquid). 14 people died the disease in 1956 in Japanese city of Minamata.

Production wastes of the plant manufacturing acetaldehyde (1), acetic acid (2), and vinyl chloride (3) turned out to be the mediated reasoning for people's deaths.

1. Determine the structure of the substance $\mathbf{S}$ used for the synthesis of products 1 – 3, and write down the reaction equations behind the industrial process indicating the reaction conditions.

Anaerobic bacteria utilizing $\mathbf{Z}$ (contains 26.12% by mass of halogen) are the immediate source of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ in nature. $\mathbf{Y}$ is formed from $\mathbf{Z}$ via two stages, both catalyzed by enzymes-transferases: $\mathbf{Z} \rightarrow \mathbf{X} \rightarrow \mathbf{Y}$

In laboratory, $\mathbf{X}$ can be obtained from $\mathbf{Y}$ using the colorless crystalline carbon-free substance $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the following equation:

$$\mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{Z} \rightarrow 2\mathbf{X}$$

0.235 g of a fine-grained black powder of metal $\mathbf{A}$ was solved in ~2.96 mL of 10% HCl ($\rho = 1.048\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) at slight heating. After the addition of $\ce{(NH4)2C2O4}$ solution taken in small excess, the deposition of 3.068 g yellow-orange precipitate $\mathbf{C}$ was observed. All the experiments were made under inert atmosphere, the solutions of HCl and $\ce{(NH4)2C2O4}$ were preliminary degassed.

Thermal analysis revealed the obtained precipitate to decompose in 3 stages in oxygen ($25\ldots900\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) with the formation of ternary mixture $\mathbf{G}$ with 57.3% mass loss. One of the stages is accompanied by an increase of the mass.

By adding an excess of $\ce{(NH4)2C2O4}$ to the solution of the salt $\mathbf{B}$ with cobalt nitrate, a red solution $\mathbf{D}$ could be prepared. $\ce{PbO2}$ and $\ce{CH3COOH}$ induces the change of the solution color from red to emerald green. Ethanol can be used to extract emerald green crystals of $\mathbf{E}$ and apple green crystals of $\mathbf{F}$. The latter becomes colorless under the light.

It was shown by the thermal analysis that the mixture of $\mathbf{E}$ и $\mathbf{F}$ crystals decomposes in oxygen ($25\ldots900\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) with the formation of mixture $\mathbf{G}$.

2. Determine the qualitative and quantitative composition (mol. %) of the mixture $\mathbf{G}$.

Problem 9 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 3). [Mixed-valence Me4O2 and Me3O groups in models of photosynthetic water oxidation]

A complex compound, that consists the group $\mathbf{Me}_4\mathrm{O}_2$, plays a great role in the oxidation process $\ce{2H2O - 4e- = O2 + 4H+}$ in the photosynthesis of green plants. The group $\mathbf{Me}_4\mathrm{O}_2$ participates in the photo-oxidation ($\overset{+2}{\mathbf{Me}}_x\overset{+3}{\mathbf{Me}}_{4-x}\mathrm{O}_2 - x\mathrm{e}^- + h\nu = \overset{+3}{\mathbf{Me}}_4\mathrm{O}_2$). Complex compounds of $\mathbf{Me}$ were synthesized to use in modelling of the similar process with participation of the group $\mathbf{Me}_3\mathrm{O}$ ($\overset{+2}{\mathbf{Me}}_x\overset{+3}{\mathbf{Me}}_{3-x}\mathrm{O} - x\mathrm{e}^- + h\nu = \overset{+3}{\mathbf{Me}}_3\mathrm{O}$). At the first step $\mathrm{K}_a\mathbf{Me}\mathrm{O}_b$ was added to 12.88 g (0.04 mol) of tetraalkylammonium bromide $\ce{[R4N]Br}$. The purple precipitate $\mathbf{A}$ with mass 14.44 g was obtained after filtration. At the second step 0.01 mol of $\ce{C5H5N}$ (Py) and $\mathbf{Me}(\ce{CH3COO})_2\cdot4\ce{H2O}$ were dissolved in alcohol, then glacial acetic acid and a part of $\mathbf{A}$ were added until a reddish brown solution $\mathbf{I}$ was produced. At the third step 0.00333 mol of $\ce{NaClO4}$ were mixed with the solution $\mathbf{I}$ and brown precipitate $\mathbf{D}$ was separated. Blackish brown crystals of $\mathbf{B}$ can be isolated by a careful evaporation of the solution $\mathbf{I}$ at $65\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The elemental composition of nonelectrolyte $\mathbf{B}$ and the cation in the salt $\mathbf{D}$ is the same (21.4% $\mathbf{Me}$, 42.0% C, 4.26% H, 5.44% N и 26.9% O).

Bond length, Å (number of bonds):

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \mathbf{Me}\text{–O}_a & \mathbf{Me}\text{–O}_b & \mathbf{Me}\text{–N} & \text{C–O}_b \\ \hline 1.94\ (3) & 2.10\ (12) & 2.17\ (3) & 1.28\ (12) \end{array}$$

Average valence angle, °:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \mathbf{Me}\text{–O}_a\text{–}\mathbf{Me} & \text{O}_a\text{–}\mathbf{Me}\text{–O}_b & \text{O}_a\text{–}\mathbf{Me}\text{–N} & \text{O}_b\text{–C–O}_b \\ \hline 120 & 94.6 & 179 & 118.3 \end{array}$$

1. Determine $\ce{[R4N]Br}$, $\mathbf{Me}$ and $\mathbf{A}$, if $M(\mathbf{A}) - M(\ce{[R4N]Br}) = 39\,\mathrm{g/mol}$, and $\mathbf{A}$ is formed in the exchange reaction.

2. Determine $\mathbf{B}$, draw the structural formula $\mathbf{B}$ and calculate $x$ in $\overset{+2}{\mathbf{Me}}_x\overset{+3}{\mathbf{Me}}_{3-x}\mathrm{O}$.

3. Determine $\mathbf{D}$. Write the formation reaction equations $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ from $\mathbf{A}$.

4. Calculate E for $\ce{O2 + 4H+ + 4e- = 2H2O}$ in water ($p(\ce{O2}) = 1$ atm, $C(\ce{H+}) = 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{mol}/L$), note that $E^0(\ce{O2}/\ce{H2O}) = 1.23\,\mathrm{V}$.

5. Calculate $E^0$ for $\overset{+3}{\mathbf{Me}}_3\mathrm{O}$ (the group in the cation of $\mathbf{D}$) + $x\mathrm{e}^-$ = $\overset{+2}{\mathbf{Me}}_x\overset{+3}{\mathbf{Me}}_{3-x}\mathrm{O}$ (the group in $\mathbf{B}$), note if the reaction proceeds 66.70% $E = 0.44\,\mathrm{V}$, concentrations of other reactants equal $C = 1\,\mathrm{mol}/L$.

6. Calculate e.m.f. at standard concentrations except $C(\ce{H+}) = 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{mol}/L$ and determine the possibility of complex $\mathbf{D}$ with group $\mathbf{Me}_3\mathrm{O}$ to participate in the photosynthesis.

problems.title: [Analysis of an ice-melting product]
problems.problem:
Problem 13 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Analysis of an ice-melting product]

Ice-melting chemicals reduce the freezing point of water by increasing the number of particles (both neutral particles and ions) present in a solution. This effect is quantitatively described as $\Delta T_m = imK$, where $K$ is cryoscopic constant of the solvent ($1.86\,\mathrm{K\cdot kg/mol}$ for water), $m$ is molality (amount of the solute (in mol) divided by the mass of the solvent (in kg)), $i$ is isotonic coefficient (number of particles produced upon the dissolution of the solute molecule). The acidity constant of formic acid is $10^{-3.75}$.

Ice-melting product $\mathbf{A}$ consists of NaCl, $\ce{CaCl2}$, calcium and ammonium formate and sand. This product may optionally be used with non-dissociating anticaking agent $\mathbf{X}$.

1. What is substance $\mathbf{X}$, if it contains only C, H, N and O atoms, and the solution obtained by adding 16.15 g of this substance to a 1 L portion of water freezes at $-0.50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

2. Aqueous solution of $\mathbf{A}$ (30.0 g/L) was filtered to remove sand, and four 10 mL aliquots were taken. An excess of formaldehyde was added to aliquot no. 1 which was then titrated with a 0.1000 M solution of KOH with phenolphthalein indicator; the endpoint titrant volume was 7.2 mL (this reaction yields hexamethylenetetramine $\ce{(CH2)6N4}$). 30 mL of 0.1000 M standard solution of alkaline $\ce{Br2}$ and then an excess of acidic solution of KI were added to aliquot no. 2; iodine in the resultant solution was titrated with 0.1000 M solution of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ (the endpoint titrant volume was 27.2 mL). Ammonia and metal indicator were added to aliquot no. 3 and the solution was titrated with 0.1000 M solution of EDTA until the color changed (the endpoint volume of EDTA was 12.7 mL). After addition of a $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ indicator to aliquot no. 4 it was titrated with 0.1000 M solution of $\ce{AgNO3}$ until the precipitate became pale orange (the endpoint titrant volume was 23.9 mL). Write down the reactions corresponding to the titrations and calculate the weight fractions of NaCl, $\ce{CaCl2}$ and the both formats in the dry sample.

3. Choose the most efficient component of the ice-melting chemical $\mathbf{A}$ by finding the weight of ice (g) which can be melted by 1 g of each of the following individual substances at $-10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: (a) NaCl, (b) $\ce{CaCl2}$, (c) ammonium formate.

4. Determine the isotonic coefficient of calcium formate in a 1 M solution. Write the equations corresponding to dissociation and hydrolysis of this salt. Calculate the contribution (in %) of hydrolysis into the value of isotonic coefficient.

problems.title: [Winkler titration of dissolved oxygen and its interferences]
problems.problem:
Problem 14 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 2). [Winkler titration of dissolved oxygen and its interferences]

Winkler titration is one of the methods of quantitative determination of oxygen in water. According to this method, manganese sulphate is added to an alkalized aliquot of water sample and allowed to react for a period of time. Then the sample is acidified with diluted sulphuric acid, followed by addition of potassium iodide. Next, iodine is titrated with standardized sodium thiosulphate solution.

1. Please write (and balance) all reactions this method relies on.

2. The method described above was applied to an aliquot of 0.500 L of water sample, and the volume of sodium thiosulphate (0.0423 M) spent was 8.43 mL. Please determine the concentration of oxygen in this sample in mg/L.

Winkler titration results may be affected by redox-active compounds. In particular, nitrite ions present in water samples may oxidize iodide ions, which may lead to a positive bias in the determination (overestimated results). This interference may be reduced by addition of sodium azide, urea or sulphamic acid $\mathrm{NH_3^+SO_3^-}$.

3. Write down the reactions occurring between nitrite ions and these compounds in weak acid medium (assume that all these reactions do not yield any nitrogen oxides).

4. During a Winkler test, a sample was pre-treated with an excess of sodium azide, which lead to incorrect final results. Write the reaction which caused this error (take into consideration that one of its products is molecular nitrogen) and indicate whether the bias in determination was positive or negative.

5. Both Fe(II) and Fe(III) salts are also among the known interferences to the Winkler method.

a) A sample containing 30 mg/L of Fe(III) was taken for analysis. The concentration of oxygen determined by Winkler titration in this sample was higher by 1.3 mg/L than the actual concentration of oxygen. This can be explained by a slow reaction which occurs between Fe(III) and iodide ions in acidic medium. Please write the equation of this reaction.

b) Fe(II) also interferes with this method. Please write the reactions explaining the causes of this interference. Would the bias be positive or negative?

c) A sample of water contains 15 mg/L of Fe(II) and 15 mg/L of Fe(III). What would be the result of determination of $\ce{O2}$ by Winkler titration if the actual concentration of $\ce{O2}$ is 9.0 mg/L? The analysis is carried under identical conditions in both parts 5a and 5c of this problem.

d) An amount of NaF was added to an aliquot of the same sample (5c), so that the concentration of NaF was 0.005 M. Determine the sign of the bias of determination of oxygen. Take into account that $\ce{Fe(OH)3}$ reacts with $\ce{F-}$ significantly faster than with $\ce{I-}$. Please write the reactions explaining this bias.

problems.title: [Greenhouse fumigants of Nero Wolfe]
problems.problem:
Problem 2. [Greenhouse fumigants of Nero Wolfe]

Nero Wolfe, a fictional character created by the mystery writer Rex Stout, was not only excellent armchair detective but also well-known amateur orchid grower. Some stories, devoted to Wolfe, includes description of the greenhouse disinfection using fumigation with cyanogas G, Nico Fume and ciphogene. Ciphogene is a fictional fumigant but two others were really used for this goal. Cyanogas G (compound $\mathbf{A}$) is a poisonous liquid with b.p. $26.7\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. For safety, this was producing directly in a greenhouse from the “black cyanide” (compound $\mathbf{B}$ containing 30.4% of nitrogen). In the pure form, $\mathbf{B}$ is a white powder but commercial product contains some impurities providing black-gray coloration. In the presence of water (even in the wet air) $\mathbf{B}$ undergoes hydrolysis producing $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

problems.title: [Rotation and vibration of diatomic molecules]
problems.problem:
Problem 8. [Rotation and vibration of diatomic molecules]

Diatomic molecule with masses of atoms $m_1$ and $m_2$ can be considered as a rigid rotator, if rotation doesn’t affect the equilibrium internuclear distance $r_e$. In quantum mechanics rotation energy of a molecule $E_\mathrm{rot} = B_eJ(J+1)$, where $J = 0, 1, 2\ldots$ – rotational quantum numbers, $B_e = \hbar^2/2I$ – rotational constant, $I = \mu r_e^2$ – moment of inertia, $\mu = m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ – the reduced mass of the molecule. In the ideal gas of diatomic molecules the occupancies of rotational levels are governed by Boltzmann distribution ($N_J$ – number of molecules on the level with rotational number $J$, $N$ – total number of molecules in the gas):

$$\frac{N_J}{N} \sim (2J+1)\exp\left[-\frac{B_eJ(J+1)}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right]$$

1. Determine the value of $J$, corresponding to the rotation level most highly occupied by the $\ce{N2}$ molecules at 298 K? $I = 1.401\cdot10^{-46}\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2}$?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2015-1-8-fig1.png

Lennard-Jones potential is used for description of the potential energy curves of diatomic molecules:

$$U(r) = 4\varepsilon\left[\left(\frac{r_0}{r}\right)^{12} - \left(\frac{r_0}{r}\right)^{6}\right],$$

where $r$ – distance between the nuclei, $\varepsilon$ and $r_0$ – curve parameters. Zero energy level corresponds to the total energy of two atoms at infinite distance between them.

2. a) On the axes of the graph $U(r)$ mark the points, corresponding to the parameters $\varepsilon$ and $r_0$. b) Find the equilibrium internuclear distance in the units of $r_0$.

For gases of polar molecules the pure rotational spectra can be detected.

3. Calculate the frequencies (Hz) of the first two lines of the absorption spectrum BrF. $B_e = 7.093\cdot10^{-24}\,\mathrm{J}$. According to the selection rules only transitions $J \rightarrow J+1$ are possible at absorption.

If along with the rotation one takes into account the molecular vibration motion, its energy equals to the sum of $E_\mathrm{rot} + E_\mathrm{vib}$ ($k$ – the force constant, $n = 0, 1, 2\ldots$ – the vibration quantum number):

$$E_\mathrm{vib} = \hbar\omega\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right) = \hbar\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)$$

4. For the molecule $\ce{^{127}I^{35}Cl}$ $k = 239\,\mathrm{N/m}$, $B_e = 2.26\cdot10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J}$. Find the wavelength at which light is absorbed by these molecules in the transition from the state with $J = 0$, $n = 0$ to the state with $J = 1$, $n = 1$?

In contrast to vibration frequency the force constant $k$ does not change at isotopic substitution.

5. The line $1326\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ is observed in the IR spectrum of $\ce{^{79}Br^{19}F}$. Calculate the frequency ($\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) of the corresponding line in the IR spectrum of $\ce{^{81}Br^{19}F}$.

Physical constants: Planck constant $h = 2\pi\hbar = 6.63\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J{\cdot}s}$, the light speed $c = 3\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, Avogadro number $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.02\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, 1 a.m.u. $= 1.66\cdot10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, Boltzmann constant $k_\mathrm{B} = 1.38\cdot10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}$.

Problem 1 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Dissolving rusty iron pins in citric acid]

Young chemistry fan Vasya weighed out 1.5 g of iron drawing pins and heated them in a 100 mL portion of citric acid ($\ce{H3Cit}$, see the scheme) solution. As soon as rust disappeared from the surface of the pins (but before the dissolution of iron started), he poured the liquid away and repeated heating with a fresh portion of citric acid solution. When the reaction finished, he filtered the solution (the weight of non-dissolved pins was 0.1 g) and evaporated it to dryness. Then Vasya placed the remaining dry salt (a neutral citrate monohydrate) into a weighed tube, sealed it with glass wool and ignited it in a ventilated room to prevent intoxication with the evolving gas. The solid product (its total weight was 1.0 g) was attracted by a magnet. When Vasya poured out the substance from the tube, he observed beautiful sparks appearing due to its spontaneous burning in air. Some soot was left on the tube walls after the experiment.

problems.title: [Gold nanoparticles and Rayleigh light scattering]

Problem 3 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Gold nanoparticles and Rayleigh light scattering]

A solution of $\ce{HAuCl4}$ ($c_\mathrm{Au} = 4\cdot10^{-6}\,\mathrm{M}$) containing a stabilizer was heated in the presence $\ce{H2O2}$, which yielded a colloidal solution of gold metal nanoparticles (AuNPs) of diameter $d = 10\,\mathrm{nm}$; the AuNPs concentration $c_\mathrm{AuNP}$ was $2.5\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{M}$ (in gold), while the rest of gold was left in the form of Au(III) (solution $\mathbf{1}$).

Problem 6 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 3). [Solubility of chlorine in water and a binary disinfectant gas]

Gaseous chlorine was first obtained by the Swedish chemist Carl Scheele in 1774 when interacting pyrolusite with hydrochloric acid. Currently, chlorine is produced on an industrial scale in large quantities.

1. Give the equation of the reaction, which allowed K. Scheele first obtain chlorine.

Chlorine is a very toxic gas. Several deep breaths of air, in which the chlorine content of 1000 ppm, is sufficient for death coming (ppm – one millionth fraction or parts per million).

The partial pressure of chlorine in the gaseous phase above the solution equilibrium is in direct ratio to the molar concentration of these particles in the solution. The value of the proportionality coefficient ($k(\ce{Cl2})$, $\mathrm{atm{\cdot}dm^3/mol}$) depends on many factors: temperature, ionic strength, presence of other substances. In a first approximation for solutions with zero ionic strength its temperature dependence may be written as:

$$k(\ce{Cl2}) = 6.554\cdot10^{5}\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{3163.7}{T}\right).$$

2. Calculate the mass concentration of molecular chlorine (in $\mathrm{mg/dm^3}$) in saturated at $20.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ solution, which occurs in equilibrium with air at atmospheric pressure of 750 mm Hg and with chlorine content equal to 1000 ppm.

The dynamic equilibrium between dissolved chlorine and water in solution is established. This equilibrium constant ($K$, $\mathrm{mol^2/dm^6}$) and acid dissociation rate constant of the weak hypochlorous acid (p$K_\mathrm{a}$) for solutions with low ionic strength in the temperature range 0 – $45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ depend on the temperature ($T$) as follows:

$$\lg K = -\frac{982798}{T^2} + \frac{5485.7}{T} - 10.7484; \qquad \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = \frac{3000.0}{T} - 10.0686 + 0.0253T.$$

3. Calculate the molar concentration of hypochlorous acid and the pH in the solution of question 2.

4. For the purification of waste water the concentrated solutions obtained by dissolving chlorine in water at elevated pressure are used. Calculate solubility of chlorine (in $\mathrm{g/dm^3}$) at $10.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a partial pressure in the gaseous phase equal to 1.50 atm.

5. How will the solubility of chlorine change qualitatively in comparison with the solubility calculated in question 4, if it is used water with temperature $5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Briefly explain your answer.

6. Experimental solubility of chlorine in water is higher on about 0.6% compared with the value calculated in question 4. Briefly explain the cause of this phenomenon and write the corresponding reaction equation.

7. Since 1999 it is known the disinfection water technology using a binary gas $\mathbf{X}$, with a density at STP more than $3\,\mathrm{g/dm^3}$. One of methods of producing a gas $\mathbf{X}$ in an industrial scale is the action of chlorine gas on solid substance containing chlorine. Write the reaction equation for obtaining $\mathbf{X}$ by this method in industrial scale and write the reaction equation of obtaining of gaseous $\mathbf{X}$ in the laboratory. Draw the structural formula and specify the spatial structure of the molecule $\mathbf{X}$.

8. Gas $\mathbf{X}$ is a reactive compound. Which products are formed by reacting $\mathbf{X}$ with an aqueous solution of NaOH? Write the equation of the corresponding reaction.

9. As a result of the impact of ozone on $\mathbf{X}$ substance $\mathbf{Y}$ is obtained. Write the equation of the corresponding reaction. Draw the structural formulae of particles present in liquid $\mathbf{Y}$.

problems.title: [Kinetic isotope effects and heavy water]
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Kinetic isotope effects and heavy water]

Substitution of an element in the molecule by another isotope changes the reaction rate, if the atom is involved in breaking or forming of chemical bonds at the rate-limiting stage of the reaction. This phenomenon is called kinetic isotope effect (KIE) and numerically it is characterized by the rate constants ratio $k_\mathrm{H} / k_\mathrm{D}$ of the reaction involving hydrogen and deuterium substituted reagents. With the help of KIE the mechanisms of a large number of reactions were investigated.

1. Calculate the KIE for the reaction of bromination of acetone in acidic medium at 298 K. Assume that KIE is caused only by the difference in the activation energies of the reactions.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Reaction} & \ce{CH3COCH3 + Br2} & \ce{CD3COCD3 + Br2} \\ \hline E_\mathrm{A},\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} & 31.0 & 35.8 \end{array}$$

The rate of this reaction is described by the kinetic equation:

$$v = \frac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{CD3OCD3}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k[\ce{CD3OCD3}]^n[\ce{Br2}]^m[\ce{H+}]^l,$$

where $n$, $m$, $l$ – reaction orders for acetone, bromine and $\ce{H+}$, respectively.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} & [\ce{CD3COCD3}],\ \mathrm{M} & [\ce{Br2}],\ \mathrm{M} & [\ce{H+}],\ \mathrm{M} & v,\ \mathrm{M{\cdot}s^{-1}} \\ \hline 1 & 0.3 & 0.05 & 0.05 & 5.7\cdot10^{-5} \\ \hline 2 & 0.3 & 0.1 & 0.05 & 5.7\cdot10^{-5} \\ \hline 3 & 0.3 & 0.05 & 0.1 & 1.2\cdot10^{-4} \\ \hline 4 & 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.2 & 3.1\cdot10^{-4} \end{array}$$

2. a) Determine the $n$, $m$, и $l$ from the given above experimental data.

b) What is the overall reaction order?

The mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution has the form:

$$\ce{C6L6 + E^{\oplus} <=>[$k_1$][$k_2$] C6L6E^{\oplus} ->[$k_3$] C6L5E + L^{\oplus}} \qquad (\mathrm{L} = \mathrm{H\ or\ D})$$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Electrophile} & \ce{NO2+} & \ce{CH3COCl/SbCl5} \\ \hline \text{KIE} & 1 & 2.22 \end{array}$$

3. Based on the above data, indicate the limiting stage for both reactions.

Solution of $\ce{CuSO4}$ in normal water has blue color. The split energy ($\Delta_\mathrm{o}$) of $d$-level of $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ions in the octahedral ligand field for the complex $\ce{[Cu(D2O)6]^{2+}}$ is equal to $14403\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. The Jahn – Teller effect is ignored. $1\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}} = 1.986\cdot10^{-22}\,\mathrm{J}$.

$$\begin{array}{ll|c} \text{Absorption region} & \lambda,\ \mathrm{nm} & \text{Substance color} \\ \hline \text{Violet} & 400 - 424 & \text{Yellow} \\ \text{Green} & 490 - 575 & \text{Purple} \\ \text{Yellow} & 575 - 585 & \text{Blue} \\ \text{Red} & 647 - 710 & \text{Green} \end{array}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2015-2-7-fig1.png

4. a) Write down the configuration of $d$-electrons of $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ion. b) Write down the configuration (in terms of t and e) of $d$-electrons $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ion in $\ce{[Cu(D2O)6]^{2+}}$. c) Calculate the ligand field stabilization energy in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. d) Calculate the wavelength absorbed by the complex and specify the color of copper sulfate in heavy water $\ce{D2O}$. e) Is this complex paramagnetic or diamagnetic?

If the presence of oxygen isotopes is ignored, there are three isotopic species of water: $\ce{H2O}$, HDO and $\ce{D2O}$. In the mixture, the high rate isotope exchange takes place according to the reaction $\ce{H2O + D2O = 2HDO}$ with the equilibrium constant $K_x = 4$.

5. Calculate the molar fraction of each species in natural water. Natural abundance (mol %) of isotopes H and D is equal to 99.985 and 0.015, respectively.

Many believe that prolonged boiling of drinking water is dangerous to health since the concentrations of heavy forms (HDO, $\ce{D2O}$) significantly increase due to higher volatility of ordinary water ($\ce{H2O}$).

6. Verify the validity of this statement by calculating for how many times the initial volume of water $V_i$ exceeds the final volume $V_f$, remaining after evaporation, so that the concentration of HDO would increase by 15%. The liquid – vapor partition coefficient $\alpha$ at given temperature does not depend on the isotopic ratio D : H, and at the boiling point $\alpha = 1.013$. At the beginning of evaporation the mole fraction HDO was $3\cdot10^{-4}$.

Notes: 1) Coefficient $\alpha$ shows, for how many times the evaporation rate of pure ordinary water $\ce{H2O}$ exceeds the rate for pure water HDO. 2) Neglect the presence $\ce{D2O}$ in water. 3) Assume that $\ce{H2O}$ – HDO solution is perfect and that the molar volumes of these substances are equal. Physical constants: gas constant $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J/mol{\cdot}K}$, Plank constant $h = 6.63\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J{\cdot}s}$, Avogadro's number $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.02\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, speed of light in vacuum $c = 3\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Problem 8 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 2). [Hydrolysis kinetics of bis(ethylenediamine)cobalt(III) complexes]

The rate of acidic hydrolysis $\ce{Co(en)2Cl2+ + H2O -> Co(en)2(H2O)Cl^{2+} + Cl-}$ is not depend on $[\ce{H+}]$, is described by the kinetic equation $w = kC_{\ce{Co(en)2Cl2+}}$ and has rate constants $k = 2.4\cdot10^{-4}$ ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and $k = 8.1\cdot10^{-4}$ ($35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) for $cis$-complex, $k = 3.5\cdot10^{-5}$ ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and $k = 1.5\cdot10^{-4}$ ($35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) for $trans$-complex. However, in the case of complexes with ligands, which are hard bases capable to form hydrogen bonds, the rate of hydrolysis depends on pH. Kinetic characteristics of the acid-basic hydrolysis $\ce{Co(en)2F2+}$ (table) were described by the mechanism:

$$\begin{array}{rl} \ce{Co(en)2F2+ + H2O -> Co(en)2(H2O)F^{2+} + F-} & (k_3) \\ \ce{Co(en)2F2+ + H+ <=> Co(en)2F2H^{2+}} & (K = 10.20) \\ \ce{Co(en)2F2H^{2+} + H2O -> Co(en)2(H2O)F^{2+} + HF} & (k_4) \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} [\ce{H+}],\ \mathrm{mol/L} & 10^{-4} & 10^{-3} & 10^{-2} & 5\cdot10^{-2} & 10^{-1} \\ \hline k_\mathrm{H}\cdot10^{3},\ \mathrm{min^{-1}} & 6.173 & 7.716 & 21.74 & 63.42 & 91.84 \end{array}$$

1. Describe the hydrolysis of $\ce{Co(en)2Cl2+}$ by the two-stage mechanism ($k_1$; $k_{-1}$; $k_2$).

2. Using the method of stationary concentrations derivate the kinetic equation and indicate the condition of its agreement with the experimental one ($w = kC_{\ce{Co(en)2Cl2+}}$).

3. Derivate the expressions for $\alpha$, calculate the mole fractions of $\ce{Co(en)2F2+}$ and $\ce{Co(en)2F2H^{2+}}$ at pH = 2.

4. Display graphically the dependence $k_\mathrm{H} = f(\mathrm{pH})$ and derivate the equation for $k_\mathrm{H}$, which describe the dependence $k_\mathrm{H} = f([\ce{H+}])$, using the expression for $\alpha$.

5. Calculate the rate constants $k_3$ and $k_4$.

6. Indicate the process, which explain the sharp rise of $k_\mathrm{H}$ at pH < 2.

7. Write down the structural formula of the possible intermediates in the two-stage mechanism in the case of $trans$-$\ce{Co(en)2Cl2+}$.

8. Calculate activation energy ($E_\mathrm{A}$) for $cis$- and $trans$-$\ce{Co(en)2Cl2+}$ and enthalpy ($\Delta H^\#$) and entropy ($\Delta S^\#$) of formation of activated complex only for $cis$-complex ($k = Ae^{-E_\mathrm{A}/RT} = 2.08\cdot10^{10}\,T\,e^{-\Delta G^\#/RT}$, $\Delta H^\# = E_\mathrm{A} - RT$, $T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$).

problems.problem:
Problem 9 (Physical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Phase equilibria: ideal solutions, a eutectic and the triple point of gallium]

A liquid mixture of substances 1 and 2 forms an ideal solution, so the Raul’s law is valid $P_i = x_iP_i^0$, where $P_i^0$ – vapor pressure of pure component at a certain temperature. Let $P_1^0 / P_2^0 = r$, $x$ and $y$ – the molar fraction of the substance 2 in the liquid solution and its vapor, respectively, $P$ – the total vapor pressure above the solution.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2015-2-9-fig1.png

1. Based on the Raul’s and Dalton's ($P_i = y_iP$), laws obtain the dependencies: a) $P$ from $x$, b) $y$ from $x$, c) $P$ from $y$.

2. Using the lever rule, according to the diagram (see left figure) determine the composition (mol %) of both phases at the point A and the relative composition of phases of 1 mol of toluene – cyclohexane mixture at this point.

The Gibbs phase rule determines the number of thermodynamic degrees of freedom ($f$), i.e. the number of variables (pressure, temperature, concentration), which can be changed without changing the number of phases ($F$) in the system: $f = 2 + K - F$, where $K$ – the number of components. The right figure shows a phase diagram $T - x$ ($P$ = const) of Ag – Pb with eutectic point.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2015-2-9-fig2.png

3. Determine the nature of the phases and the number of degrees of freedom at points A – D (see the table in the answer sheet).

If in the binary system A – B the liquid phase can be considered as ideal solution, for the construction of the liquidus line (line E – C – F) you can use the Schroeder equation:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln x_\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{\Delta H_\mathrm{A}}{RT^2}, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}\ln x_\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{\Delta H_\mathrm{B}}{RT^2},$$

where $T_\mathrm{A}$, $T_\mathrm{B}$; $\Delta H_\mathrm{A}$, $\Delta H_\mathrm{B}$ – temperature and melting enthalpy of the pure components.

4. Considering the melt (Ag – Pb) as ideal solution, determine the coordinates of the eutectic point (mole fraction of Pb and eutectic temperature $T_\mathrm{E}$). The mole fraction of the silver is equal to 0.264, the melting point of silver $T_\mathrm{m} = 1235\,\mathrm{K}$, enthalpy of fusion of silver $\Delta H_\text{пл} = 11.95\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

In the single-component system dependence of vapor pressure on temperature is determined by the Clausius – Clapeyron equation

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln P}{\mathrm{d}T} = \frac{\Delta H_\mathrm{vap}}{RT^2},$$

where $\Delta H_\mathrm{vap}$ – heat of vaporization, which is assumed to be constant.

5. a) Find the temperature of the triple point $T_\mathrm{tr}$ of gallium from temperature dependence of the saturated vapor pressure of solid and liquid substances (atm):

$$\ln P_\mathrm{s} = -32254 / T + 14.97, \quad \ln P_\mathrm{liq} = -31582 / T + 12.75.$$

b) Calculate the enthalpy of sublimation $\Delta H_\mathrm{sub}$, evaporation $\Delta H_\mathrm{vap}$ and melting $\Delta H_\mathrm{m}$ of the gallium (kJ/mol).

c) Calculate the standard entropy of vaporization $\Delta S^0_\mathrm{vap}$ and entropy of melting $\Delta S_\mathrm{m}$ (J/mol·K), $T_\mathrm{m} = 303\,\mathrm{K}$, $T_\mathrm{boil} = 2477\,\mathrm{K}$.

problems.problem:
Problem 10 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem 1). [Chemistry behind amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)]

In 2014 the World was conquered by an “epidemics” of ice-cold water dousing. This philanthropic effort known as ALS Ice Bucket Challenge was aimed at fund raising to investigate the reasons behind amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a serious neurodegenerative decease with yet unrevealed mechanisms of progress. In this task we will analyze the information about ALS known up-to-date.

A genetic defect of enzyme $\mathbf{E}$ is sometimes behind ancestral ALS cases. $\mathbf{E}$ catalyzes the reaction with the total equation:

$$2\mathbf{A1} + 2\mathbf{A2} \rightarrow \ce{H2O2 + O2}$$

Particle $\mathbf{A1}$ non-enzymatically reacts with molecule $\mathbf{A3}$ containing the same number of atoms as $\mathbf{A1}$. As a result, $\mathbf{A4}$ (77.41% O by mass) is formed according to the following reaction equation:

$$\mathbf{A1} + \mathbf{A3} \rightarrow \mathbf{A4}$$

1. Determine molecular formulae of $\mathbf{A1}$ – $\mathbf{A4}$.

Particle $\mathbf{A5}$ found in nature is isomeric $\mathbf{A4}$.

2. Draw structural formulae of $\mathbf{A4}$ and $\mathbf{A5}$, and compare their toxicity to man.

$\mathbf{E}$ is encoded by the gene SOD1. ALS was found to be a result of single point mutations of SOD1, which appear as a change of the second nucleotide in the corresponding codons. As a result, an “improper” amino acid is incorporated into polypeptide chain (initial amino acid → mutant amino acid). Two major SOD1 mutations can be written as Mut1 ($\mathbf{B1} \rightarrow \mathbf{B2}$) and Mut2 ($\mathbf{B3} \rightarrow \mathbf{B1}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2015-2-10-fig1.png

3. Using the table of genetic code determine the amino acids $\mathbf{B1}$ – $\mathbf{B3}$ if it is known that these amino acids are encoded by the same number of codons, whereas the total number of purine bases in this codons exceeds that of pyrimidine ones.

4. Indicate in the Answer Sheet whether the mutations Mut1 and Mut2 can be due to single-step chemical modifications of nitrogen bases in human DNA?

In March 2014 Nature published an article which reported that four-strain DNA fragments in non-coding region of gen C9orf72 are responsible for sporadic cases of ALS (like that observed in the case of a well-known theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking). DNA quadruplexes are known to form in gene fragments containing repeated hexanucleotide sequences involving only two major (one purine and one pyrimidine) nitrogen bases. The molecular mass of the hexanuclotide with totally protonated phosphate groups is of 1913 Da.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2015-2-10-fig2.png

5. Draw the pair of major nitrogen bases linked by three hydrogen bonds (use dashed lines to show the hydrogen bonding).

6. Determine the nitrogen bases present in the hexanucleotide. Determine the number of each of these bases in the hexanucleotide.

7. Draw the cross section of the DNA quadruplex (see the above figure) with 8 hydrogen bonds (use dashed lines to show these bonds). Note that in this case the hydrogen bonds formation involve also atoms which do not participate in hydrogen bonding in conventional DNA duplexes.

Problem 3. [Metal A from polymetallic sulfide ores and its oxidants]

The metal $\mathbf{A}$ obtained by coal reducing of its oxide $\mathbf{B}$ after sulfide burning. This sulfide is produced by processing polymetal (CuS, PbS) sulfide ores. Metal $\mathbf{A}$ is known as one of the major components of Wood's metal.

$\mathbf{A}$ is dissolved only in oxidizing acids. For example, reaction with 30% $\ce{HNO3}$ leads to nitrate $\mathbf{C}$, which is easily hydrolysed in water forming the basic salts, one of which composition can be written as $[\mathrm{A}_6\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{OH})_4](\mathrm{NO}_3)_6\cdot4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$. Therefore, metal salts of $\mathbf{A}$ are dissolved in solution of the corresponding acids.

Addition of alkali to $\mathbf{C}$ leads to the precipitation of hydroxide $\mathbf{D}$. The compound $\mathbf{E}$ is produced by oxidation of $\mathbf{D}$ by potassium persulfate in alkaline medium. $\mathbf{E}$ is used in the practice of inorganic synthesis as a strong oxidant. Thus, the reaction of $\mathbf{E}$ with a transition metal sulfate affords another colored oxidant $\mathbf{F}$, which solution has an intense broad absorption band in the green region (550 nm).

$\mathbf{B}$ is formed when $\mathbf{D}$ is heated to $150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, (the weight loss in this process is 10.4%). Compound $\mathbf{B}$ is a yellow crystals, it is usually prepared by thermolysis of various metal organic compounds of $\mathbf{A}$: acetates, β-diketonates and other MOCs. Sodium analogue of $\mathbf{E}$ is synthesized by fusion of $\mathbf{B}$ with sodium peroxide in an oxygen atmosphere.

The solution is left to crystallize in a mixture of ice and salt for 2 hours. The crystalline precipitate (potassium mass fraction is 23.92%) is separated on a sintered glass filter and dried at the room temperature in the air.

problems.title: [Hydrogen atom: from the Rydberg formula to the Bohr model]
problems.problem:
Problem 6. [Hydrogen atom: from the Rydberg formula to the Bohr model]

In 1888 Rydberg and Ritz discovered an empirical formula which determines the positions of spectral lines of hydrogen atoms by light absorption:

$$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right),$$

where $\lambda$ – wavelength, $R$ – Rydberg constant, $n_1$ and $n_2$ – natural numbers. A given spectral series corresponds to transfer (jump) of electron from different states $n_2$ to a given state $n_1$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Spectral series} & n_1 & n_2 & \lambda,\ \mathrm{nm} \\ \hline \text{Layman} & 1 & 3 & \sim100 \\ \text{Layman} & 1 & & 121 \\ \hline \text{Brackket} & 4 & & 1456 \\ \hline \text{Ballmer} & & 3 & \end{array}$$

1. Using the data from the table, calculate the Rydberg constant $R$ and complete this table with the absent data.

In 1913 Bohr developed his model of Hydrogen atom. This model is based on the supposition that the atom has stationary circular orbits where electron is located without emission of energy. Electron transfer from orbit $n_1$ to $n_2$ is accompanied by absorption or emission of light (photon) with specific wavelength.

The potential energy of electron in the electrostatic field of the nuclei is

$$E_\mathrm{p} = -\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n},$$

where $e = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$ – elementary charge, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$ – electric constant, $r_n$ – radius of $n^\text{th}$ orbit. And $r_n = a_0 n^2$, $a_0$ – radius of $1^\text{st}$ Bohr orbit (Bohr's radius).

It is known that the value of kinetic energy of electron in Hydrogen atom is twice smaller than those of potential energy and it is opposite in sign.

2. Which series does correspond to transfer of electron to the ground state?

3. Knowing constant $R$, calculate the energy of 1 mole of hydrogen atoms in the ground state.

4. Calculate the Bohr's radius $a_0$ and minimal distance between $3^\text{rd}$ and $2^\text{nd}$ orbits.

5. Find the ionization energy of hydrogen atom.

6. Taking into account that the total energy of $\ce{H2}$ molecule is $-3070\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ (energy is measured from the energy of nuclei and electrons at rest, situated at infinite distance from each other), calculate the bond energy between H atoms in this molecule.

Additional data: $h = 6.627\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}$, $c = 3\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$.

2. Write down the resultant thermochemical equation of the reaction between $\mathbf{B}\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\ce{H2O2}$.

problems.title: [Conductometric titrations]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 1). [Conductometric titrations]

Conductometry is the one of the oldest electrochemical methods of analysis. It is based on the measurement of conductivity $\sigma$ [S/m]. Conductivity is related to the existence of ions in solution. Each ion is characterized by the molar conductivity $\lambda$ [$\mathrm{S\cdot m^2/mol}$], which depends on its charge $z$ and mobility $\mu$ [$\mathrm{S\cdot m^2/C}$]: $\lambda = |z|\cdot\mu\cdot F$, where $F$ is Faraday constant. The total conductivity is the sum of the conductivities of each ion: $\sigma = \sum\sigma_\mathrm{i} = \sum\lambda_\mathrm{i}\cdot c_\mathrm{i}$ where $c_i$ is the concentration of the ion [$\mathrm{mol/m^3}$].

1. The mobilities of $\ce{OH-}$ and $\ce{H+}$ are $2.07\cdot10^{-7}$ and $3.63\cdot10^{-7}\,\mathrm{S\cdot m^2/C}$, respectively. Calculate the molar conductivities $\lambda(\ce{OH-})$, $\lambda(\ce{H+})$ and the conductivity ($\sigma$) of pure water.

In the first experiment, 50.0 mL of strong acid $\mathbf{HA}$ was titrated by a 0.500M solution of alkali. The graph represents the conductivity as function of the volume of the alkali solution (see Figure).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2016-2-1-fig1.png

2. Which ions contribute to the conductivity before equivalence point, in the equivalence point and after the equivalence point? Consider the water dissociation as negligible.

3. Determine the acid $\mathbf{HA}$ (HCl, $\ce{HClO4}$ or HBr) and alkali (LiOH, KOH or NaOH), taking into account that the molar conductivities of ions [$\mathrm{mS\cdot m^2/mol}$] are as follows:

$$\lambda(\ce{K+}) = 7.35,\ \lambda(\ce{Na+}) = 5.01,\ \lambda(\ce{Li+}) = 3.86,\ \lambda(\ce{Cl-}) = 7.63,\ \lambda(\ce{Br-}) = 7.80.\ \lambda(\ce{ClO4-}) = 6.52.$$

4. Calculate the solution conductivity after addition of 6.0 mL of the alkali solution.

In the second experiment, 20 mL of a mixture of HCl with a weak organic acid $\mathbf{H_nB}$ ($K_\mathrm{a}\sim10^{-5}$) was diluted to 100 mL and titrated by a 0.600M KOH solution. The results of titration are given in the table:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} V,\ \mathrm{mL} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 & \mathbf{10} & \mathbf{12} \\ \hline \sigma,\ \mathrm{S/m} & 0.600 & 0.489 & 0.377 & 0.267 & 0.233 & 0.278 & 0.324 & 0.489 & 0.655 & 0.985 & 1.312 \end{array}$$

5. How many protons of the weak acid $\mathbf{H_nB}$ have been titrated?

Problem 3 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Polarography]

Polarography is a technique applied for the determination of metal ions. The potential between a dropping mercury cathode and a mercury pool anode is varied (for example, from 0.0 to –1.5 V), and the corresponding changes in current $I$ are measured. When reducible substances are present in the solution, a sharp rise in current occurs at the certain potential. The recorded plot of current against applied voltage $I = f(E)$ (polarogram) is characterized by wave height $h$ (cm), or diffusion current $I_\mathrm{max}$ (A), that are proportional to the concentration of the unknown ion, and by the potential at the midpoint of the wave $E_{1/2}$ (half-wave potential) depending on the nature of the analyte.

problems.title: [Classical and nonclassical tautomers of Luo and Crabtree]
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 1). [Classical and nonclassical tautomers of Luo and Crabtree]

For the investigation of equilibrium between classical ($\mathbf{J}$) and nonclassical ($\mathbf{G}$) tautomers Luo and Crabtree in 1990 synthesized a set of mononuclear complexes ($\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{J}$) of d-metal ($\mathbf{Me}$). $\mathbf{B}$ was used as an initial compound, 4.098 g of which can be obtained by the addition reaction from 3.273 g $\mathbf{Me}\mathrm{O_n}$ and the equimolar mass of $\mathrm{NaO}_n$ at $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The synthesis of complexes was as follows: $\mathbf{B}$ was dissolved in alcohol, then 6.210 g of $\ce{(CH3)2C6H5P}$ ($\ce{Me2PhP}$) were added, and after addition of concentrated HCl the reaction mixture was boiled during 18 hours with reflux condenser and the orange $\mathbf{C}$ was formed (m g, yield 80%). CO was bubbled at boiling through the alcohol solution of $\mathbf{C}$ until 4.408 g of yellow $\mathbf{D}$ was formed (50% yield). To the etheric solution of $\mathbf{D}$ $\ce{LiAlH4}$ was added and boiled with reflux condenser during 40 hours till yellow $\mathbf{E}$ ($w_\mathrm{Me} = 29.50$; $w_\mathrm{P} = 14.73$; $w_\mathrm{O} = 2.53\%$) was formed, which contained ligand $\mathbf{L}$, but no $\ce{Cl-}$. $\mathbf{E}$ was dissolved in $\ce{CH2Cl2}$, then it was protonated using $\ce{HBF4}$ at 208 K and a daffodil solution of equilibrium mixture of $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ was obtained, which has conductivity close to $\ce{LiAlH4}$. The complexes $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{G}$ have c.n. = 7, and in $\mathbf{J}$ c.n. = 8. For $\mathbf{G} \rightleftarrows \mathbf{J}$ Luo and Crabtree obtained $\Delta H^0 = -4.6\,\mathrm{kJ/mole}$, $\Delta S^0 = -10\,\mathrm{J/mol\cdot K}$.

1. Determine $\mathbf{Me}$ and define the formula of $\mathbf{B}$.

2. Determine the formulae of nonelectrolytes $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$, if they are complexes $\mathbf{Me}$(3+), and calculate m.

3. Determine $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{J}$, if the IR-spectrum of $\mathbf{J}$ contains $1832\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ band, and $\mathbf{G}$ – two bands 1838 and $2692\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ (the IR-spectra of $\mathrm{K}\mathbf{MeL}_4$ contain band $1828\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and $\mathbf{L}_2$ – $4159\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$).

4. Write the reaction equations of complex formation.

5. Calculate $\Delta G^0$ and the composition of the equilibrium mixture $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ in mol.% at 208 K, considering that $\Delta H^0$ and $\Delta S^0$ do not depend on temperature.

6. Propose the structure of intermediate fragment at the transition of $\mathbf{G}$ to $\mathbf{J}$, if the bond distances: L–L in $\mathbf{G}$ – 0.084; in $\mathbf{J}$ – 0.160; in the intermediate 0.138 nm.

7. Draw MO diagram for $\mathbf{L}_2$ and the overlapping of orbitales in $\mathbf{G}$ in bond formation of $\mathbf{Me}$ with ligands containing $\mathbf{L}$.

Problem 5 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem 2). [A family of halogen compounds]

Learning without reflection is a waste, Reflection without learning is dangerous — Confucius (551 – 479 BC)

The halogens atoms have a large gamma of possible oxidation numbers which leads to a great diversity of compounds and interesting structures. However, it is important to remember that some halogens compounds could be very toxic and explosive and it is very important to pay attention working and exploring the halogen compounds.

Compounds $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}_{1,2}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ have the same qualitative composition. The oxidation number of central atom is growing in the row $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Z}$. The compound $\mathbf{B}$, which was obtained by fluorination of the binary compound $\mathbf{A}$ ($\omega_\mathrm{F}$ = 34.86%), could produce compounds $\mathbf{Y}_1$ ($\omega_\mathrm{F}$ = 52.53%) or $\mathbf{Y}_2$ by partial hydrolysis. Pure compound $\mathbf{Y}_2$ could be obtained by three methods: a) by the reaction of compound $\mathbf{A}$ with the brownish- yellow gas $\mathbf{C}$, b) by the fluorination of yellow-orange gas $\mathbf{D}$ or c) by the hydrofluorination of dark red liquid $\mathbf{E}$. Binary compounds $\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{E}$ have the same qualitative composition. One of the elements of compounds $\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{E}$ is the same that the central atom of $\mathbf{X}$-$\mathbf{Z}$ molecules. The oxidation number of this element is growing in a row $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$; moreover the oxidation number of this element is the same in $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ compounds. The synthesis of $\mathbf{C}$ from simple compound $\mathbf{F}$ and mercury (II) oxide is one of the few methods to obtain compound $\mathbf{C}$ in a pure state.

The compound $\mathbf{Y}_2$ was oxidized by strong oxidizing agent as $\ce{PtF6}$ to obtain equimolar quantity of salts $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$. During the action of nitryl fluoride on $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ it was obtained respectively $\mathbf{Y}_2$ and new product $\mathbf{Z}$.
