problems.problem:
Problem 12 (Organic Chemistry section, problem 3). [gem-Dimethylcycloalkanes and the synthesis of hirsutene]

In synthesis of a number of natural polycyclic compounds used in perfumery, medicine, in prediction of oil reserves, an important role belongs to medium-sized cycles containing heme-dimethyl fragment. Synthesis of heme-dimethylcyclopentane $\mathbf{I}$ is presented in the scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-12-fig1.png

1. What is the structures of compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, if $\mathbf{A}$ has the simplest formula $\mathrm{C}_x\mathrm{H}_{x+y}\mathrm{O}_y$, $w(\mathrm{H}) = 6.85\%$, $\mathbf{A}$ is titrated with two equivalents of alkali; $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are monocycles; $\mathbf{D}$ is a spirocycle, its $^1$H NMR spectrum has three signals of the same intensity.

Heme dimethylcycloalkenes are used for cascade polycyclization. The synthesis of 3,3-dimethylcyclopentene ($\mathbf{II}$) was carried out in several stages:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-12-fig2.png

2. What is the structures of compounds $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{J}$, $\mathbf{K}$, if $\mathbf{G}$ is a homologue of $\mathbf{A}$, $^1$H NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{G}$ has three singlets (3 : 2 : 1); $\mathbf{J}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ are cyclic structures.

3. Select a reaction condition $\mathbf{E}$ + 2$\mathbf{F}$: a) t; b) [the reagent drawn below]; c) $\mathrm{LiN}(i\text{-Pr})_2$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-12-fig3.png

Synthesis of the natural hirsutene polycycle ($\mathbf{X}$), including tandem cyclization, was carried out starting from heme-dimethylcyclopentene $\mathbf{II}$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-12-fig4.png

4. What is the structures of compounds $\mathbf{L}$, $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{HM}$, $\mathbf{N}$, $\mathbf{O}$, $\mathbf{HO}$, $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{S}$, if the stages $\mathbf{L}\rightarrow\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{N}\rightarrow\mathbf{O}$ pass with the extension of the cycle through the formation of unstable zwitterions $\mathbf{L'}$ and $\mathbf{N'}$; there is a band ~ $1750\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in the IR spectra of $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{N}$, $\mathbf{O}$, $\mathbf{S}$.

5. Propose the structure of intermediate $\mathbf{L'}$ obtained as a product of the nucleophilic addition of $\ce{CH2N2}$ to $\mathbf{L}$.

6. Determine the reagents from which ketenes were obtained for the reactions: $\mathbf{II}\rightarrow\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{IV}\rightarrow\mathbf{N}$: 1) $\ce{CH3CHClCOCl}$; 2) $\ce{Cl3CCOCl}$; 3) Zn/Cu; 4) $\ce{(C2H5)3N}$.

7. Specify the configuration of atoms a, b, c, d in hirsutene $\mathbf{X}$.

problems.title: [A complex chromium(III) salt P]
problems.problem:
Problem 13 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 1). [A complex chromium(III) salt P]

The anion of a complex salt $\mathbf{P}$, containing trivalent chromium, is used to detect and identify certain amines and drugs based on them. A number of experiments was carried out to confirm the composition of the salt. Nitrogen in salt $\mathbf{P}$ was determined by two methods.

Method 1. A weighed amount of salt $\mathbf{P}$ (0.10 g) was placed in a round bottom flask, 40 mL of 5% NaOH added, and the flask was stoppered with a gas outlet tube leading to a receiver containing 50 mL of 2% boric acid. The mixture was distilled for 10 min and the receiver contents was titrated with hydrochloric acid solution using bromocresol green as indicator (pH of the color transition is 3.8–5.4); 14.13 mL of 0.0600 M HCl solution was used for that titration.

Method 2. The ability of ammonium cations to form hexamethylene tetramine with formaldehyde with the release of acid was used. An excess of formaldehyde was added to a weighed amount of salt $\mathbf{P}$ (0.10 g) and the solution was titrated, during which 5.65 mL of 0.0500 M alkali solution was spent.

1. Write down the equation of reaction occurring when ammonia is absorbed by the solution of boric acid (reaction 1) and the reaction of titration of the receiver contents with hydrochloric acid (reaction 2).

2. Write down the ionic form of reaction occurring upon addition of formaldehyde to a solution of salt $\mathbf{P}$ (reaction 3).

3. Calculate the amount of nitrogen in the original salt, determined by methods 1 and 2. What kind of particles contain nitrogen determined by these methods?

4. What is the pH value of the solution (pH < 7, pH > 7, pH = 7) in the equivalence point of titration by method 2? Is it possible to apply the indicator used in method 1 for visual end point indication?

A weighed amount of salt $\mathbf{P}$ (0.10 g) was transferred into a conical flask, 10 mL of 0.1 M NaOH solution was added and the solution was heated. On boiling, the complex was destroyed with the release of a gas with a strong odor and formation of a green precipitate. The suspension was cooled and 10 mL of 2 M nitric acid added along with a few drops of a $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ solution as indicator. A bright red solution was formed, which was then titrated by Volhard technique with a solution of silver salt until the color turned from red to pale gray-green; 22.6 mL of 0.0500 M $\ce{AgNO3}$ solution was used for that titration.

5. What ion was determined by Volhard titration?

6. Based on the above data, calculate the amount of this ion in salt $\mathbf{P}$.

To determine the mass loss during heating, a portion of salt $\mathbf{P}$ (1.000 g) was kept for three hours at $105\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The losses amounted to 5.085% by weight.

7. Calculate the amount of the component that evaporates while heating salt $\mathbf{P}$.

8. Based on the data obtained, derive the formula for salt $\mathbf{P}$, if its molecular weight does not exceed 600 g/mol.

9. Propose the reaction equation of the salt $\mathbf{P}$ decomposition by alkali with a release of gas and precipitate formation (reaction 4).

For the synthesis of salt $\mathbf{P}$, ammonium thiocyanate is fused under constant stirring and a mixture of ammonium dichromate and thiocyanate is added. After a while, a violent reaction 5 begins, accompanied by the release of ammonia. The reaction mixture is cooled, the product is triturated and treated with cold water. The undissolved precipitate is separated from the mother liquor under vacuum and introduced into water heated to $70\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The solution is filtered and placed overnight in a refrigerator, where crystals of salt $\mathbf{P}$ are precipitated from it.

10. Propose the reaction equation of salt $\mathbf{P}$ synthesis in the melt in molecular form (reaction 5b). Consider that the main products of thiocyanate oxidation are sulfate and cyanate ions. To simplify the arrangement of the coefficients, write down the reaction in the melt in ionic form (reaction 5a) with the reduction of dichromate to $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ ion.

problems.title: [pKa of ferulic acid by HPLC]
problems.problem:
Problem 14 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 2). [pKa of ferulic acid by HPLC]

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is a powerful technique for separation, quantitative and qualitative analysis of complex mixtures of compounds. By means of this tool some other analytical tasks can be solved, for example, it can be used to determine the dissociation constants of acids in aqueous–organic solvent systems. In this problem you are offered to estimate the $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ value of ferulic acid (trans-4-hydroxy-3-methoxycinnamic acid, HA) in the mixture of 30% $\ce{CH3CN}$ – 70% formate buffer ($\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{a},\,\ce{HCOOH}} = 3.75$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2019-2-14-fig1.png

1. Draw the structural formula of ferulic acid and encircle the functional group which is ionizable in formate buffer solutions.

The method is based on the dependence of retention factor $k$, which is calculated using retention times of the retained ($t_\mathrm{r}$) and unretained ($t_\mathrm{m}$) components, on the pH ($\mathrm{pH} = -\lg a_{\mathrm{H^+}}$). The retention factor $k$ for a weak acid is, in its turn, connected with mole fractions of protonated ($\chi_{HA}$) and deprotonated ($\chi_{A^-}$) forms and corresponding retention factors ($k_{HA}$ and $k_{A^-}$):

$$k = \frac{t_\mathrm{r}-t_\mathrm{m}}{t_\mathrm{m}} = \chi_{HA}k_{HA} + \chi_{A^-}k_{A^-}.$$

For diluted aqueous solutions the impact of ionic strength and activity coefficients are usually not considered, but for the investigated buffer–acetonitrile system it can be significant. Therefore, the expression for acid dissociation constant should be written as:

$$K_\mathrm{a} = \frac{a_{\mathrm{H^+}}a_{A^-}}{a_{HA}} = \frac{a_{\mathrm{H^+}}\gamma_{A^-}[A^-]}{[HA]}.$$

2. Get the expression for the dependence of retention factor $k$ from $K_\mathrm{a}$ and $a_{\mathrm{H^+}}$.

The activity coefficient $\gamma_{A^-}$ can be estimated from the Debye–Hückel equation and the expression for ionic strength of a solution $I$, which takes into account the impact of all ions $X_\mathrm{i}$ presented in the solution and their charge $z_\mathrm{i}$: $-\lg\gamma = \frac{A\sqrt{I}}{1+a_0B\sqrt{I}}$, $I = 0.5\sum z_\mathrm{i}^2[X_\mathrm{i}]$.

For the investigated mixture of solvents: $A = 0.6476\,\mathrm{M^{-1/2}}$, $a_0B = 1.5918\,\mathrm{M^{-1/2}}$.

In the performed chromatographic experiment three buffer–acetonitrile systems with pH values 3.15, 3.93 and 4.35 were used. The total concentration of HCOONa and HCOOH in these solutions was 0.010 M.

3. Fill in the following table, which describes the composition of analyzed solutions:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{№} & \text{pH} & c_\mathrm{HCOONa},\ \mathrm{M} & c_\mathrm{HCOOH},\ \mathrm{M} & I,\ \mathrm{M} & \gamma_{A^-} \\ \hline \mathbf{1} & 3.15 & & & & \\ \hline \mathbf{2} & 3.93 & & & & \\ \hline \mathbf{3} & 4.35 & & & & \end{array}$$

The retention time of unretained component $t_\mathrm{m}$ (0.01% solution of KBr) was 100.0 s, while the retention times of ferulic acid were 233.3, 229.7 and 223.3 s for solutions 1, 2 and 3, respectively.

4. Calculate the retention factors $k$ for three investigated solutions.

5. Using the expression obtained in question 2, determine the $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of ferulic acid and the retention factors for its protonated and deprotonated forms $k_{HA}$ and $k_{A^-}$. If you did not get the answer on questions 3 and 4, use the following values for $\gamma_{A^-}$: 0.90, 0.85, 0.80 and $k$: 1.482, 1.350, 1.151 for solutions 1, 2 and 3, respectively.

6. What will be the value for $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of ferulic acid in aqueous solution in comparison with buffer–acetonitrile system (higher, lower or the same)?

problems.title: [Wine diamonds: potassium hydrotartrate]
problems.problem:
Problem 15 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem 3). [Wine diamonds: potassium hydrotartrate]

Enology is the study of wine, which includes the investigation of processes taking place under the fermentation of grape juice. One of these processes is the formation of “wine diamonds” – the crystals, consisting mainly of potassium hydrotartrate ($\ce{KHC4H4O6}$) and formed by storage of wine at low temperatures. The acid dissociation constants of tartaric acid are $9.12\cdot10^{-4}$ and $4.26\cdot10^{-5}$.

1. Calculate the values of $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{a},1}$ and $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{a},2}$ for tartaric acid.

2. At what value of $\mathrm{pH_{max}}$ the fraction of hydrotartrate ion is the maximum?

3. Sketch a distribution diagram for all the forms of tartaric acid ($\ce{H2A}$, $\ce{HA^-}$, $\ce{A^{2-}}$) as a function of pH. Show $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{a},1}$, $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{a},2}$ and $\mathrm{pH_{max}}$ on it.

Solubility product of potassium hydrotartrate at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is $5.00\cdot10^{-5}$, but in most cases its solubility is increased due to equilibria between tartaric acid and other ions or organic compounds. The average concentration of potassium ions in wine is 1.0 g/L, total concentration of tartaric acid is 1.4 g/L and the pH of wine is about 3.5.

4. How in theory should the pH of wine be changed when the crystals of wine diamonds are formed due to the cooling of solution, if the pH is lower than $\mathrm{pH_{max}}$? If it is higher than $\mathrm{pH_{max}}$? Specify the equilibria responsible for these effects.

5. What percentage of tartaric acid relative to the total amount is presented in wine in the form of free hydrotartrate anion ($\ce{HA^-}$)?

6. What percentage of tartaric acid relative to the total amount does not take part in acid-base equilibria, i.e. is involved in complexes with other ions (not $\ce{H+}$) and organic compounds?

7. What is the pH range for precipitation of potassium hydrotartrate from aqueous solution, containing potassium ions and tartaric acid in the same total concentrations as in wine?

problems.title: [Salt X from sodium carbonate and a simple substance A]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [Salt X from sodium carbonate and a simple substance A]

Salt $\mathbf{X}$ exists as orange-yellow crystals that are highly soluble in water. To synthesize $\mathbf{X}$ a charge of 6.360 g of sodium carbonate mixed with 6.414 g of solid simple substance $\mathbf{A}$ and obtained mixture was left at $280\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ during 2 hours. In so doing gas $\mathbf{B}$ was evolved, total volume of which was equal $1.967\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ (at $128\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $101.7\,\mathrm{kPa}$). Resulting from synthesis solid residue contains 27.25% of sodium by mass and represents the mixture of two salts $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$. One of them is soluble in ethanol, the second one is insoluble essentially. This can be used to isolate the desired product from the resulting solid mixture. Theoretically, in the described synthesis, 6.968 g of salt $\mathbf{X}$ can be obtained.

1. Define the content of gas $\mathbf{B}$. Write down your calculations.

2. Determine the composition and give the formulas for $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$. Write down your calculations.

3. Give the reaction equation carrying out at producing of $\mathbf{X}$.

4. Draw the spatial structure of anions of salts $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$, indicate valence angles.

5. Suggest two more procedure of synthesis of $\mathbf{X}$.

problems.title: [Quantum dots XY: synthesis, band gap and binding to cysteine]
problems.problem:
Problem 2. [Quantum dots XY: synthesis, band gap and binding to cysteine]

Colloidal quantum dots are semiconductor nanocrystals with a size of 2–10 nm. In this range, the electro physical and optical properties depend on the size of the nanoparticles and differ from the properties of bulk material of a similar chemical composition due to quantum confinement effects. One of the first quantum dots were studied had an $\mathbf{XY}$ composition from the number of semiconductors of the $\mathrm{A^{II}B^{VI}}$ group. Roman numerals indicate the numbers of groups in the periodic table.

1. Determine the composition of $\mathbf{XY}$, if it is known that 1) 598 $\mathbf{X}$ atoms contain in one quantum dot with radius $r = 2.0\,\mathrm{nm}$; 2) $\rho(\mathbf{XY}) = 5.67\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, the number of formula unit’s $z$ in a unit cell is 2; 3) when $\mathbf{XY}$ is dissolved in hyperchloric acid, a gas with a strong unpleasant odor with a density of $3.31\,\mathrm{g/L}$ at 1 atm and 298 K is produced.

There are numerous $\mathbf{XY}$ synthesis methods, some of which are presented in the scheme (TMS – tetramethylsilane):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2020-1-2-fig1.png

2. a) Identify substances $\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{G}$. b) Write the equations of reaction (1 – 8).

The band gap of quantum dots ($E_\mathrm{g}^\mathrm{nano}$) is determined as

$$E_\mathrm{g}^\mathrm{nano} = E_\mathrm{g}^\mathrm{bulk} + \frac{h^2}{8r^2\mu} - \frac{1.8e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon\varepsilon_0 r},$$

where $E_\mathrm{g}^\mathrm{bulk}$ – band gap for bulk material, $h$ – Planck constant, $r$ – quantum dot radius, $\mu$ – reduced mass of electrons and holes, $e$ – elementary charge, $\varepsilon_0$ – electric constant, $\varepsilon$ – dielectric permeability.

3. Determine in which color region quantum dots with radius 3.3 nm will luminesce if the maximum luminescence of nanoparticles with $r = 2.0\,\mathrm{nm}$ are at $\lambda = 446\,\mathrm{nm}$ in the blue region. $\varepsilon(\mathbf{XY}) = 10.6$, $1/\mu = 1.37\cdot10^{31}\,\mathrm{kg^{-1}}$.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Color:} & \text{blue} & \text{green} & \text{yellow} & \text{orange} \\ \hline \lambda,\ \mathrm{nm}: & 435 – 480 & 500 – 560 & 580 – 600 & 600 – 615 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

$\mathbf{XY}$-based quantum dots have intense narrow bands of luminescence spectra in the visible light region, which almost don’t overlap with absorption spectra, which makes it possible to obtain displays with high color rendering quality. However, due to the toxicity of $\mathbf{X}$ and all its compounds, it usage in electronics is strictly limited in most countries. One of the main causes of $\mathbf{X}^{2+}$ toxicity is the ability to bind to sulfur-containing proteins, inhibiting the activity of enzyme systems. The simplest sulfur containing amino acid is cysteine $\ce{C3H7NO2S}$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2020-1-2-fig2.png

4. a) Calculate the isoelectric point (pI) of cysteine, if $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}(\text{–COOH}) = 1.9$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}(\text{–}\ce{NH3+}) = 10.4$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}(\text{–SH}) = 8.2$; b) Determine the total charge of the amino acid at pH = 8.5; c) c) To which electrode, anode (+) or cathode (–), moves cysteine during the electrophoresis at pH = 8.5?

To determine the thermodynamically preferred Cd/Cys ratio during the formation of the organometallic complex, the temperature dependences of the equilibrium constants of the reactions

$$\mathbf{X}^{2+}\mathrm{(aq)} + \mathrm{CysH} + \ce{H2O} = \mathbf{X}\text{–}\mathrm{Cys}^{+} + \ce{H3O+} \qquad (1)$$

$$\mathbf{X}^{2+}\mathrm{(aq)} + 2\mathrm{CysH} + 2\ce{H2O} = \mathrm{Cys}\text{–}\mathbf{X}\text{–}\mathrm{Cys} + 2\ce{H3O+} \qquad (2)$$

were studied. As a result, the equations for $\ln K$ dependencies on $1/T$ are obtained: $y_1 = -2.93 + 29348/T$ and $y_2 = -3.50 + 37400/T$ for reactions (1) and (2) respectively.

5. Calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ_{298}$ for both reactions based on the presented data.

6. Draw possible structures of the complexes $\mathbf{X}^{2+}$ and cysteine preferably formed in solution at a) pH = 8.5; b) pH = 11.

Physical constants:

$h = 6.63\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}$, $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.02\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, $c = 2.998\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$, $1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$, $e = 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J/mol\cdot K} = 0.082\,\mathrm{L\cdot atm/mol\cdot K}$.

problems.title: [Element X: two series of binary compounds A and B]
problems.problem:
Problem 3. [Element X: two series of binary compounds A and B]

The element $\mathbf{X}$ as simple substance exists in the form of several allotropic modifications, including $\mathbf{X_1}$ and $\mathbf{X_2}$, which differ greatly in their reactivity. Compounds of $\mathbf{X}$ with most metals and non-metals are known. Consider two similar classes of binary compounds formed by element $\mathbf{X}$.

Substance $\mathbf{A_1}$ ($\omega(\mathbf{X}) = 56.34\%$) is formed by comproportionation of substances: elemental $\mathbf{X_1}$ with $\mathbf{A_5}$. Substance $\mathbf{A_2}$ ($\omega(\mathbf{X}) = 52.54\%$) is obtained by oxidation of $\mathbf{A_1}$ at $190–210\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ with small amounts of colorless gas $\mathbf{G}$. If the same reaction is carried out at elevated temperature – in the range $280–320\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, then the mixture of binary compounds $\mathbf{A_2}$, $\mathbf{A_3}$, $\mathbf{A_4}$ and $\mathbf{A_5}$ is formed. Oxidation state of $\mathbf{X}$ increases in the row. Gas $\mathbf{G}$ is obtained by decomposition of black-brown binary compound $\mathbf{D}$, the second product of the decomposition reaction is a simple compound $\mathbf{D_1}$. Compound $\mathbf{A_6}$ ($\omega(\mathbf{X}) = 30.10\%$) is obtained recently by interaction $\mathbf{A_1}$ with the blue gas $\mathbf{G_1}$ received from $\mathbf{G}$ at $-78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in solution $\ce{CH2Cl2}$.

Substances of series B in most cases can be synthesized by direct interaction of simple substances. Substance $\mathbf{B_1}$ is formed at $180\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in inert atmosphere as a result of interaction of $\mathbf{X_2}$ with the simple substance $\mathbf{Y}$. Molar mass of $\mathbf{B_1}$ and $\mathbf{A_1}$ are the same. Substance $\mathbf{B_1}$ can be oxidized further by substance $\mathbf{Y}$ in $\ce{CS2}$ solution with trace amounts $\ce{I2}$, as catalyst, the substance $\mathbf{B_2}$ is formed at these conditions. Molar mass of $\mathbf{B_2}$ is equal to molar mass of $\mathbf{A_5}$. Substances $\mathbf{B_5}$ and $\mathbf{B_3}$ are produced by interaction of simple substances $\mathbf{X_1}$ or $\mathbf{X_2}$, respectively, with $\mathbf{Y}$. Substance $\mathbf{B_4}$ ($\omega(\mathbf{X}) = 30.10\%$) is a product of comproportionation $\mathbf{B_5}$ and $\mathbf{B_3}$.

1. Decipher the substances and write the reaction equations.

2. Draw substance structures $\mathbf{A_1}$ and $\mathbf{A_6}$, $\mathbf{B_1}$ – $\mathbf{B_5}$. In $\mathbf{A_6}$, the same fragment can be distinguished in the structure of the molecule as in $\mathbf{A_1}$, as well as the same fragments from $\mathbf{G}$ atoms can be distinguished similar to $\mathbf{G_1}$. Data for $\mathbf{B_1}$ – $\mathbf{B_5}$ series are presented in the table. Substance $\mathbf{B_2}$ has two isomers. $\mathbf{B_1}$ has 3-fold axis.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Bond type} & \mathbf{B_1} & \mathbf{B_2(1)} & \mathbf{B_2(2)} & \mathbf{B_3} & \mathbf{B_4} & \mathbf{B_5} \\ \hline \mathbf{X}\text{–}\mathbf{X} & 3 & 1 & 2 & 1 & – & – \\ \hline \mathbf{X}\text{–}\mathbf{Y} & 6 & 10 & 8 & 10 & 12 & 12 \\ \hline \mathbf{X}\text{–}\mathbf{Y}\ \text{terminal} & – & – & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

problems.title: [Cope, oxy-Cope and Claisen rearrangements; the synthesis of barbaralane]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [Cope, oxy-Cope and Claisen rearrangements; the synthesis of barbaralane]

The Cope rearrangement is [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of 1,5-dienes, which mechanism for parent hexa-1,5-diene depicted on Figure 1. The reaction goes through a 6-electron concerted transition states and follow rules of orbital symmetry.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2020-1-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Mechanism of Cope rearrangement.

1. Propose the structure of two diasteromeric hydrocarbons $\ce{C8H14}$, whose comparable behavior in Cope rearrangement proves the synchronous mechanism of the reaction. Also provide the structure of the rearranged products in each case.

The Cope rearrangement can be extended to hetero-atoms and substituents. In such cases, we have the oxy-Cope and Claisen rearrangement, depending whether the heteroatom is part of the rearrangement system, or acts as initially a pendant group, but undergoes a keto-enol tautomerisation afterwards.

2. Determine the products of the following reactions. (Note: all of the reactions below fall into the same class determined in question no. 1.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2020-1-4-fig2.png

Scheme 1. Examples of oxy-Cope and Claisen rearrangements.

Another interesting feature of the Cope rearrangement is the degenerate variant (the product is structuraly identical to the starting material), as in the parent hexa-1,5-diene. This fact has been subjected to a large number of theoretical studies. In the 60’s the hydrocarbon barbaralane ($\ce{C9H10}$) was designed and synthesized. The compound was named after Professor Barbara M. Ferrier. This compound enters degenerate rearrangement at room temperature and the rearrangement stops only at $-110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Scheme 2 depicts an optimized synthesis of barbaralane from 1983.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2020-1-4-fig3.png

Scheme 2. Synthesis of barbaralane.

3. Decode Scheme 2 and draw the structure of compounds $\mathbf{E}$ – $\mathbf{H}$ and barbaralane.

4. How many signals are observed in the $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ NMR spectra of barbaralane at room temperature and at $-110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

problems.title: [Favorsky isomerization, the zipper reaction and elenic acid]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Favorsky isomerization, the zipper reaction and elenic acid]

In 1884 A. E. Favorsky discovered that the heating of hydrocarbon $\mathbf{I}$ ($w_\mathrm{C} = 88.89\%$) with alcoholic solution of KOH at $170\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ leads to its isomerization to product $\mathbf{Ia}$. When $\mathbf{Ia}$ is shaken with a mixture of water and sulfuric acid (1:3) in a sealed tube, crystals of hydrocarbon $\mathbf{A}$ ($\ce{C12H18}$, $T_\mathrm{melt} = 164\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) are formed, and compound $\mathbf{A}$ possess only one singlet in the $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectrum ($\delta$ = 2.2 м.д.).

1. Decode structure $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{Ia}$ and $\mathbf{A}$, if $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{Ia}$ – position isomers of multiple bond. The mechanism of the isomerization was investigated in 1951 using the hydrocarbon $\mathbf{II}$, which is homologue of $\mathbf{I}$. It was found that the treatment of $\mathbf{II}$ by KOH solution in alcohol ($175\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, 3 h) leads to isomer $\mathbf{IIa}$ formation. The isomerization process is reversible and proceeds through isomeric compound $\mathbf{IIb}$.

2. Decipher the structure of $\mathbf{II}$, $\mathbf{IIa}$ and $\mathbf{Iib}$. Take into account, that $\mathbf{II}$ and $\mathbf{IIa}$ contain the equal number of sp-hybridized carbon atoms, but its amount in $\mathbf{IIb}$ two times less. Upon oxidation of the equilibrium mixture by $\ce{KMnO4}/\ce{H+}$, only $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{CH3COOH}$, $\ce{CH3CH2COOH}$ and $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CHOOH}$ are formed as carbon-containing products.

3. Write reaction equation of oxidation $\mathbf{II}$, $\mathbf{IIa}$ and $\mathbf{IIb}$ by $\ce{KMnO4}$ in acidic media.

The reverse conversion of $\mathbf{IIa}$ to $\mathbf{II}$ can also be carried out in practice. For this purpose $\mathbf{IIa}$ is treated by base $\mathbf{X}$ with further hydrolysis of the reaction mixture. Compound $\mathbf{X}$ could be obtained by the reaction of equimolar amount of KH with liquid compound $\ce{C3H10N2}$.

4. Indicate the structural formulas of $\ce{C3H10N2}$ and $\mathbf{X}$. The $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectra of $\ce{C3H10N2}$ has a quintet, singlet and triplet with the integral ratio 1:2:2, and the singlet could exchange with $\ce{D2O}$. In the answer sheet indicate the role of the bases KOH and $\mathbf{X}$ in the transformations $\mathbf{II} \rightarrow \mathbf{IIa}$ and $\mathbf{IIa} \rightarrow \mathbf{II}$.

A rearrangement $\mathbf{IIa} \rightarrow \mathbf{II}$ can multiply occur inside the molecule in the presence of $\mathbf{X}$. Such transformation called zipper-reaction. The reaction was used as a key step of the synthesis of natural Elenic acid:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2020-1-5-fig1.png

5. Decipher structures $\mathbf{B}$ – $\mathbf{G}$. The $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{B}$ ($w_\mathrm{C} = 32.73\%$, $w_\mathrm{H} = 2.27\%$) showed a singlet at 4.9 ppm (1H) and two doublets at 6.6 ppm (2H) and 7.5 ppm (2H). Compound $\mathbf{C}$ is the unbranched homologue of $\mathbf{I}$ ($w_\mathrm{C} = 86.33\%$).

problems.title: [The lead battery]
problems.problem:
Problem 6. [The lead battery]

The lead battery was invented by the French chemist Louis Gaston Plante in 1859. In the charged state, the left electrode of the battery (with a more negative potential) consists of metallic lead, and the right one of lead oxide $\ce{PbO2}$. The electrolyte is a solution of sulfuric acid (20–30 weight %). When two lead plates are immersed in acid (uncharged state), a thin layer of $\ce{PbSO4}$ is formed on the electrodes and the solution is saturated with the same salt. When the battery is charged at its electrode connected to the positive pole of the source, lead is oxidized to $\ce{PbO2}$, and the second electrode turns into pure lead. The concentration of sulfuric acid increases.

1. Draw the simplest circuit diagram of the electrical circuit of a lead battery with the polarity of the electrodes and interface surfaces (vertical bar).

Below are the half-reactions 1 and 2 occurring on the electrodes:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline & \text{Half-reaction} & E^0,\ \mathrm{V} \\ \hline 1 & \ce{PbSO4 + 2e^- = Pb + SO4^{2-}} & -0.359 \\ \hline 2 & \ce{PbO2 + SO4^{2-} + 4H+ + 2e^- = PbSO4 + 2H2O} & +1.682 \\ \hline 3 & \ce{Pb^{2+} + 2e^- = Pb} & -0.126 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

2. a) Write the total reaction expressing the final products of chemical transformations in the battery; b) Find the standard EMF of the electrochemical cell; c) Calculate the standard Gibbs energy of the total reaction; d) Calculate the equilibrium constant of this reaction at a temperature of $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

At the interface of the Pb | electrolyte, a chemical interaction should take place with the formation of $\ce{PbSO4}$.

3. Write the corresponding chemical reaction.

The $\ce{Pb(SO4)2}$ salt is first formed on the $\ce{PbO2}$ | electrolyte interface, but due to its instability, extremely low solubility and ability to decompose with oxygen evolution, the surface of the $\ce{PbO2}$ electrode is also covered with a thin layer of $\ce{PbSO4}$.

4. Write chemical reactions of a) $\ce{Pb(SO4)2}$ formation and b) $\ce{Pb(SO4)2}$ decomposition.

In a fully charged battery at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the concentration of $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ ions in solution is $0.93\cdot10^{-6}\,\mathrm{M}$.

5. Determine the potential of the lead electrode Pb | $\ce{H2SO4}$ in this state.

In some working condition at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the electrolyte contains 376 g of $\ce{H2SO4}$ per 1000 g of water. The acid activity coefficient in such a solution is $\gamma(\ce{H2SO4}) = 0.165$, and the water activity is $a(\ce{H2SO4}) = 0.7$.

6. Calculate the EMF of the electrochemical cell of the battery with this electrolyte.

Additional information:

I. Gas constant $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{j\cdot mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$;

II. Faraday Constant $F = 96485\,\mathrm{C\cdot mol^{-1}}$;

III. The relationship of the Gibbs energy of the reaction with the EMF: $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G = -nFE$;

IV. In concentrated solutions, the molality of $m_i$ components (mol/1000 g of solvent) is replaced by $a_i$ activities. The relationship between these quantities is $a_i = \gamma_i m_i$, where $\gamma_i$ – is the activity coefficient. In extremely dilute solutions, the activity became concentration ($a_i \rightarrow \gamma_i m_i$ at $m_i \rightarrow 0$)

V. Nernst formula for electrode potential

$$E = E^0 + \frac{RT}{nF}\ln\frac{a(\mathrm{Ox})}{a(\mathrm{Red})},$$

where $a$ is the activity of the oxidized and reduced forms, $n$ is the number of electrons in the half-reaction.

Problem 7. [Thyroglobulin and the biosynthesis of a hormone: compounds A–F]

Biosynthesis of an important hormone starts from thyroglobulin, a protein produced in the thyroid body and enriched with the tyrosine ($\alpha$-amino acid) residues. The peroxide oxidation in the presence of anions $\mathbf{X}^-$ leads to the transformation of the aromatic rings of tyrosine into the $\mathbf{Y}$ moieties, further oxidation of which is accompanied by intraprotein rearrangement yielding the dehydroalanine and another amino acid units (see the scheme). As required, the formed prohormone is hydrolyzed with elimination of compound $\mathbf{A}$ (65.34% of element $\mathbf{W}$), which is further transformed into a more efficient compound $\mathbf{B}$ (58.48% of $\mathbf{W}$); the inactive $\mathbf{B'}$ isomer is formed as a by-product. Deactivation of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ occurs via several paths with the formation of metabolites $\mathbf{C}$ – $\mathbf{E}$. Under certain conditions, deactivation of $\mathbf{A}$ affords compound $\mathbf{F}$ (67.88% of $\mathbf{W}$) exhibiting anticancer action.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2020-1-7-fig1.png

Problem 8. [Glycerophospholipids, liposomes and doxorubicin delivery]

Glycerophospholipids are important components of cell membranes. Their biosynthesis starts with the modification of hydroxyl group of glycerol by phosphate group, which results in the chiral product.

1. The R-isomer of glycerol 3-phosphate is given in the Answer sheet. Draw the Fischer projection of this compound showing free OH-group at the top. Specify its relative configuration (D or L).

The phosphate group of glycerol 3-phosphate affords esters as a result of the reaction with alcohols, e.g. with compound $\mathbf{D}$ formed in the organism from the canonical amino acid $\mathbf{X}$. Biosynthesis of $\mathbf{X}$ starts from a glycolysis intermediate, 3-phosphoglycerate. Equations of the reactions are presented in the scheme.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2020-1-8-fig1.png

SAM is S-Adenosyl methionine, SAH is the demethylated product, S-Adenosyl homocysteine; $\ce{NAD+}$ and NADH are oxidized and reduced forms of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, respectively.

2. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{X}$, if there is one more (except $\mathbf{X}$) canonical amino acid in the above scheme.

Free OH-groups of glycerol 3-phosphate are esterified by fatty acid residues resulting in phospholipids, which contain both hydrophobic and hydrophilic moieties. In aqueous solutions, phospholipids spontaneously form bilayer structures which finally affords spherical liposomes.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2020-1-8-fig2.png

3. Estimate the internal cavity volume of a liposome with the external diameter of 100 nm composed of glycerol 3-phosphate-based lipids modified with $\mathbf{D}$ and two residues of palmitic (hexadecanoic) acid (these lipids further referred to as DPPC). When estimating the length of the lipid molecule, consider the valence angles and the C–C bond length of 0.154 nm; neglect the size of the hydrophilic fragment. Take the carbonyl carbon as the beginning of the hydrophobic fragment.

Liposomes were prepared by solvent evaporation from 0.02 mL of DPPC solution in chloroform (with the concentration of 25 mg/mL), subsequent addition of 5 mL of water and ultrasonic treatment of the resulting system.

4. a) Calculate the concentration of the obtained liposomes (diameter of 100 nm). Take the surface area occupied by a single DPPC molecule on both external and internal sides of the lipid bilayer equal to $0.44\,\mathrm{nm^2}$. Note that all lipid molecules are included in the liposomes, whereas all liposomes consist of the same number of DPPC molecules.

b) Calculate the total internal volume of the liposomes in the resulting system.

Note. If you failed to answer question 3, take the entire volume of a liposome as that of its internal cavity.

Liposomes are widely used for targeted delivery of drugs. A medicine is typically incorporated into the internal cavity, which leads to an enhanced time of the drug circulation in blood и.

5. Calculate the biological half lifetimes of free doxorubicin (Dox) and the liposomes with Dox, if the process of the drug clearance is described by the first-order kinetics. Both drugs are administered in the concentration of $75.0\,\mathrm{mg/m^2}$ (referred to the body surface area). After 4 h, the concentration of Dox and liposomes were found equal to 66.8 and $67.4\,\mathrm{mg/m^2}$, respectively.

6. Calculate the amount of free Dox and Dox entrapped into the liposomes that would be found in man 2 h after administration of the drugs. Dox concentration inside the liposomes is of 25 mg/mL. The dose of 5 mL of the liposomes described in i. 4 was administrated to a patient. Equal initial masses of Dox were introduced with both drugs.

Problem 3. [Metal X discovered by Scheele in mineral A; coloured compounds X1–X4]

Mineral $\mathbf{A}$ was used in ancient times for refining glass. For some time, it was considered a type of magnetite, although it is not attracted by a magnet. Subsequently, the Swedish chemist Scheele discovered a new metal $\mathbf{X}$ in this mineral, which can exhibit different oxidation states. As a consequence, solutions of compounds of this metal can have different colors. Compound $\mathbf{X_1}$, which is blue-colored, can be turned into $\mathbf{X_2}$, that has a green color and can be further converted into violet $\mathbf{X_3}$ and then into pink $\mathbf{X_4}$.

$$\mathbf{X_1}\ \text{(blue)} \underset{\mathbf{2}}{\overset{\mathbf{1}}{\rightleftarrows}} \mathbf{X_2}\ \text{(green)} \underset{\mathbf{4}}{\overset{\mathbf{3}}{\rightleftarrows}} \mathbf{X_3}\ \text{(violet)} \underset{\mathbf{6}}{\overset{\mathbf{5}}{\rightleftarrows}} \mathbf{X_4}\ \text{(pink)}$$

3. Write equations for the reactions $\mathbf{1}$ – $\mathbf{6}$.

4. When $\mathbf{X_4}$ interacts with ammonium hydrogen phosphate in ammonia aqueous solution, a white precipitate $\mathbf{X_5}$ is formed, which decomposes on heating to form $\mathbf{X_6}$. Draw the structure of the $\mathbf{X_6}$ anion, give the reaction equations and the composition of the resulting compounds taking into account that the mass fraction of $\omega(\mathbf{X})$ in $\mathbf{X_6}$ is 38.73%.

problems.title: [The mercury thermometer: thermal expansion, freezing point, entropy, amalgams and spilled mercury]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [The mercury thermometer: thermal expansion, freezing point, entropy, amalgams and spilled mercury]

In connection with the COVID-19 pandemic additional sanitary and epidemiological requirements were introduced. Thus it was impossible to get into public places without measuring body temperature, which was carried out using pyrometers and thermal imagers. These devices provide fast data acquisition, but their accuracy is much lower than contact thermometers, among which mercury is the most widely used. Upon contact with the object of measurement, the volume of mercury changes due to thermal extension according to the formula: $V = V_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$, where $V_0$, $V$ are the initial and final volume of Hg, $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient of volumetric expansion, $\Delta T$ is the difference between the initial and final temperatures.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2021-1-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Mercury thermometer before starting measurements

1. Determine if a person is sick if, when measuring his temperature 115 J of heat was transferred to mercury. Hg density $\rho = 13.55\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, heat capacity of liquid Hg $c = 27.88\,\mathrm{J/mol\cdot K}$, $\alpha = 1.8\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The scale division is 1 mm (Fig. 1), the initial temperature of mercury is $35.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The signal of the onset of the disease is $37.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The diameter of the column of mercury $d = 1\,\mathrm{mm}$.

The mercury thermometer has a number of disadvantages, including difficulty of using it in the regions with cold climate.

2. Based on the equilibrium condition $\Delta_\mathrm{melt}G = 0$, determine the freezing point of Hg; $\Delta_\mathrm{melt}H = 2.29\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, $\Delta_\mathrm{melt}S = 0.034\,\mathrm{J/K}$. The thermometer contains 0.7 g Hg.

3. Using the relation $\delta Q = T\mathrm{d}S$, determine the change in entropy of 0.7 g of mercury when the temperature rises from $T_\mathrm{i} = -60$ to $T_\mathrm{f} = +40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $c(\mathrm{Hg,\ s}) = 28.28\,\mathrm{J/mol\cdot K}$. Note that the desired change is the sum of the entropy changes in the tree stages of heating. If you failed answering question 2, provide a formula for calculating $\Delta S$ with an unknown melting point.

Electrochemically produced mercury amalgams are used to lower the freezing point.

4. a) Write down the process equations; b) Determine the composition $\omega(\mathrm{wt\,\%})$ of thallium amalgam $\mathrm{Tl\cdot}n\mathrm{Hg}$, obtained by electrolysis of thallium formate solution for 5 min with a current of 0.73 A using a mercury cathode weighing 5 g; c) Determine the density of gases evolved at the anode at 298 K and $p = 1\,\mathrm{atm}$.

The main disadvantage of mercury thermometers is high toxicity of Hg, which can lead to spilled mercury poisoning. To remove small drops of mercury that cannot be collected mechanically, a solution of potassium permanganate with hydrochloric acid or a dilute solution of iron(III) chloride are used.

5. Write down the equations for the reactions mentioned.

Physical constants: $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J/mol\cdot K}$, Faraday constant $F = 96\,485\,\mathrm{C/mol}$.

problems.title: [Acetic acid in canning and baking: vinegar, marinade pH and baking powder]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Acetic acid in canning and baking: vinegar, marinade pH and baking powder]

Acetic acid ($K_\mathrm{a} = 1.75\cdot10^{-5}$) is often used as a preservative, which contributes to the making of acidic medium and prevents the multiplication of botulism spores under anaerobic conditions, which can accidentally get into the canned food with soil particles. At pH < 4.6 botulism spores are not reproduced and the toxin is not produced. Vinegar (9% aqueous solution (density $1011.0\,\mathrm{g/dm^3}$)), is most often used as a seasoning and for canning in domestic conditions as well as vinegar essence, which is a 70% aqueous solution (density $1068.5\,\mathrm{g/dm^3}$) of acetic acid.

1. At $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, there are two glass cylinders $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ by volume on the table, both contain $200\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 70% and 86% aqueous solutions of acetic acid, respectively. How can one determine what solution is contained in each of the cylinders if it is not possible to carry out a chemical analysis, but there is reference data?

2. What volume of 9% vinegar should be taken to prepare $12.0\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of a marinade for preserving mushrooms with a pH = 3.5?

3. The young chemist made a mistake in his calculations and prepared a marinade with a pH 2.5. Calculate the mass of baking soda that should be added to $12.0\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of such a marinade in order to raise its pH to 3.5 (when calculating, assume that the volume of the solution and its density do not change with the addition of soda).

In everyday life, vinegar is also used in baking pastry from yeast-free dough. To make the confectionery "pomp", baking soda is used, which is "quenched" beforehand – a small amount of vinegar is added and only then the resulting mixture (baking powder) is added to the dough. The amount of vinegar should be strictly defined (about a teaspoon of baking soda – the same amount of vinegar), since an excess of baking soda in a confection greatly impairs its quality (gives a "metallic" taste) due to the formation of sodium carbonate when heated during baking.

4. Give the chemical reaction equations occurring during the baking process, in which, due to the non-gaseous product at normal conditions it becomes possible to subsequently increase the volume (pomp) of the dough based on flour, water, sugar and salt.

5. Calculate the maximum volume (at normal conditions) of carbon dioxide that can be released during baking of a dough with added baking powder, consisting of 1 teaspoon (5.0 g) baking soda and 1 teaspoon ($5.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$) 9% vinegar.

Anionic chain polymerization includes the stages of initiation (1 and 2), chain propagation (3), and chain termination (4). https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2021-1-7-fig1.png

If the rate constants of the given stages are related as $k_\mathrm{t} \ll k_\mathrm{p} = k_\mathrm{i,2} \ll k_\mathrm{i,1}$ and the monomer reactivity is independent of the nature of the anionic species it is added to, the polymerization affords almost monodisperse polymer (that consisting of the molecules of equal molecular mass).

To obtain a nanocomposite material, compound $\mathbf{A}$ (0.52 g) was stirred with aqueous suspension of 1.00 g of sodium form of montmorillonite $\mathbf{MontONa}$ until equilibrium.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2021-1-7-fig2.png

The lifetime of bringing novel drugs to the market on average takes around 20 years and over 1 billion dollars. Problem 1. [A battery from “The Mysterious Island”]

In Jules Verne's novel “The Mysterious Island”, the chemical engineer Smith built a battery to power the telegraph:

«Smith decided to make the simplest battery, similar to the one invented by Becquerel in 1820. The engineer made several glass jars and filled them with nitric acid. Then he plugged each jar with a stopper, passing through it a glass tube, the lower end of which was plugged with a clay sleeve wrapped with a piece of rag. Through the upper end of this tube he poured a solution of potash. Smith then took two zinc plates and immersed one in nitric acid and the other in a solution of potash. An electric current immediately arose and went from the plate inserted in (1) to the plate inserted in (2). When these plates were connected with a metal wire, the plate in the tube became (3), and the plate in the jar became the (4) pole of the device. The result was a source of current, quite sufficient to set in motion an electric telegraph.»

Standard potentials (V) (pH = 0)

6. How many ($N$) batteries must be connected in series in order for the telegraph to work, which needs a voltage of $4.5\,\mathrm{V}$?

7. Calculate the Gibbs energy and the equilibrium constant of the reaction in the battery.

Reference data: $E^\circ(\ce{K+}/\ce{K}) = -2.93\,\mathrm{V}$, $E^\circ(\ce{O2}/\ce{H2O}) = 1.23\,\mathrm{V}$, $E^\circ(\ce{Zn^{2+}}/\ce{Zn}) = -0.76\,\mathrm{V}$, $F = 96485\,\mathrm{C/mol}$, $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}$.

problems.title: [Adsorption of n-pentanol]
problems.problem:
Problem 2. [Adsorption of n-pentanol]

Surface-active species (surfactants) are adsorbed at an interface between phases, thus reducing its tension. The surface tension of aqueous $n$-pentanol solution under air can be described via the Szyszkowski equation $\sigma = K - L\ln(1 + Mc)$, with $K = 72.8\,\mathrm{mN/m}$, $L = 16.7\,\mathrm{mN/m}$, $M = 66\,\mathrm{L/mol}$, and $c$ being concentration of the alcohol in the solution.

1. Determine the surface tension of pure water.

2. Determine the lowest limit of $n$-pentanol detection in the aqueous solution by measuring the surface tension, if the latter can be measured with accuracy of ±2%.

Adsorption ($\Gamma$, $\mathrm{mol/m^2}$) of a surfactant with the formation of its monolayer at the interface can be described via the Gibbs equation $\Gamma = \dfrac{\Gamma_\mathrm{max}\cdot Mc}{1 + Mc} = \dfrac{L}{RT}\,\dfrac{Mc}{(1 + Mc)}$, with $\Gamma_\mathrm{max}$ being the highest possible adsorption ($\mathrm{mol/m^2}$), $L$ and $M$ being the Szyszkowski equation parameters.

3. Calculate $\Gamma_\mathrm{max}$ for $n$-pentanol adsorption at the water–air interface and determine the area $s_0$ per a molecule in the saturated adsorbed monolayer.

If the area of the surface at which the adsorption occurs can hardly be measured, the adsorption can be expressed per mass of the sorbent (mol/g). In this case, the Gibbs equation is still correct, yet the parameters $M$, $L$ are different from these for the water–air interface. To study $n$-pentanol adsorption at active carbon, 1 g of the carbon sample was put in the alcohol solutions (25 mL each) with different concentration ($c_0$). Upon the equilibration, the carbon was filtered off, and surface tension of the filtrate ($\sigma$) was determined. The obtained data are in the table below:

$$\begin{array}{c|c} c_0,\ \mathrm{mol/L} & \sigma,\ \mathrm{mN/m} \\ \hline 0.05 & 59.4 \\ 0.10 & 50.8 \\ 0.15 & 44.2 \\ 0.2 & 38.9 \end{array}$$

4. Determine the alcohol concentration in the filtrate at its different starting concentrations and calculate the $n$-pentanol adsorption on carbon (mol/g) in each of the four experiment runs.

5. Draw a plot of $c/\Gamma$ as a function of $c$ ($c$ being the equilibrium alcohol concentration). Using the obtained data, determine the highest possible adsorption $\Gamma_\mathrm{max}$ of the alcohol on the carbon (mol/g).

6. Assuming that the area per molecule is the same in the adsorption layer at the water–air and water–carbon interfaces, calculate specific surface area of the carbon ($\mathrm{m^2/g}$).

problems.title: [A ladybug defence alkaloid]
problems.problem:
Problem 3. [A ladybug defence alkaloid]

Ladybugs play an important ecological role in controlling the population of some harmful insects such as aphids. Ladybugs have few natural enemies due to their defense mechanism based on releasing a fluid that contains cokyneline ($\mathbf{J}$, $\ce{C13H23NO}$). Below its synthesis is presented.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-1-3-fig1.png

The key step in this synthesis is the Robinson-Schepf reaction, which was first used as a method for obtaining the bicyclic compound $\mathbf{X}$ from which tropinone ($\mathbf{Y}$) was obtained:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-1-3-fig2.png

1. Decipher the structures of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ considering that the Robinson-Schepf reaction is a sort of a double Mannich reaction.

2. Decode substances $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{J}$ if the IR spectrum of $\mathbf{A}$ contains a band at $1720\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and $^1$H NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{D}$ contains 5 signals in with integrated intensities 6:2:2:2:1.

problems.title: [Stereochemistry of the aldol reaction]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [Stereochemistry of the aldol reaction]

Aldol condensation is a universal method for the formation of a C–C bond. It is important to discuss the stereochemical regularities of this reaction.

1. Give the structures of achiral carbonyl compounds and products of their aldol condensation if this product contains: a) 0 chiral centers; b) 1 chiral center; c) 2 chiral centers.

To minimize side processes, pre-prepared enolates are often used, the stereochemistry of which depends significantly on the structure of the starting carbonyl compound.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-1-4-fig1.png

2. Determine the structure of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, lithium enolates $Z$-$\mathbf{I}$ and $E$-$\mathbf{II}$ if the $^1$H NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{A}$ contains quadruplet (2H), triplet (3H) and singlet (9H). The $^1$H NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{B}$ contains singlet (2H), quadruplet (2H), singlet (3H), triplet (3H), singlet (6H). $\mathbf{B}$ is obtained regioselectively by the reaction: $\ce{C_{x}H_{y} + RCOCl/AlCl3 -> }\mathbf{B}$. Determine the structures of $\ce{C_{x}H_{y}}$ and RCOCl.

Aldol condensation exhibits high stereoselectivity when pre-prepared enolates are used. The stereochemistry of the products is determined by the geometry of the enolate ($Z$/$E$). To predict the predominant diastereomer (syn-/anti-) of the condensation product, it was proposed to use the 6-membered transition state ($\mathbf{TS}$):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-1-4-fig2.png

3. Add substituents in $\mathbf{TS}$ for the reactions of $Z$-$\mathbf{I}$ and $E$-$\mathbf{II}$ with PhCHO. Based on structure of $\mathbf{TS}$, determine the structure of predominantly formed diastereomer of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$. Consider the geometry of the enolate ($Z$/$E$) and the fact that the bulky substituent occupies the equatorial position preferentially.

4. Indicate how the geometry of the initial enolate is related to the stereochemistry of the final condensation product

5. Indicate the configurations of the chiral centers ($R$/$S$) in your product $\mathbf{C}$.

Dubois found that the carbonyl compound $\mathbf{E}$ is converted to enolate $\mathbf{III}$ by treatment with LiOH. Subsequent reaction with i-PrCHO followed by hydrolysis leads to the product $\mathbf{F}$ ($w_\mathrm{O}$ = 20.51%).

6. Based on paragraphs 2–4, depict the structures of $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{III}$ and $\mathbf{F}$, taking into account stereochemistry. $^1$H NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{F}$ contains 2 signals of the same intensity.

problems.title: [Metabolites of lomerizine and doping control]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Metabolites of lomerizine and doping control]

During the recent Winter Olympics in Beijing, serious attention was drawn to the skater K. Valieva, who had been tested positive for Trimetazidine.

A version was suggested in media that the drug appeared in the organism due to administration of Lomerizine ($\mathbf{Y}$, $M = 468\,\mathrm{g/mol}$), a pain killer approved by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and widely used for treatment of migraines. According to the WADA protocols, $\mathbf{X}$ is one of metabolites of $\mathbf{Y}$, which complicates search for of intentional Trimetazidine administration.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-1-5-fig1.png

1. Deduce all possible structures of $\mathbf{Y}$, if all its unknown substituents (those but H) totally contain four elements (e1, e2, e3, e4) in the molar ratio of 2:3:3:9. Show calculations.

Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS) is the major method used for determination of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$. The drug actually used by an athlete can by distinguished by the presence of the compound $\mathbf{Z}$ in the urine. $\mathbf{Z}$ is formed from $\mathbf{Y}$ in a one-step process catalyzed by the same enzyme responsible for the one-step transformation of $\mathbf{Y}$ into $\mathbf{X}$. The LC-MS spectra of both $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ contain one peak of the protonated molecule ($[\mathbf{X}+\mathrm{H}]^+$ in the case of $\mathbf{X}$ and $[\mathbf{Z}+\mathrm{H}]^+$ in the case of $\mathbf{Z}$), as well as the signals from the major destruction products ($\mathbf{X}_1^+$ and $\mathbf{Z}_1^+$ ions, respectively). The difference in the $m/z$ values in the case of both ions ($[\mathbf{X}+\mathrm{H}]^+ - \mathbf{X}_1^+$ and ($[\mathbf{Z}+\mathrm{H}]^+ - \mathbf{Z}_1^+$) is the same and equals 86.

2. Determine the sum of the molecular masses of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ with an accuracy to integer. Note that this question is independent of the previous one.

An oxygen containing compound $\mathbf{Z}_2$ is the major metabolite of $\mathbf{Z}$. $\mathbf{Z}_2$ is formed in one enzymatically catalyzed step and contains 4 types of H atoms.

3. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{Z}$ and $\mathbf{Z}_2$.

Formation of more hydrophilic metabolites is the major strategy of clearance of $\mathbf{Y}$ in organisms. Three of its metabolites $\mathbf{Y}_1$ – $\mathbf{Y}_3$ are structural isomers, whereas the fourth one ($\mathbf{Y}_4$) has the molecular mass by $30\,\mathrm{g/mol}$ higher than that of $\mathbf{Y}_1$.

4. Draw only one of the possible structures of each of $\mathbf{Y}_1$ and $\mathbf{Y}_4$, if $\mathbf{Y}_1$ – $\mathbf{Y}_4$ contain one and only one group identical for all the compounds, the group contributing to higher hydrophilicity. $\mathbf{Y}_1$-$\mathbf{Y}_4$ are formed from $\mathbf{Y}$ in one step.

5. Draw the finally disclosed formula $\mathbf{X}$.

Organisms use the same metabolic strategies for $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$. When using LC-MS to check the fact of administration of $\mathbf{X}$, one should monitor the signals from the protonated molecules of two metabolites ($\mathbf{X}_1$ and $\mathbf{X}_2$) with $m/z$ of 253 and 333, respectively, and from the common major product of their destruction in the form of $\mathrm{M}^+$ ion with $m/z$ of 167.

6. Propose one variant of the structures of each of $\mathbf{X}_1$ and $\mathbf{X}_2$, if the hydrophilicity increases in the sequence of $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{X}_1$, and $\mathbf{X}_2$, whereas $\mathbf{X}_2$ is formed in man directly from $\mathbf{X}_1$.

problems.title: [Iodine solutions and extraction]
problems.problem:
Problem 6. [Iodine solutions and extraction]

Iodine is widely used in medicine as an antiseptic. Since this substance is slightly soluble in water (3450 ml of water is needed to dissolve 1.00 g of the substance), an alcoholic solution of iodine and a Lugol’s solution are practically used.

1. Calculate the molar concentration (M) of iodine in a saturated aqueous solution (consider that the volume does not change when iodine is dissolved).

When iodine is extracted from the aqueous phase by an organic solvent, for example, carbon tetrachloride ($\ce{CCl4}$), an equilibrium $\ce{I2_{(aq)} <=> I2_{(org)}}$ is established, which is described by the distribution constant

$$K_D = \frac{[\ce{I2}]_{org}}{[\ce{I2}]_{aq}}.$$

A certain amount of $\ce{CCl4}$ was added to the saturated iodine solution in water, and the extraction was performed. The mass fraction of iodine in the organic phase was 57.2 times greater than in the aqueous phase. Consider the densities of aqueous solutions equal to the density of water (1 g/ml) and organic solutions – the density of $\ce{CCl4}$ (1.59 g/ml).

2. Calculate $K_D$ for iodine distribution between the aqueous phase and $\ce{CCl4}$.

Lugol’s solution is a solution of $\ce{I2}$ in a 10% (by weight) aqueous solution KI. In such a solution, the iodine solubility is increased due to the formation of a complex ion $\ce{I3^-}$ according to the equation:

$$\ce{I2_{(aq)} + I^-_{(aq)} <=> I3^-_{(aq)}} \qquad K_I = \frac{[\ce{I3^-}]_{aq}}{[\ce{I2}]_{aq}[\ce{I^-}]_{aq}}.$$

3. Analyze the structure of $\ce{I3^-}$ ion using the valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory – specify the type of the molecule ($\mathrm{AX}_n\mathrm{E}_m$, X – ligands, E – electron pairs bonded to the central atom A) and the I–I–I angle.

To find $K_I$, 100 ml of Lugol’s solution was taken (take the density also equal to 1 g/ml) and extracted with tetrachloromethane with a volume of 50 ml. Titration of 10.00 ml of aliquots of organic and aqueous phases required 3.70 and 13.90 ml of sodium thiosulfate solution with a concentration of 0.2500 M, respectively.

4. Write equations for the reactions of thiosulfate ions with $\ce{I2}$ and $\ce{I3^-}$ that occur during titration.

5. Calculate the mass fraction of $\ce{I2}$ in the analyzed Lugol’s solution and the $K_I$ constant. If you haven’t got an answer to question 2, use the value $K_D = 150$.

problems.title: [Pyrophoric iron]
problems.problem:
Problem 7. [Pyrophoric iron]

If you heat the tip of a steel needle to red heat in the flame of an alcohol lamp, and then quickly bring it into a flask with oxygen, then the needle burns with a bright flame, scattering sparks like a Bengal fire. This forms a solid black substance.

1. Give the equation for the reaction that occurs when a steel needle burns in oxygen.

Iron will not burn without heating and without oxygen, as you know. You can find a description of experiments on the preparation of "pyrophoric iron" in books on entertaining chemistry and in the Internet, "pyrophoric iron" burns out without heating on contact with air, almost like a steel needle. At the first stage of its preparation, a solution of potassium oxalate (or oxalic acid) should be added to an excess of an aqueous solution of ferrous sulfate. In this case, a yellow compound $\mathbf{A}$ precipitates (mass fraction of oxygen 53.36%).

2. Determine the formula of $\mathbf{A}$.

At the second stage, the resulting precipitate should be filtered, dried, and then strongly heated in a test tube closed with a cotton swab. As a result, according to the authors, "pyrophoric iron" is obtained. If the test tube with the resulting black powder is cooled to room temperature, and then, after removing the cotton swab, the contents are slowly poured out, then upon contact with air, the resulting product “lights up”, scattering bright sparks.

3. Give the equation of the chemical reaction of obtaining "pyrophoric iron" proposed by the authors of the publications.

An experimental study showed that if the thermal decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$ is carried out in a vacuum, then after its complete decomposition, a gas mixture is formed, the density of which at $280\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $110.8\,\mathrm{kPa}$ is $0.6507\,\mathrm{g/dm^3}$.

4. Determine the formulas of the substances that are contained in the gas mixture formed after the complete decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$ in a vacuum, and calculate their mole fractions.

5. Give the equation for the reaction that occurs during the decomposition of $\mathbf{A}$ in vacuum.

6. Give the equation for the combustion of "pyrophoric iron".

7. Why does the resulting product "burn" when exposed to air?
7.1. the resulting product is a very strong reducing agent;
7.2. the product is formed in the form of very small particles (nanoparticles);
7.3. combustion of the product starts due to the presence of impurities in the air;
7.4. the enthalpy of reaction between the product and oxygen is positive;
7.5. along with the main product during decomposition, a catalyst is formed, which sharply accelerates the reaction of the main decomposition product with oxygen;
7.6. combustion starts due to gases formed during decomposition.

problems.title: [Oxyacids of element X]
problems.problem:
Problem 8. [Oxyacids of element X]

Element $\mathbf{X}$ forms a wide variety of oxyacids in which it exhibits different oxidation states. Despite this, the structural principle underlying these compounds is not complicated – they always contain the element $\mathbf{X}$ in a tetrahedral (or slightly distorted tetrahedral) environment and contain a double bond with oxygen $\mathbf{X}$=O.

An elementary substance $\mathbf{X}$ reacts and dissolves in a concentrated solution of sodium hydroxide upon the heating. There are many products of this reaction, but the main ones are gas $\mathbf{G}$ and salt $\mathbf{B1}$. Acidification of a solution of salt $\mathbf{B1}$ produces acid $\mathbf{A1}$, which can be isolated individually by prolonged extraction with diethyl ether from aqueous solutions. The acid $\mathbf{A1}$ is white crystals with a melting point of $26.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

If another allotropic modification of $\mathbf{X}$ is oxidized by sodium chlorite or hydrogen peroxide in an alkali, salt $\mathbf{B2}$ is formed. The dihydrate of acid $\mathbf{A2}$ ($\omega(\ce{H2O})$ = 18.18%) is isolated from salt $\mathbf{B2}$ by ion exchange on a cation exchange column. The dihydrate of $\mathbf{A2}$ is further subjected to vacuum dehydration over $\ce{P2O5}$ to obtain an anhydrous acid. The $\mathbf{A2}$ acid molecules have such symmetry elements as the inversion center, the 2-fold rotation axis, and the mirror plane perpendicular to it.

The acid $\mathbf{A2}$ decomposes at $73\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, however, even with slight heating, two processes can proceed in parallel: isomerization (rearrangement) to acid $\mathbf{A3}$, as well as disproportionation with the formation of a mixture of equimolar amounts of two acids – $\mathbf{A4}$ and $\mathbf{A5}$. The $\mathbf{A3}$ acid molecules no longer have a 2-fold rotation axis and a mirror plane, and according to NMR spectroscopy on $\mathbf{X}$ nuclei, there are two nonequivalent $\mathbf{X}$ atoms in the structure. The $\mathbf{A4}$ and $\mathbf{A5}$ acid molecules are very similar – both have a mirror plane, but $\mathbf{A5}$ contains a larger number oxygen atoms, which gives it another mirror plane (perpendicular to the first plane) and a 2-fold rotation axis that passes along the line of intersection of the planes.

The formal oxidation state of element $\mathbf{X}$ increases in the series of acids $\mathbf{A1}$ – $\mathbf{A4}$ – $\mathbf{A2}$ – $\mathbf{A5}$.

1. Identify the unknown compounds and write down the equations of the mentioned chemical reactions.

2. Draw the structure of the molecules of acids $\mathbf{A1}$ – $\mathbf{A5}$, taking into account the indicated symmetry elements.

There are other oxyacids of $\mathbf{X}$, but many of them are difficult to isolate in pure form, and their salts are mainly known. Thus, the series of normal sodium salts $\mathbf{B6}$ – $\mathbf{B7}$ – $\mathbf{B8}$ contains the same number of sodium and $\mathbf{X}$ atoms. The number of oxygen atoms in this series increases by one, and the mass fraction of oxygen in $\mathbf{B6}$ and $\mathbf{B7}$ is 38.10% and 40.91%, respectively.

3. Determine the composition of salts $\mathbf{B6}$ – $\mathbf{B8}$.

4. Suggest the structure of anions of acidic residues in $\mathbf{B6}$ – $\mathbf{B8}$.

problems.title: [Thermonuclear fusion and reactor wall materials]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (Physical chemistry section, problem 1). [Thermonuclear fusion and reactor wall materials]

One of the topical areas of energy is thermonuclear fusion. In 2007, the development of a thermonuclear reactor was launched in France, the goal of which is to show by 2025 the possibility of controlling thermonuclear reactions and creating a thermonuclear station for generating energy. Artificial nuclear fusion is based on the interaction of a stable nucleus $\mathbf{X}$ with a radioactive nucleus $\mathbf{Y}$ with the formation of a stable nucleus $\mathbf{Z}$ and one neutron. The nuclei $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are isotopes. Synthesis takes place at high temperatures ($T \sim 10^8\,\mathrm{K}$) in plasma, which is held by a magnetic field in the shape of a toroid (see Fig. 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-1-fig1.png

The content of $\mathbf{Y}$ nuclei on our planet is very low, they are formed under the action of cosmic radiation on $^{14}$N atoms (interaction with a neutron), but are not able to accumulate due to the short half-life $t_{1/2} \sim$ 10–16 years. Artificially, $\mathbf{Y}$ nuclei are synthesized by irradiating a stable target A with neutrons (one neutron bombards one $\mathbf{A}$ nucleus). In addition to the $\mathbf{Y}$ nucleus, only $\mathbf{Z}$ nuclei are formed. The specific activity of the $\mathbf{Y}$ nuclei is $9650\,\mathrm{Ci/g}$. A sample containing $2.82\cdot10^{21}$ nuclei loses $14.475\,\mathrm{Ci}$ of activity in 2 years. The cost of producing $\mathbf{Y}$ nuclei is quite high: \$30 million/kg. Keep in mind that all stable nuclei have the same number of protons and neutrons.

1. Calculate the exact half-life of the nuclei $\mathbf{Y}$.

2. Calculate the financial losses for 2 months of storage of 600 g of $\mathbf{Y}$ nuclei.

3. a) Decipher the nuclei $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ and $\mathbf{A}$; b) Write three nuclear reactions: fusion of $\mathbf{Y}$ nuclei from $^{14}$N, artificial synthesis of $\mathbf{Y}$ and reaction in a thermonuclear reactor.

The energy released during the effective collision of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ nuclei is $3\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{J}$.

4. What quantity (mol) of the propane-butane (1:1) mixture burned is energetically equivalent to the reaction of the same number of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ nuclei with a total concentration of $10^{16}$ particles/L?

$\Delta_\mathrm{f}H(\ce{CO2}) = -393.5\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H(\ce{H2O}) = -285.8\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$,
$\Delta_\mathrm{f}H(\ce{C3H8}) = -103.9\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H(\ce{C4H10}) = -126.2\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$,
Toroid volume $V = 2\pi^2R^2r$. Assume $R = 9\,\mathrm{m}$, $r = 52\,\mathrm{cm}$.

The high temperature of the reaction medium is necessary to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between the nuclei. One of the main problems is the thermal stability of the reactor walls, for which two materials are tested – metal $\mathbf{M}$ and its binary compound $\mathbf{N} = \mathbf{AM}$. Metal $\mathbf{M}$ has a cubic lattice (without specifying which of the three) with a parameter of 3.16 Å and an atomic mass of more than 140 g/mol. The lattice of the $\mathbf{N}$ compound is hexagonal (see Fig. 2). The mass fraction of metal $\mathbf{M}$ is more than 50%. The compound density $\mathbf{N}$ is 1.23 times less than the density of pure metal $\mathbf{M}$. Cell parameters: $a = b = 2.92$ Å, $c = 2.82$ Å.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-1-fig2.png

5. Using the given data, decipher $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{N}$.

problems.title: [Anation kinetics of iron(III) aqua complexes]
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (Physical chemistry section, problem 2). [Anation kinetics of iron(III) aqua complexes]

Anation reactions (substitution of $\ce{H2O}$ by $\ce{X^-}$) in easily hydrolyzed complexes $\ce{[Me(H2O)6]^{3+} <=> [Me(H2O)5OH]^{2+} + H+}$ ($K_\mathrm{a}$) roceed along two routes ($k_1$ and $k_2$) at a rate of $r = (k_1[\ce{Me^{3+}}] + k_2[\ce{MeOH^{2+}}])\cdot C(\ce{X^-})$.

1. For $\ce{[Me(H2O)6]^{3+} + X^- ->}$, using its short form ($\ce{Me^{3+} + X^- ->}$), write down the reaction equations for the indicated two routes.

Connick and Coppel showed that if $\ce{X^-}$ is an anion of strong acid, then $k_\mathrm{obs} = (k_1[\ce{H+}] + k_2K_\mathrm{a})/([\ce{H+}] + K_\mathrm{a})$ and the rate increases with decrease of $[\ce{X^-}]$. Pouli and Smith established that for the weak acids HX $k'_\mathrm{obs} = (k_3[\ce{H+}] + k_4K_\mathrm{a})/K$, rate decreases with reducing $[\ce{X^-}]$ and there action proceeds via two routes: $\ce{Fe^{3+} + HX <=> FeX^{2+} + X^-}$ ($k_3$, $k_{-3}$, $K = k_3/k_{-3}$) and $\ce{FeOH^{2+} + HX <=> FeX^{2+} + H2O}$ ($k_4$, $k_{-4}$). For the anation reactions of $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ with participation of $\ce{Cl^-}$ and $\ce{HN3}$ at 25 C it was obtained:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} [\ce{H+}],\ \mathrm{mol/L} & 1.0 & 0.5 & 0.1 & 0.05 & 0.01 \\ \hline k_\mathrm{obs},\ \mathrm{L/(mol\cdot s)} & 83.60 & 156.9 & 709.2 & 1325.2 & 4458.0 \\ \hline k'_\mathrm{obs},\ \mathrm{L/(mol\cdot s)} & 85.15 & 81.76 & 79.05 & 78.71 & 78.44 \end{array}$$

2. Derive the kinetic equation for the reaction rate of $\ce{Fe^{3+} + Cl^- ->}$, assuming that the ions $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ and $\ce{FeOH^{2+}}$ are in equilibrium. The concentrations of chloride complexes can be neglected ($[\ce{Fe^{3+}}]$ and $[\ce{FeOH^{2+}}] \gg [\ce{FeCl^{2+}}]$ and $[\ce{FeOHCl+}]$), and $C(\ce{Fe}) = [\ce{Fe^{3+}}] + [\ce{FeOH^{2+}}]$. Calculate $k_1$, $k_2$ and $K_\mathrm{a}$ for $[\ce{H+}] < 0.5\,\mathrm{mol/L}$, using the table data.

3. Derive the kinetic equation for the reaction rate of $\ce{Fe(H2O)6^{3+} + HN3 <=>}$ and the expression for $k'_\mathrm{obs}$, if the rate of the forward reaction is the same as in the case of $[\ce{Cl^-}]$, and the sum $k_{-3}[\ce{H+}] + k_{-4}$ for the reverse reaction can be obtained from the equilibrium condition ($r = 0$). Note that at equilibrium $r_+ = r_-$, and $C(\ce{FeN3^{2+}}) = [\ce{FeN3^{2+}}]$. Consider the concentrations $C(\ce{HN3}) = [\ce{HN3}]$ and $C(\ce{Fe}) \gg C(\ce{FeN3})$ and $C(\ce{FeOHN3})$. Calculate $k_3$, $k_4$ and $k_{-3}$ for $[\ce{H+}] < 0.5\,\mathrm{mol/L}$.

It was established that in the case of anions of weak acids, the anation mechanism $\ce{Fe(H2O)6^{3+} + N3^-}$ includes two stages: reversible with formation of $\ce{HN3}$ and constant of $K_x$ and irreversible with $k_4$, and $k''_\mathrm{obs}$ does not depend on pH.

4. Give the reaction mechanism and expression for $k''_\mathrm{obs}$. Calculate $K_x$ and $k''_\mathrm{obs}$, if thnd e dissociation constant of $\ce{HN3}$ $K_\mathrm{a1} = 1.9\times10^{-5}$. For the reaction $\ce{Fe(H2O)6^{3+}}$ with $\ce{Cl^-}$ at $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and pH = 0, $k_1 = 275.9$.

5. Calculate the activation energy ($E_\mathrm{a}$) for $\ce{Fe(H2O)6^{3+} + Cl^- -> Fe(H2O)5Cl^{2+} + H2O}$.

In the reaction mechanism of $\ce{Fe(H2O)6^{3+} + X^-}$ the first stage depends on the strength of the acid HX and can proceed in two ways: either with the formation of a trigonal bipyramid (C. N. = 5), or an ion pair in the form of an octahedral wedge (C.N. = 7).

6. Describe a two-stage mechanism in the case of $\ce{Cl^-}$ and $\ce{N3^-}$.

problems.title: [Smart materials in sportswear]
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (Physical chemistry section, problem 3). [Smart materials in sportswear]

Smart materials can significantly increase the effectiveness of athletes. At the 2008 Olympiad games, some swimmers used swimming suits created with participation of NASA. As a result, 94% of gold medals were received by athletes in this sportswear. The key to success was the cross-linking of polymer fibers with a unique composition that reduces water resistance, which increased the speed of swimmers by 4%.

1. From the structures below, select two examples of polymers that could be used in such effective swimsuits.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-3-fig1.png

Sewing microcapsules from materials with a reversible phase transition coated with a hydrophobic shell into the fibers of the fabric allows for the body's thermoregulation during intensive training, both indoors and outdoors. Such materials are capable of absorbing heat with its subsequent release upon returning to the initial temperature and phase state. One of example of such materials is polymer $\mathbf{F}$ ($t_\mathrm{melt} = 38\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) obtained by cationic polymerization of $\mathbf{G}$ at low temperatures. $\mathbf{G}$ is released in the composition of an equimolar gas mixture with $M_\mathrm{av} = 44\,\mathrm{g/mol}$ during the thermal decomposition of ethylene carbonate. Cationic polymerization of $\mathbf{G}$ is carried out according to the scheme:

$$\begin{array}{lll} \text{1) initiation} & \mathrm{H^+}\mathbf{A}^- + \mathbf{G} \rightarrow \mathrm{M^+}\mathbf{A}^- & k_\mathrm{i} = 9.5\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{L/(mol\cdot s)}, \\ \text{2) propagation} & \mathrm{M^+}\mathbf{A}^- + \mathbf{G} \rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{i+1}^{\,+}\mathbf{A}^- & k_\mathrm{p} = 0.94\ \mathrm{L/(mol\cdot s)}, \\ \text{3) chain transfer} & \mathrm{M^+}\mathbf{A}^- + \mathbf{G} \rightarrow \mathrm{P} & k_\mathrm{tr} = 8.0\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{L/(mol\cdot s)}, \\ \text{4) termination} & \mathrm{M^+}\mathbf{A}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{M}_i + \mathrm{H^+}\mathbf{A}^- & k_\mathrm{term} = 7.5\cdot10^{-2}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}, \end{array}$$

where $\mathrm{H^+}\mathbf{A}^-$ – polymerization initiator, $\mathrm{M^+}\mathbf{A}^-$ – active site of the growing chain, $k_j$ – the rate constants of the corresponding stages.

2. a) Determine $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$; b) Using the approximation $V_\mathrm{i} = V_\mathrm{t}$, get the expression for the rate of cationic polymerization; c) Get an expression for the average degree of polymerization $X_\mathrm{av} = V_\mathrm{p}/(V_\mathrm{term} + V_\mathrm{tr})$.

3. a) Calculate the value of heat a runner releases into the surrounding space, exercising on a treadmill for 1 hour, if the change in internal energy is $-3.38\,\mathrm{MJ}$ and the power generated is 235 W. b) By how many degrees does a runner raise the temperature of the surrounding air while exercising in a room with area of $2500\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and a ceiling height of 5 m? $\rho_\mathrm{air} = 1.165\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, heat capacity $c_\mathrm{air} = 1.005\,\mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$.

4. a) What amount of microcapsules of polymer $\mathbf{F}$ with a diameter of $40\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ can be obtained by polymerization of 2.15 mol of $\mathbf{G}$ in 1 L of the reaction mixture if the reaction yield is 95%? Take $\rho_\mathbf{F} = 1200\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
If You didn’t determine the degree of polymerization, accept $M(\mathbf{F}) = 500\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.
b) What proportion of the heat generated by a runner can be absorbed by sportswear containing all the obtained microcapsules of polymer $\mathbf{F}$? A runner's skin temperature is $34\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at the start of a workout and $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at the end.
$c(\mathbf{F}, \mathrm{s}) = 8.48\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{kJ/(microsphere\cdot K)}$, $c(\mathbf{F}, \mathrm{l}) = 6.28\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{kJ/(microsphere\cdot K)}$,
$\Delta_\mathrm{melt}H(\mathbf{F}) = 6.11\cdot10^{-9}\,\mathrm{kJ/microsphere}$.
Assume that heat is distributed evenly from all area and clothing covers 80% of the body.

The implementation of tribo-, piezo- and thermoelectric materials into clothing allows sports to use mechanical energy and heat generated to operate vital signs sensors or more complex wearable electronics. For example, a $30\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ thick film of piezoelectric polymer $\mathbf{K}$, placed in a runner's sneakers, is capable of generating power $W = 1\,\mathrm{mW}$. Output voltage $U = \gamma Ph/\varepsilon\varepsilon_0$, where $\gamma$ – piezoelectric coefficient, $P$ – applied pressure, $h$ – film thickness, $\varepsilon$ – the dielectric constant, $\varepsilon_0$ – electrical constant.

5. a) Determine the current that can be generated while running if the mass of the runner is 55 kg, and the area of the sneakers is $189\,\mathrm{cm^2}$. Accept $\gamma(\mathbf{K}) = 49.6\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C/N}$, $\varepsilon(\mathbf{K}) = 10$; b) How many percent can runner charge a heart rate sensor with a $130\,\mathrm{mA\cdot h}$ battery in 1 hour of running? c) Identify polymer $\mathbf{K}$ and monomer $\mathbf{L}$ if the last one is known to be an unsaturated halogenated hydrocarbon containing 37.5% C and 3.1% H. The electron impact ionization mass spectrum of $\mathbf{L}$ (containing both molecular and fragment positive ions) contains intense peaks with the ratio masses of ions to their charge $m/z$ = 64, 63, 50 and 14.

Physical constants: electrical constant $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$, gravitational acceleration $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
