Problem 4 (Organic chemistry section, problem 1). [Organic “carbon oxides”]

Some carbon compounds, in particular, $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{CO2}$ oxides, are considered in the framework of inorganic chemistry. However, there are quite a lot of oxygen compounds of carbon related to organic substances. Such “carbon oxides” $\mathbf{X1}$ – $\mathbf{X11}$ will be considered in the present problem. In the mild ozonolysis of a elementary substance $\mathbf{A}$, a compound $\mathbf{X1}$ with an oxygen mass fraction of 6.24% is formed. When heated or photolyzed, it loses the oxygen molecule and forms the compound $\mathbf{X2}$.

1. Give the molecular formulas of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{X1}$, and $\mathbf{X2}$. Support the answer with calculations.

Oxygen-containing carbon compounds $\mathbf{X3}$ – $\mathbf{X6}$ are unstable substances of the cyclic structure. $\mathbf{X3}$ and $\mathbf{X6}$ decompose to form the same gas with a higher density than air. Substance $\mathbf{X4}$ is formally a dimer of compound $\mathbf{X5}$. When $\mathbf{X4}$ decomposes, an equimolar mixture of two gases and substance $\mathbf{X5}$ is first formed, which then decomposes to form a mixture of gases of the same density. The simplest dicarboxylic acid $\mathbf{B}$ can be used to obtain $\mathbf{X3}$ – $\mathbf{X5}$, while $\mathbf{X6}$ can be synthesized from isobutyraldehyde:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-4-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-4-fig2.png

2. Give the structural formulas of $\mathbf{B}$ – $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{X3}$ – $\mathbf{X6}$.

3. The adjacent homolog of substance $\mathbf{B}$ also forms a “carbon oxide” when heated with phosphorus(V) oxide. Give a reaction equation providing the structural formulas of organic substances.

Oxygen compounds $\mathbf{X7}$ – $\mathbf{X9}$ have the same empirical formula, corresponding to the lightest carbon oxide, containing two, three, and four cycles in their structures, respectively. All the substances $\mathbf{H}$ – $\mathbf{K}$ have 1 signal each in $^1$H NMR spectra, and in $^{13}$C NMR spectra there are 4 signals for substance $\mathbf{H}$, 2 signals each for compounds $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$, and just 1 signal for $\mathbf{K}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-4-fig3.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-4-fig4.png

4. Give the structural formulas of $\mathbf{H}$ – $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{X7}$ – $\mathbf{X9}$.

5. Adding substance $\mathbf{C}$ to $\mathbf{J}$ and $\mathbf{K}$, two more “carbon oxides” $\mathbf{X10}$ and $\mathbf{X11}$ can be obtained. They have the same empirical formula as $\mathbf{X7}$ – $\mathbf{X9}$ and contain 10 and 12 carbon atoms, respectively. Give the structural formulas of $\mathbf{X10}$ and $\mathbf{X11}$.

Problem 6 (Organic chemistry section, problem 3). [Fenestranes]

In 1972, the structures of polycyclic compounds were proposed, where the sp3 carbon atom should be flattened for steric reasons.

Such compounds are called fenestranes (from Latin window) because its representative [4,4,4,4]-fenestrane ($\ce{C9H12}$) resembles a window (in the case of a completely flat central carbon atom). Due to strong steric hindrance [4,4,4,4]-fenestrane has not been synthesized, although its analog [4,4,4]-fenestrane ($\ce{C8H12}$) – “broken window” exists.

Problem 8 (Life sciences and polymers section, problem 2). [Phenylketonuria and peptide sequencing]

Phenylketonuria is a genetic disease that leads to phenylalanine (Phe) metabolism abnormalities caused by mutations in the gene encoding the enzyme phenylalanine-4-hydroxylase (PAH). As a result of the disease, Phe and toxic products of its transformations accumulate in the body. The biosynthesis of some of the metabolites is shown in the scheme.

One of the mutations in the gene (R408W) responsible for phenylketonuria is associated with a single nucleotide substitution. This leads to a change in the triplet and synthesis of PAH with another amino acid. To determine which amino acid has been substituted, two pentapeptides were isolated and sequenced (determination of the amino acid sequence). b) The Bergmann degradation is a multi-step process. First, the peptides are treated with diphenyl phosphoryl azide (DPPA), affording acyl azides. The latter undergo the Curtius rearrangement. Subsequent treatment with benzyl alcohol gives carbamates, and the hydrogenolysis removes the benzyl protecting group. Finally, acid hydrolysis leads to aldehydes containing the side chain of a terminal amino acid:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-8-fig3.png

Problem 10 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 1). [Inorganic pigments]

«I often think that the night is more alive and more richly colored than the day.»
Vincent Van Gogh

A lot of inorganic compounds, especially of transition metals, have various colors, what can be used to create dyes and pigments. Important properties of inorganic dyes are their high resistance to light, high temperatures, corrosion, and also good coloring ability. Some popular inorganic dyes encrypted below are used by modern industry, others have remained only in historical references and in paintings of the great artists.

Nowadays, titanium or zinc white is often used as a white pigment, however, that was not always the case. Pigment $\mathbf{A}$ is a basic carbonate. The oldest method of producing $\mathbf{A}$ was as follows: thin sheets of metal were placed in special pots, on the bottom of which a small amount of acetic acid was poured. The pots were buried in horse manure, which released a large amount of carbon dioxide during rotting. As a result, a white layer of basic carbonate formed on the metal surface. Then it was cleaned off and used in the manufacture of paint.

1. Determine $\mathbf{A}$, if the thermal decomposition results in the mass loss of 13.7%. $\mathbf{A}$ does not contain crystallization water.

$\mathbf{A}$ stands out for its pure white color and excellent hiding power, yet $\mathbf{A}$ is hardly used today due to its high toxicity. In addition, it slowly darkens in air due to interaction with hydrogen sulfide. One way to restore such a "spoiled" white color is to treat it with hydrogen peroxide.

2. Write down the chemical reactions equations of the last two processes.

A mixed iron oxide is usually used as a black pigment, as well as substance $\mathbf{C}$, which is formed during the incomplete combustion of a hydrogen compound with a density of 0.714 g/L (under normal conditions).

Furthermore, an increase in the mass fraction of $\mathbf{D}$ leads to a color change from yellow to yellow-orange and brown. In nature, $\mathbf{D}$ is also found as a distinct mineral.

Problem 11 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 2). [Compounds of element X, from solids to liquids]

The element $\mathbf{X}$ is part of a large number of compounds and substances that have been used by humanity since ancient times. Most of these compounds under normal conditions are solid, crystalline, non-volatile substances, but there are examples of compounds whose melting points are below room temperature.

An elementary substance $\mathbf{X1}$ with slight heating can actively react with a gaseous, slightly colored substance $\mathbf{A1}$, forming compound $\mathbf{Y1}$. When heated, this substance is able to sublimate, which is often used to separate compounds which are similar in their composition. In parallel with the transition into the gas phase, $\mathbf{Y1}$ undergoes partial decomposition with the formation of compound $\mathbf{Y2}$ and an elementary substance. Substance $\mathbf{Y2}$, being crystalline, does not pass into the gas phase, but it is hygroscopic like $\mathbf{Y1}$. $\mathbf{Y2}$ can be obtained in other ways, for example, by the reaction of $\mathbf{X1}$ with $\mathbf{Y1}$, or by the reaction of $\mathbf{X1}$ with the binary compound $\mathbf{A2}$, the latter includes the lightest element. The molar fractions of element $\mathbf{A}$ in $\mathbf{Y2}$ and $\mathbf{A2}$ differ by 1.334 times, and its mass fraction differ by 1.7377 times.

1. Determine the element $\mathbf{X}$ and the composition of the compounds $\mathbf{Y1}$, $\mathbf{Y2}$, $\mathbf{A1}$ and $\mathbf{A2}$. Confirm your conclusion with calculations. Write down the equations of mentioned reactions. Draw the structure of the $\mathbf{Y1}$ molecule in the gas phase.

In addition to crystalline $\mathbf{Y1}$ and $\mathbf{Y2}$, the element $\mathbf{X}$ may be contained in the substances $\mathbf{Y3}$ and $\mathbf{Y4}$ liquid under ambient conditions.

The compound $\mathbf{Y3}$ can be obtained by the reaction of $\mathbf{Y2}$ with aluminum and a gaseous substance, the latter is isoelectronic to nitrogen molecule. The molecular fragment of the $\mathbf{Y3}$ has one 3-fold axis of symmetry, three 2-fold axes, four mirror planes, but the inversion center is absent. This compound is diamagnetic. Under the hard UV radiation it can form a diamagnetic compound $\mathbf{Y5}$, in which the mass fraction of the element $\mathbf{X}$ is 1.077 times more than the mass fraction in $\mathbf{Y3}$. The molecular fragment of the $\mathbf{Y5}$ compound has two mirror planes of symmetry, one 2-fold axis. The compound $\mathbf{Y3}$ is soluble in many organic solvents. When action of $\mathbf{A1}$ excess on a solution $\mathbf{Y3}$ in tetrachloromethane $\mathbf{Y1}$ is formed.

2. Determine the compounds $\mathbf{Y3}$ and $\mathbf{Y5}$. Confirm your conclusion with calculations. Write down the equations of these reactions. Draw structural formulas of molecular fragments, indicating all bonds.

$\mathbf{Y4}$ is used as polar solvent, catalyst, electrolyte in electrochemical devices. The scheme of obtaining the compound $\mathbf{Y4}$ is presented below in the scheme.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-11-fig1.png

3. Write down the equations of the corresponding reactions, draw the structural formulas of compounds $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{II}$, $\mathbf{Y4}$. Give an example of an inorganic compound containing the same anion as in $\mathbf{Y4}$.

4. For what reason are the compounds $\mathbf{Y3}$ and $\mathbf{Y4}$ fluids at ambient temperature and pressure? Select the answer from the proposed options. Which of these compounds can pass into the gas phase?

$\mathbf{Y3}$ is liquid under ambient conditions due to:
□ molecular structure, weak intermolecular interactions
□ ionic structure, asymmetrical anion
□ atomic type of crystal structure
□ asymmetry of structural molecular fragment
□ low oxidation state of the element X

$\mathbf{Y4}$ is liquid under ambient conditions due to:
□ molecular structure, weak intermolecular interactions
□ asymmetrical cation and charge delocalization in anion
□ atomic type of crystal structure
□ asymmetry of structural molecular fragment
□ low oxidation state of the element X

The following compound can pass to the gas phase:
□ $\mathbf{Y3}$
□ $\mathbf{Y4}$
□ $\mathbf{Y3}$ and $\mathbf{Y4}$
□ none of the compounds can pass to the gas phase

problems.title: [The oxide A2On and its complexes]
problems.problem:
Problem 12 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 3). [The oxide A2On and its complexes]

The compound $\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$ which plays an important role in the transmission of nerve signals, is obtained in the form of a bluish gas by the action of $\ce{Cr2O3}$ on a mixture of potassium salts ($3\mathrm{K}\mathbf{A}\mathrm{O}_2 + \mathrm{K}\mathbf{A}\mathrm{O}_3$). Pure $\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$ is colorless paramagnetic gas with $l_{\mathbf{A}\text{–O}} = 0.115\,\mathrm{nm}$, which condenses below $-164\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ into a colorless diamagnetic solid mixture of isomers $\mathbf{B}$: $\mathbf{B1}$ ($l_{\mathbf{A}\text{–O}} = 0.112$ и $0.240\,\mathrm{nm}$) and $\mathbf{B2}$ ($l_{\mathbf{A}\text{–O}} = 0.112\,\mathrm{nm}$; $l_{\mathbf{A}\text{–}\mathbf{A}} = 0.218\,\mathrm{nm}$; cis-isomer). In 1978 Laane obtained red modification $\mathbf{B3}$ ($l_{\mathbf{A}\text{–O}} = 0.119\,\mathrm{nm}$ and $0.174\,\mathrm{nm}$, $\angle\mathbf{A}\mathrm{O}\mathbf{A} = 107^\circ$) by $\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$ condensation in the presence of Lewis acids.

1. Decode $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$ and $\mathbf{B}$, if the mass fraction $w_\mathbf{A}$ in $\mathrm{K}\mathbf{A}\mathrm{O}_2$ and $\mathrm{K}\mathbf{A}\mathrm{O}_3$ differs by 2.61%. Write down the equation for the $\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$ synthesis reaction and the reaction explaining the bluish color of the gas.

2. Calculate the content of $\mathbf{B}$ (mol. %) in the gas at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1 atm, if $\Delta_\mathrm{f}G^\circ$, kJ/mol: 12.35 ($\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$) and 39.00 ($\mathbf{B}$). Draw the structural formulas of $\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$ (MO method) and modifications of $\mathbf{B}$.

Being in complexes monodentate $\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$ can donate an electron to the central Me atom and act as either σ-donor (1), or both σ-donor and π-acceptor (2), forming linear ($\mathbf{X}$) fragment Me$\mathbf{A}$O (170-180°), and can be one-electron (3), forming bent ($\mathbf{Y}$) fragment Me$\mathbf{A}$O (120-140°).

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{Complex} & \angle\mathrm{Me}\mathbf{A}\mathrm{O} & l_{\mathrm{Me}\text{–}\mathbf{A}},\ \mathrm{nm} & l_{\mathbf{A}\text{–O}},\ \mathrm{nm} & \nu\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\ \text{in IR-spectrum} \\ \hline [\mathrm{Fe(CN)_5}\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n]^{2-} & 178 & 0.166 & 0.112 & 1935 \\ \hline [\mathrm{IrCl(CO)(PPh_3)_2}\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n]^{+} & 124 & 0.197 & 0.119 & 1680 \\ \hline [\mathrm{RuCl(PPh_3)_2}(\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n)_2]^{+} & 178;\ 138 & 0.186;\ 0.172 & 0.118;\ 0.114 & 1845;\ 1687 \end{array}$$

3. Draw fragments 1-3 and the structural formulas of the complexes given in the table, assuming that Me in $d^2sp^3$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}sp^3$ hybridization, $\angle\mathrm{Me(PPh_3)_2} \sim 180^\circ$, and one ligand $\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$ is in the axial position.

In 1979, Schoonover and Eisenberg showed that there is equilibrium $\mathbf{X} \rightleftarrows \mathbf{Y}$ in solution. If $\mathbf{A}_2\mathrm{O}_n$ is passed through a solution of green $\ce{MeCl3}$ (3.73 g) in $\ce{CH3OH + N(C2H5)3}$ until complete sedimentation of $\mathrm{CH_3O}\mathbf{A}\mathrm{O}$, $\ce{PPh3}$ (0.025 mol) is added until a brown-red solution of the $\mathbf{E}^+$ cation (7.82 g, yield 80%, $w_\mathrm{Cl} = 4.54\%$), then salts of $\mathbf{E}$An would be obtained by the action of $\ce{BF4^-}$ and $\ce{PF6^-}$. In their solution in THF at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\ce{Cl^-}$ can be replaced with $\ce{C3H5^-}$ by action of $\ce{Sn(C3H5)4}$ with formation of light brown salt $\mathbf{D}\ce{PF6}$ ($\nu = 1763\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) and red-brown one $\mathbf{D}\ce{BF4}$ ($\nu = 1631\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$).

4. Decode mononuclear cations $\mathbf{E}^+$ and $\mathbf{D}^+$ in the salts and depict the structural formulas of $\mathbf{D}^+$ ($\ce{PPh3}$ – triphenylphosphine, $\ce{C3H5}$ – trihaptoligand $\eta^3$-).

In a solution of any of the salts with $\mathbf{D}^+$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, bands 1760 and $1630\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ of the same intensity are fixed ($I$), at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the intensity of the $1760\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ band increases by 31%, and the sum of the intensities of the two bands does not depend on temperature.

5. Estimate $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ of the transition $\mathbf{Y} \rightleftarrows \mathbf{X}$, using the intensities in the IR spectrum and the Van't Hoff equation.

problems.title: [Chemical analysis of paints]
problems.problem:
Problem 13 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 1). [Chemical analysis of paints]

Art is the highest manifestation of power in man.
L.N. Tolstoy (1828-1890)

An important and interesting application of chemical analysis is painting. Paints contain a pigment (most often it is an inorganic mineral) and a binder (oil in the case of oil paints). Analysis of paints is necessary for the purpose of restoration or verification of authenticity of a painting.

The main white pigments in paints are white lead paint $\ce{Pb2(OH)2CO3}$, zinc white paint $\ce{ZnO}$ and barium white $\ce{BaSO4}$. To determine the type of white paint, it is sufficient to dissolve it in a strong acid: two out of the three paints dissolve, and the insoluble one can be dissolved by fusion with sodium carbonate.

1. Arrange the white paints in the descending order of solubility in 0.1 M strong acid. Confirm this sequence by calculating the solubility $S$ of each of the three paints in acid, assuming that pH = 1 and it is not changing during dissolution: $K_\mathrm{S}(\ce{BaSO4}) = 1.1\cdot10^{-10}$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1}(\ce{H2SO4}) = -6.3$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2}(\ce{H2SO4}) = 1.9$, $K_\mathrm{S}(\ce{Pb2(OH)2CO3}) = 3.5\cdot10^{-46}$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1}(\ce{H2CO3}) = 6.35$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2}(\ce{H2CO3}) = 10.35$, $K_\mathrm{S}(\ce{Zn(OH)2}) = 1.2\cdot10^{-17}$.

After the dissolution of white paints, the following reagents can be used to recognize them: $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ (a yellow precipitate forms, and its amount increases when sodium acetate is added), KI (a yellow precipitate forms that dissolves easily in hot water; if the solution is cooled, the precipitate forms again, sometimes it is called "golden rain"), $\ce{(NH4)2[Hg(SCN)4] + CuSO4}$ (violet precipitate).

2. Match the identified cations and reagents, write down the corresponding reaction equations.

3. Why does the amount of the first yellow precipitate increase with the addition of sodium acetate?

Knowing the nature of the white paint is important for restoring paintings or verifying their authenticity. For example, despite the beautiful color of white lead, it will eventually turn gray and even black in air (the presence of traces of a gas with a close molecular weight to oxygen). To restore the white color, restorers use a solution of hydrogen peroxide.

4. Write the appropriate reaction equations.

In the 16th-17th centuries, paints often contained such harmful elements as lead (in white paints and pigments) and arsenic, which was a component of such infamous wallpaper paints as "Scheele green" or "Paris Green" with an amazing green tint but very toxic due to arsine release in a humid atmosphere.

5. Paris Green is a mixed salt, it is obtained by the interaction of pigment “Verdigris” ($\mathrm{CuAc_2}$) with arsenic(III) oxide.
a) Write down the reaction of Paris Green formation, if both components of the mixed salt contain copper(II) as cation.
b) When alkali are added, the Paris Green suspension changes color to red-orange. Write down the redox reaction equation, circle the compound(s) responsible for the color of the mixture.
c) Determine the formula of Paris Green if the amount of copper in the product obtained after treatment with alkali is equal to the amount of arsenite. The redox reaction is quantitative.

The amount of arsenic can be determined by the following method: a wallpaper sample ($100\,\mathrm{cm^2}$) is dissolved in fuming nitric acid, the volume of the solution is adjusted to 500 mL, and an aliquot of the solution (100 mL) is titrated with sodium bromate of a concentration of 0.002 M to the equivalence point (1.65 mL).

6. Determine what fold the amount of arsine exceeds the maximum permissible concentration ($0.1\,\mathrm{mg/m^3}$) in a room with the wall area of $50\,\mathrm{m^2}$, if the volume of the room is $60\,\mathrm{m^3}$, assuming that 1/1000 of all arsenic has turned into arsine.

Other component of paints are oils, esters of glycerol, characterized by the ability to dry, which in turn is related to the number of C=C bonds in the oil: the more of them, the faster the paint dries due to polymerization. The number of C=C bonds is characterized by the iodine number (the mass of iodine reacting with 100 g of oil). With the iodine number less than 115, the oil does not dry out, 115–130 it is semi-drying and more than 130 – well drying.

The iodine number can be determined by iodometric titration: a sample of oil (1.500 mL, $\rho = 0.92\,\mathrm{g/mL}$) is diluted with chloroform, and a known amount of bromine is added in excess. After the reaction is completed, potassium iodide is added to the mixture, the resulting iodine is titrated with a solution of sodium thiosulfate prepared using 24.81 g of salt pentahydrate in 500 mL of solution. A similar blank experiment is carried out without oil. For the titration of the first solution, 6.75 mL of thiosulfate solution was used, and for the titration of the blank sample, 56.25 mL of the same solution was spent.

7. Write down all the equations of the reactions that take place; instead of oil, write R–CH=CH–R for simplicity.

8. Calculate the iodine number and judge the suitability of the oil for use in a paint formulation.

problems.title: [Complexation of a carbocyanine dye with a surfactant]
problems.problem:
Problem 14 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 2). [Complexation of a carbocyanine dye with a surfactant]

The spectroscopic properties of dyes (absorption of light, fluorescence, etc.) can change markedly when interacting with surfactants. For example, carbocyanine $\mathbf{Z}$ in the presence of sodium $n$-dodecyl sulfate (SDS) changes its absorption spectrum as follows (1 - in the presence of SDS, 2 - without SDS):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-14-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-14-fig2.png

Dodecyl sulfate does not absorb in this range of the spectrum.

1. Choose the wavelength at which it is most convenient to observe the complexation of the dye with the surfactant.

To describe the equilibrium in solution, it is sufficient to apply the mass action law (the expression for the constant $K$ of the corresponding equilibrium), the law of conservation of matter (material balance) and the Bouguer-Lambert-Beer law $A = \varepsilon[\mathrm{X}]l$, where $A$ is absorbance, $\varepsilon$ is the molar absorption coefficient of X; [X] is the equilibrium concentration of X (mol/L), $l$ is the optical path of the cell (cm).

2. a) For the complexation reaction presented in the form: $\mathrm{Z} + n\mathrm{SDS} = \mathrm{Z(SDS)}_n$, write down the expression for the equilibrium constant. Designate the total concentration Z as $c(\mathrm{Z})$ and the equilibrium concentration as [Z]. Write down the expression for the material balance of the dye (Ignore the material balance for SDS, because the surfactant concentration is significantly higher than the dye concentration.)
b) Write the experimental value of absorbance $A$ as the absorbance of the $\mathrm{Z(SDS)}_n$ complex according to the Bouguer–Lambert–Beer law for a cell with $l = 1$ cm (neglect the absorbance of the free dye).

3. a) From the written equations, obtain an expression relating the optical density $A$, the molar absorption coefficient of the complex $\varepsilon$, the total concentrations of the dye $c(\mathrm{Z})$ and dodecyl sulfate $c(\mathrm{SDS})$ and the complex formation constant $K$.
b) Bring the resulting expression to the form $y = y_0 + Bx$, where $y = 1/A$, and $x = 1/c(\mathrm{SDS})^n$.

4. The following values of absorbances were obtained experimentally in the presence of various concentrations of SDS ($l = 1$ cm; the total dye concentration $c(\mathrm{Z})$ is constant and equal to $1\cdot10^{-5}$ M):

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} c_\mathrm{SDS},\ \mathrm{M} & 2.0\cdot10^{-4} & 2.9\cdot10^{-4} & 3.8\cdot10^{-4} & 6.0\cdot10^{-4} \\ \hline A & 0.10 & 0.20 & 0.33 & 0.67 \end{array}$$

a) Plot the graphs $1/A$ – $1/(c_\mathrm{SDS})^n$ for n = 1, 2, and 3.
b) Determine the composition of the complex.
c) How to calculate the value of the complex formation constant? Give the formula (do not give a numerical value).

problems.title: [Extraction of iodine in the presence of halide ions]
problems.problem:
Problem 15 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 3). [Extraction of iodine in the presence of halide ions]

Extraction is a method of separating substances based on their different distribution between two immiscible solvents (phases). For example, when iodine is extracted from the aqueous phase with an organic solvent, an equilibrium described by the distribution constant is established:

$$\ce{I2_{(aq)} <=> I2_{(org)}} \qquad K_D = \frac{[\ce{I2}]_{org}}{[\ce{I2}]_{aq}}.$$

The following organic substances were added to the saturated aqueous iodine solution: tetrachloromethane, cyclohexene, benzene, ethyl alcohol, starch, isoamyl alcohol.

1. Assign the added organic substance with the observed effect: a) separation into two phases, the upper one is colored purple; b) separation into two phases, the lower one is colored purple; c) dark blue solution; d) brown solution; e) separation into two phases, the upper one is colored brown; f) separation into two phases, the upper one turns purple, which fades over time, and the third phase forms on the bottom.

The iodine solubility in water is increased in the presence of halide ions due to the formation of complex ions of type $\ce{I2X^-}$, where X = F, Cl, Br, I, according to the equation:

$$\ce{I2_{(aq)} + X^-_{(aq)} <=> I2X^-_{(aq)}} \qquad K_X = \frac{[\ce{I2X^-}]_{aq}}{[\ce{I2}]_{aq}[\ce{X^-}]_{aq}}.$$

The $D_X$ distribution coefficient is the ratio of the sums of all forms concentrations of the extracted substance in the organic phase to the aqueous. When extracting an iodine solution in the presence of halide ions, only neutrally charged iodine molecules are transferred into the organic phase.

2. Get an expression that explains the linear correlation $\dfrac{1}{D_X} = a + b[\ce{X^-}]_{aq}$. How are the constants $K_D$ and $K_X$ related to coefficients $a$ and $b$?

To determine the equilibrium constants $K_D$ and $K_X$, a series of experiments was conducted to extract iodine from some organic solvent into aqueous solutions of potassium halides with a known salt concentration. After separating the phases, the iodine concentrations were determined by titration with a standard sodium thiosulfate solution.

3. Derive the expression for the relation of $D_X$ to the volumes of thiosulfate $V(\ce{Na2S2O3})_{aq}$ and $V(\ce{Na2S2O3})_{org}$, which went to titration of aliquots of the aqueous and organic phases with volumes $V_{aq}$ and $V_{org}$, respectively.

The graph shows the dependencies of $1/D_X$ on the initial concentration of three halide ions in the aqueous phase (cases $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{C}$). It is known that the stability of $\ce{I2X^-}$ complexes increases in the series of $\ce{I2F^-} < \ce{I2Cl^-} < \ce{I2Br^-} < \ce{I3^-}$, and in the case of one of the halides (case $\mathbf{D}$), dependence $1/D_X$ from $[\ce{X^-}]_0$ stops to be linear.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2022-2-15-fig1.png

4. What approximation should be allowed for the expression in question 2 to explain the linear dependence of $1/D_X$ also on $[\ce{X^-}]_0$? Please provide your calculations.
$K_X[\ce{I2}]_{aq} \ll 1$ $\qquad$ $K_X[\ce{I2}]_{aq} \approx 1$ $\qquad$ $K_X[\ce{I2}]_{aq} \gg 1$

5. Assign the cases $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{D}$ to the corresponding halides $\ce{F^-}$, $\ce{Cl^-}$, $\ce{Br^-}$ and $\ce{I^-}$.

6. Estimate the values of $K_D$ and $K_X$ for the three halides $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{C}$.

problems.title: [Sparkling water and Henry's law]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [Sparkling water and Henry's law]

Natural carbonated water has been known for a long time. The effort to produce artificial sparkling water (SW) using bicarbonates or dissolving $\ce{CO2}$ under pressure was successful in 1740–1760. Due to the widespread demand, industrial production began in 1783. The dissolution of $\ce{CO2}$ in water is described by Henry's law, which states that the molar concentration of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the solution: $C = k_\mathrm{H}\cdot P$, where $k_\mathrm{H}$ – Henry's temperature-dependent constant according to Arrhenius' law:

$$k_\mathrm{H}(T) = k_\mathrm{H}(298\,\mathrm{K})\exp\left[-\frac{\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{diss}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T}-\frac{1}{298}\right)\right],$$

where $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{diss}$ – enthalpy of dissolution equal to for $\ce{CO2}$ in water $-19.9\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$, $k_\mathrm{H}(298\,\mathrm{K}) = 3.3\cdot10^{-2}\,\mathrm{M\cdot atm^{-1}}$.

Artificial SW contains considerably more gas than natural, and is divided into low-, medium- and high-gas content by mass $\ce{CO2}$ content in the ranges of 0.2–0.3, 0.3–0.4 and >0.4%, respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-1-1-fig1.png

Figure 1

1. Determine the category of a 500 mL SW that is saturated with carbon dioxide at a pressure of 2 atm and temperature $5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

2. Obtain an expression for the pressure of $\ce{CO2}$ in the closed bottle shown in Fig. 1. Region I has volume $V_\mathrm{gas}$ and is filled with ideal gas, region II is carbonated water with volume $V_\mathrm{liq}$ and the concentration of carbon dioxide is determined by Henry's law. The total amount (mol) of $\ce{CO2}$ is determined by the contribution of gaseous and aqueous phases: $n_\Sigma = n_\mathrm{gas} + n_\mathrm{liq}$.

3. Using the expression obtained in step 2, calculate the pressure of carbon dioxide in a closed bottle (Fig. 1) containing 500 mL of SW at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The diameter of the bottle neck $d = 28\,\mathrm{mm}$, $h = 4\,\mathrm{cm}$, take $n_\Sigma(\ce{CO2})$ to be 45 mmol.

4. Calculate the pH of pure water at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in contact with air. Partial pressure of $\ce{CO2}$ in the air $3.0\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{atm}$. Accept that $[\ce{H+}] \approx [\ce{HCO3^-}]$, and do not take into account the contribution to the pH value of the dissociation of the carbonic acid in the second step.

$$\ce{CO2 + H2O <=> H2CO3}\qquad K = 3.3\cdot10^{-2}\,\mathrm{M\cdot atm^{-1}},$$

$$\ce{H2CO3 <=> H+ + HCO3^-}\qquad k_\mathrm{a1}(\ce{H2CO3}) = 4.3\cdot10^{-7}.$$

5. How will the radius of a carbon dioxide bubble rising from the bottom of a natural spring 30 m deep increase? The hydrostatic pressure increases linearly with depth: $P = P_\mathrm{atm} + \rho_{\ce{H2O}}gh$. The initial bubble radius is 0.4 mm. Assume that the temperatures at the bottom and the surface of the spring are the same.

Physical constants: $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}$, $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m\cdot c^{-2}}$.

Problem 3. [Two-dimensional particles and adsorption on graphite]

Two-dimensional particles are characterized by thickness as well as length and width (size in the particle plane). Other important parameters of the particles are specific surface area (the ratio between the particle surface area and its mass) and dispersity (the ratio between the particle surface area and its volume).

1. For a flat square (length is equal to width) particle, write the expressions relating its specific surface area $S_\mathrm{sp}$ and dispersity $D$ with the thickness $d$, square side length $a$, and the particle density $\rho$.

2. At which $a/d$ ratios dispersity of the flat square particle is independent of the length and width (the difference in the dispersities calculated accounting for and neglecting $a$ does not exceed 1%)?

Study of adsorption at flat graphite particles revealed that the maximum amount of the adsorbate per 1 g of graphite is $10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol}$. Length of the C–C bond in the graphite layer is 0.142 nm, graphite density is $2.15\,\mathrm{g\cdot cm^{-3}}$. Cross-section area of the adsorbate molecule is $0.025\,\mathrm{nm^2}$.

3. Calculate specific surface area of graphene (a single graphite layer), available for the adsorption.

4. Calculate maximum amount of the adsorbate which can be bound by 1 g of graphene. If you have failed to get numeric answer in question 3, denote the corresponding value as $x$.

5. Write the equation relating the maximum amount of the adsorbate which can be bound by 1 g of multilayered graphite with the number of the layers in the nanoparticles $n$. If you have failed to get numeric answer in question 4, denote the corresponding value as $y$. Calculate the number of layers in the considered graphite nanoparticles. Neglect the adsorption at the side surface and penetration of the adsorbate between the graphite layers.

6. Determine the thickness of the considered graphite nanoparticles. If you have failed to get numeric answer in question 5, denote the corresponding value as $z$.

problems.title: [Elements X and Y of the same period]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [Elements X and Y of the same period]

Elements $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are located in the same period of the Periodic Table. Both the simple substance of $\mathbf{X}$ and one of the allotropic modifications of $\mathbf{Y}$ have characteristic red-orange colors. Hydrolysis of the binary compound of Al with $\mathbf{Y}$ leads to the emission of poisonous gas $\mathbf{Y1}$ with a strong unpleasant odor. $\mathbf{Y1}$ exhibits reducing properties. Thus, when $\mathbf{Y1}$ is passed into a solution of a salt obtained by heating $\mathbf{X}$ in concentrated sulfuric acid, a colored precipitate $\mathbf{X1}$ is formed among the reaction products. Combustion of $\mathbf{Y1}$ in an excess of oxygen leads to the production of a white crystalline (NC) substance $\mathbf{Y2}$, which is highly soluble in water to form a solution of $\mathbf{Y3}$. A concentrated hydrogen peroxide solution oxidizes the $\mathbf{Y3}$ solution to $\mathbf{Y4}$.

$\mathbf{Y2}$ can also be obtained by oxidizing $\mathbf{Y}$ substance with gas $\mathbf{G}$ ($D_\mathrm{He} = 11.5$) under heating. Fusion of equal amounts of $\mathbf{Y2}$ with an oxide of $\mathbf{X}$ element, in which the mass fraction of oxygen is 4 times less than the mass fraction of $\mathbf{X}$, leads to the formation of $\mathbf{X2}$ substance, which occurs in nature as a mineral. $\mathbf{X2}$ reacts with ammonia gas under heating to form $\mathbf{X3}$. $\mathbf{X3}$ – a binary compound of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$.

1. Identify unknown substances $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{X1}$ – $\mathbf{X3}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Y1}$ – $\mathbf{Y4}$, $\mathbf{G}$, and also write down the equations of chemical reactions. It is known that the qualitative composition of $\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{X3}$ is the same.

Gradual dehydration of $\mathbf{Y4}$ with phosphorus oxide $\ce{P2O5}$ first leads to the formation of acid $\mathbf{Y5}$ ($\omega(\mathrm{O}) = 0.4117$, $\omega(\mathbf{Y}) = 0.5809$), and $\mathbf{Y6}$ is formed at the final stage. $\mathbf{Y6}$ has a molecular structure, the molar mass of its structural unit lies in the range of 400–520 g/mol.

2. Identify the composition of $\mathbf{Y5}$ and $\mathbf{Y6}$, and also draw their structure.

problems.title: [Slaked lime and nitric acid]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Slaked lime and nitric acid]

A weight of slaked lime, stored for some time in air, was dried at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to a constant weight and a sample weighing 34.85 g was obtained, which was completely dissolved in $85.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of nitric acid solution (density $1138\,\mathrm{g/dm^3}$). The resulting solution was evaporated double by weight and cooled to $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In this case, a precipitate of substance $\mathbf{A}$ was formed weighing 24.98 g. The resulting filtrate weighing 40.02 g was again evaporated by a quarter and after cooling to $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, an additional 26.64 g of $\mathbf{A}$ was obtained. The resulting portions of $\mathbf{A}$ were combined and kept for a long time at $220\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ drying oven, as a result of which the mass decreased by 30.50% and substance $\mathbf{B}$ was formed.

Half of the obtained substance $\mathbf{B}$ was placed in a quartz ampoule and heated at a rate of $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C/min}$ to $580\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and kept at this temperature until the mass change ceased. In this case, $26.52\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of gas was obtained (the volume was measured at $580\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 102.3 kPa). With the second half of $\mathbf{B}$, the same experiment was carried out, but the final temperature was $600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In this case, $22.99\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ of gas was released (the volume was measured at $600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 103.5 kPa). In each of the experiments, the mass of the final solid residue $\mathbf{C}$ was 34.2% of the initial one.

1. Give the equations of the reaction that occurs when a sample of lime is dissolved in nitric acid.

2. Establish the composition of substances $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

3. Calculate the mass fraction of impurities in the dry lime sample.

4. Make the reaction equations that occur when $\mathbf{B}$ is heated to $580\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Bring your calculations.

problems.title: [Nafion and its cheaper analog]
problems.problem:
Problem 6. [Nafion and its cheaper analog]

Nafion is a polymer characterized by both ion-exchange properties and chemical resistance. It is thus used as a material for production of semipermeable membranes, which let through the molecules of low-molecular compounds and retain polymers. The equivalent weight (mass of the material per 1 mol of ionic groups) depending on the content ($y$) and length ($z$) of the pendant substituents is an important parameter of Nafion.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-1-6-fig1.png

1. Calculate the equivalent weight of Nafion at $x = 100$, $y = 50$, $z = 3$.

2. Nafion with the equivalent weight of 1100 g/mol and $z = 1$ is most suitable for the membranes production. Calculate the average polymerization degree of the backbone of such macromolecules, if each contains 55 ionic groups.

Once swollen in water, the membrane described in i. 2 contains 30% of $\ce{H2O}$ by mass with the density of $1.45\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. The membrane is prepared via casting of the 15% polymer solution in an alcohol with the density of $1.1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

3. Calculate the solution volume needed to prepare the swollen membrane of A4 size (210×297 mm) with the thickness of $120\,\mathrm{\mu m}$.

The prepared membrane was used to remove the salt present in a solution of lysozyme (globular protein, $M$ 14300 g/mol) by dialysis. To do so, 100 mL of the starting lysozyme solution with the protein concentration of 1 mmol/L and sodium chloride concentration of 4 mol/L was separated from 1 L of distilled water (take the salt concentration in the latter as 0) by a piece of the Nafion membrane with the diameter of 10 cm.

4. Calculate the fraction of the sodium chloride (referred to the starting mixture with the protein) removed after 5 min of dialysis (assume that the sodium chloride flow across the membrane is constant and equals $10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol/(cm^2\cdot s)}$.

5. Calculate the mass fraction of sodium chloride in the dried mixture with the protein after three cycles of dialysis (each time the dialysis was conducted until equilibrium followed by an exchange of the obtained solution of the salt with 1 L of distilled water). Neglect both the water flux across the membrane and the salt content inside it.

High price turns out to be a serious drawback of Nafion. If an enhanced chemical resistance of the membrane is not important, Nafion can be substituted by a cheaper, still less stable analog. Synthesis of such an alternative material $\mathbf{B}$ is given on the scheme below. The polymer $\mathbf{A}$ was obtained by polymerization of 4,4'-difluorobenzophenone with hydroquinone in the presence of $\ce{Na2CO3}$, and the polymer $\mathbf{B}$ by treatment of $\mathbf{A}$ with concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-1-6-fig2.png

6. Draw the structure of the repeat unit of $\mathbf{A}$.

7. Calculate the equivalent weight of $\mathbf{B}$ (neglect the terminal groups), if the mass fraction of sulfur in it equals 2.13%.

problems.title: [Bromatometric titration of anilines and phenols]
problems.problem:
Problem 7. [Bromatometric titration of anilines and phenols]

Bromatometric titration is used to determine amounts of anilines and phenols. The method is based on the bromination of these compounds into the aromatic ring. For example, when aniline is brominated, 2,4,6-tribromaniline is formed.

1. Write the equation for this reaction, indicate the amount of bromine consumed per mole of aniline.

2. When disubstituted derivatives are brominated, the result depends on the mutual arrangement of the substituents. Thus, aqueous solutions of 1,3- and 1,4-dihydroxybenzenes (resorcinol and hydroquinone) containing potassium bromide and acid were titrated with a bromate solution until a non-vanishing color of bromine appeared, after which an excess of KI was introduced and the released iodine was titrated with thiosulfate. It was found that one of the isomers absorbed 3 mol of bromine per mol of analyte (case $a$), while in the case of the other isomer, the consumption of bromine was significantly lower (case $b$). Which of the cases refers to resorcinol, and which one to hydroquinone? Write down the structures of their bromination products.

3. Predict the products of a titration with a bromide-bromate mixture of 2,4-dimethylaniline and 2,5-dimethylaniline. Specify the amount of bromine consumed per mole of analyte for these compounds.

4. Para-substituted anilines and phenols react with bromine in more complicated way. The conditions for quantitative determination have been found (control of temperature, acidity, and interaction time). Thus, 4-aminobenzenesulfonic acid (sulfanilic acid) reacts with 2 mol of bromine at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and with 3 mol at $20$–$25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. In the latter case, the sulfo group is replaced by bromine. Give the structures of bromination products for $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $20$–$25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

5. Bromatometry is used for the analysis of pharmaceutical preparations. To determine sulfapyridine (Fig.), one of the first sulfanilamide antibiotics, an excess of potassium bromide, 5.0 ml of a 1.00 M potassium bromate solution and acid were added to the analyte solution placed in a 50.0 ml flask. The flask was closed with a stopper, after 5 min an aliquot of 5.0 ml was taken.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-1-7-fig1.png

Next, an excess of KI was added to the aliquon and it was titrated with a 0.100 M solution of thiosulfate. Determine the initial mass of sulfapyridine if 12.0 ml of titrant was used. It is known that sulfapyridine is brominated similarly to sulfanilic acid, and the reaction proceeds with strict observance of stoichiometry. Write down the structure of the sulfapyridine bromination product.

problems.title: [Lead-acid batteries and desulfation]
problems.problem:
Problem 8. [Lead-acid batteries and desulfation]

Lead-acid batteries are the most common type of car batteries. The operation of such batteries is based on the electrochemical transformation of lead metal present in the cathode plates and powdered lead dioxide placed in the anode plates, in the presence of an electrolyte, an aqueous solution of sulfuric acid.

1. Write down half-reactions for the main processes occurring at the cathode and anode and the overall reaction during discharge.

2. At the end of battery charging, when insufficient lead compounds are available and current continues to flow through the battery, there can be a so-called "boiling" of the battery, which is dangerous and may result in explosion. What processes correspond to "boiling" and a potential explosion? Write down the reactions.

3. One of the significant problems of such batteries is sulfation – the accumulation of insoluble precipitate during non-optimal charge-discharge cycles, which has a negative effect on the electrochemical processes. What is this precipitate?

4. The technical service of such batteries includes desulfation for removing the precipitate. For example, this can be done by draining the electrolyte from the battery, rinsing it with water, and filling it with a solution which can be prepared by diluting 45 mL of 25% (w/w) ammonia and 20 g of Trilon B (EDTA, $\ce{Na2H2Y}$) with water to yield 1 L of solution. What chemical reaction is this method based on? Write down the main equilibria that exist in such a system.

5. Calculate the solubility of the sulfation-causing precipitate in the described desulfation solution.

6. How much precipitate can be removed from the battery plates by a single application of this solution?

For reference: Solubility product of lead sulfate: $K_\mathrm{s}^0 = 2.2\cdot10^{-8}$. The complexation constant of lead with EDTA: $\beta = [\ce{PbY^{2-}}]/([\ce{Pb^{2+}}][\ce{Y^{4-}}]) = 1\cdot10^{18}$; $K_\mathrm{b}(\ce{NH3}) = 1.76\cdot10^{-5}$. Density of 25 w/w % solution of ammonia: 0.9070 g/mL. The molar weight of EDTA: 336 g/mol. Mole fractions of the EDTA $\ce{Y^{4-}}$ form:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{pH} & \alpha(\ce{Y^{4-}}) & \text{pH} & \alpha(\ce{Y^{4-}}) & \text{pH} & \alpha(\ce{Y^{4-}}) \\ \hline 10.00 & 0.36 & 10.75 & 0.76 & 11.50 & 0.95 \\ \hline 10.25 & 0.49 & 11.00 & 0.85 & 11.75 & 0.97 \\ \hline 10.50 & 0.64 & 11.25 & 0.91 & 12.00 & 0.98 \end{array}$$

problems.title: [Thiocarboxylic acids and the Willgerodt–Kindler reaction]
problems.problem:

Thio- ($\mathbf{I}$) and dithiocarboxylic ($\mathbf{II}$) acids are sulfur-containing analogs of carboxylic acids in which one or two oxygen atoms of the carboxyl group are replaced by sulfur. Thiocarboxylic acids exist as a mixture of tautomers $\mathbf{Ia}$ and $\mathbf{Ib}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-2-1-fig1.png

The Wilgerodt-Kindler (WK) reaction allows to obtain compounds containing a thiocarbonyl group. One of the reactants in the WK reaction is $\mathbf{D}$ which is obtained according to the scheme:

The WK reaction can be demonstrated by the example of the interaction of ketone $\mathbf{E}$ ($\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_n\mathrm{O}$) with $\mathbf{D}$ in the presence of sulfur. problems.title: [Cis–trans isomerization of Me(en)₂Cl₂⁺ and ion pairs]
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (Physical chemistry section, problem 1). [Cis–trans isomerization of Me(en)₂Cl₂⁺ and ion pairs]

Isomerization cis-$\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+ \leftrightarrows$ trans-$\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+$ can be carried out according to the scheme: green $\mathbf{A}$ → violet $\mathbf{B}$ → green $\mathbf{D}$ → green $\mathbf{A}$.

1. Decipher chlorides $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ if they contain 42% ethylendiamine (en), cation $\mathbf{A}$ has the element of symmetry $I$ (center of inversion), but $\mathbf{B}$ has no such symmetry element.

Drew and Patt suggested that the $\mathbf{Me}$–N bond is broken during isomerization and $\mathbf{D}$ contains the en–$\ce{H+}$ cation. But the XRD and $^1$H NMR methods showed the presence of another cation in solid $\mathbf{D}$ - $\ce{H5O2+}$.

2. Decipher $\mathbf{D}$, if after the loss of 10% HCl and $\ce{H2O}$, it turns into $\mathbf{A}$.

Later, Brown established that an ion pair is formed during isomerization, and the observed constant ($k_\mathrm{obs}$) at $[\ce{Cl-}] > 0.1\,\mathrm{mol\cdot l^{-1}}$ does not depend on $[\ce{Cl-}]$. In 1965 Bosnich, Ingold and Tobe studied isomerization in $\ce{CH3OH}$ at $35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $[\ce{Cl-}] = 0 - 0.1\,\mathrm{mol\cdot l^{-1}}$ and found that $k_\mathrm{obs}$ depends on $[\ce{Cl-}]$ (Table).

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c} [\ce{Cl-}]\cdot10^2,\ \mathrm{mol\cdot l^{-1}} & 0 & 0.5 & 1.0 & 5.0 & 7.5 & 10 \\ \hline k_\mathrm{obs}\cdot10^3,\ \mathrm{min^{-1}} & 3.2 & 5.5 & 6.1 & 6.9 & 7.0 & 7.1 \end{array}$$

They proposed an equation $k_\mathrm{obs} = (k_\mathrm{o} + k_\mathrm{ip}K[\ce{Cl-}])/(1 + K[\ce{Cl-}])$ describing the two stream mechanism of isomerization:

$$\begin{array}{lll} \text{1st stream:} & \text{cis-}\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+ \rightarrow \text{trans-}\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+ & (k_\mathrm{o}); \\ \text{2st stream:} & \text{cis-}\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+ + \mathrm{Cl}^- \leftrightarrows \text{cis-}\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+{,}\mathrm{Cl}^- & (K); \\ & \text{cis-}\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+{,}\mathrm{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{trans-}\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+{,}\mathrm{Cl}^- & (k_\mathrm{ip}); \\ & \text{trans-}\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+{,}\mathrm{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{trans-}\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+ + \mathrm{Cl}^- & (k_1). \end{array}$$

3. Calculate $k_\mathrm{o}$, $k_\mathrm{ip}$, $K$ using $[\ce{Cl-}] = 0.5\cdot10^{-2}$ and $7.5\ 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\cdot l^{-1}}$.

4. State the conditions under which $k_\mathrm{obs}$ matches Brown’s data. Confirm this by calculating $k_\mathrm{obs}$ for $[\ce{Cl-}] = 0.5$ and $1.0\,\mathrm{mol\cdot l^{-1}}$.

The calculated value of $K$ turned out to be too large for an ion pair with $z = |1|$, overlooked by Bosnich, Ingold и Tobe. The value of $K$ can be estimated from the equation $\Delta G^\circ = (z_+\cdot z_-\cdot e^2\cdot N_\mathrm{A})/(4\pi\cdot\varepsilon_\mathrm{o}\cdot\varepsilon\cdot r) = -RT\ln K$, where $e = 1.602\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, $\varepsilon_\mathrm{o} = 8.854\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F\cdot m^{-1}}$ - the electric constant, $\varepsilon = 32$ – the dielectric constant of $\ce{CH3OH}$, $r = 6.2\cdot10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$ – distance between ions in a pair.

5. Calculate $\Delta G^\circ$ and $K$ for $\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+{,}\mathrm{Cl}^-$ and $\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}^{2+}{,}\mathrm{Cl}^-$ at $35\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and indicate which of $K$ best describes the experiment.

The experimental results without changing the equation for $k_\mathrm{obs}$ can be described using the $\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}^{2+}{,}\mathrm{Cl}^-$ ion pair and the complete dissociation of $\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}_2^+$ in the mechanism.

6. Suggest your own two stream mechanism if it is similar to the one proposed by Bosnich, Ingold and Tobe but with the ion pair $\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}^{2+}{,}\mathrm{Cl}^-$.

7. Use the method of stationary approximations to derive an equation for $k_\mathrm{obs}$, using the mole fractions of $\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}^{2+}$ and $\mathbf{Me}(\mathrm{en})_2\mathrm{Cl}^{2+}{,}\mathrm{Cl}^-$ and your mechanism.

problems.title: [Ammonium compounds and the Kapustinsky equation]
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (Physical chemistry section, problem 2). [Ammonium compounds and the Kapustinsky equation]

The ionic model is based on the assumption that spherical ions with certain charges are located at the nodes of the crystal lattice. The model often works well even for polyatomic ions. A common cation of this kind is the ammonium ion $\ce{NH4+}$. The idea of the radii of polyatomic ions made it possible to introduce the theory of Kapustinsky, who in 1956 proposed a universal formula for the energy of the crystal lattice ($T = 0\,\mathrm{K}$):

$$L_0 = W\nu\frac{|z_+z_-|e^2}{r_+ + r_-}, \qquad (1)$$

where $\nu$ - number of ions in one molecule, $r_\pm$ - ion radii, $z_\pm$ - charge numbers, $e$ – elementary charge, $W = 1.079\cdot10^5\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot pm\cdot mol^{-1}}$ – constant.

Table 1. Enthalpies of formation of ammonium and rubidium salts, $\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} \mathrm{X^-} & -\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{NH4X}, \mathrm{s}) & -\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{RbX}, \mathrm{s}) & \text{Difference} \\ \hline \ce{Cl-} & 314 & 435 & 121 \\ \hline \ce{Br-} & 271 & 394 & 123 \\ \hline \ce{I-} & 201 & 333 & 132 \\ \hline \ce{NO3-} & 366 & 494 & 128 \\ \hline \ce{ClO4-} & 295 & 434 & 139 \end{array}$$

Table 2. Crystalline radii of some ions, pm

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \ce{Li+} & \ce{Na+} & \ce{K+} & \ce{NH4+} & \ce{Rb+} & \ce{Cs+} \\ \hline 74 & 102 & 138 & 146 & 149 & 170 \end{array}$$

Table 3. Enthalpies of formation of some compounds at 298.15 K, $\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \ce{RbOH}(\mathrm{s}) & \ce{RbNH2}(\mathrm{s}) & \ce{RbH}(\mathrm{s}) & \ce{NH3}(\mathrm{g}) & \ce{NH3*H2O}(\mathrm{l}) & \ce{NH4+}(\mathrm{g}) & \ce{Rb+}(\mathrm{g}) \\ \hline -418.4 & -109.6 & -47.7 & -46.1 & -361.2 & 619 & 490 \end{array}$$

Table 1 compares the enthalpies of formation of a number of ammonium salts and their rubidium analogues. It can be seen that the difference is almost constant, and with a good approximation we can assume that it is equal to $128\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

1. Analyzing equation (1) and the data in Table 2, explain why a constant difference is not observed when comparing ammonium and sodium salts.

2. a) Calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(298.15\,\mathrm{K})$ of the solid ammonium compounds $\ce{NH4+OH-}$, $\ce{NH4+NH2-}$ and $\ce{NH4+H-}$, using the above difference and the data in Table 3;

b) Which compounds are unstable with respect to their constituent elements?

3. For the three compounds in question 2, predict a reasonable decomposition path at 298.15 K other than decomposition into elements, and calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ of the corresponding reactions using the data in Table 3.

At 194.2 K molar mixture (1 : 1) water and ammonia solidifies to form a hydrate $\ce{NH3*H2O}$ (melting temperature 201.7 K). At 110 K crystals of this hydrate belong to the rhombic (orthogonal) system corresponding to the point group $\mathbf{D}_{2h}$. Unit cell parameters: $a = 451\,\mathrm{pm}$, $b = 558.7\,\mathrm{pm}$, $c = 970\,\mathrm{pm}$ with four molecules $\ce{NH3*H2O}$ per unit. It is known that the molar volume $\ce{NH4+OH-}$(s) at 110 K equals to $27.8\,\mathrm{cm^3\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

4. a) What is the geometric shape of the cell (draw)?

b) Specify the location of nodes in the drawing;

c) For reaction $\ce{NH3*H2O}(\mathrm{s}) = \ce{NH4+OH-}(\mathrm{s})$ calculate the change in molar volume $\Delta_\mathrm{r}V_\mathrm{m}$ ($\mathrm{cm^3\cdot mol^{-1}}$) at 110 K.

According to literature data $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{NH3*H2O}, \mathrm{s}, 110\,\mathrm{K}) = -368.9\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

5. Assuming that $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{NH4+OH-}, \mathrm{s})$ is independent of temperature, use the estimation from question 2 to calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ$ of the reaction $\ce{NH3*H2O}(\mathrm{s}) = \ce{NH4+OH-}(\mathrm{s})$ at 110 K. Accept $\Delta_\mathrm{r}S^\circ = 0$.

6. Assuming that $\Delta V_\mathrm{m}$ calculated in question 4, is independent of pressure, determine the pressure at which $\ce{NH4+OH-}$(s) becomes the stable phase at 110 K. Use the relation $dG = -SdT + VdP$ and the result from question 5. If you have no solvution of this question, write a formula for the isothermal change in $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ$ with increasing pressure by $\Delta P$.

7. On which planets of the Solar system can a stable phase $\ce{NH3*H2O}$(s) exist under natural conditions?

• Mercury
• Venus
• Earth
• Mars
• Jupiter
• Saturn
• Uranus
• Neptune

There are some estimates of the stability of metallic ammonium $\ce{NH4}$(s). For example, the enthalpy of the process $\ce{NH4}(\mathrm{s}) = \ce{NH4+}(\mathrm{g}) + \ce{e-}(\mathrm{g})$ $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ = 500\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$ is estimated.

8. a) Use this result to calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{NH4}, \mathrm{s})$; b) Determine $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ of reaction $\ce{NH4}(\mathrm{s}) = \ce{NH3}(\mathrm{g}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\ce{H2}(\mathrm{g})$ and determine whether the metal is stable under standard conditions ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, 1 atm); c) How will the answer change if the entropy factor is taken into account for the reaction.

Physical constants: Avogadro’s number $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.022\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$; standard atmosphere $P^\circ = 101325\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

problems.title: [Fluorescent carbon nanoparticles as a mercury sensor]
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (Physical chemistry section, problem 3). [Fluorescent carbon nanoparticles as a mercury sensor]

Carbon nanoparticles (CNP) exhibit pronounced fluorescence. Upon absorption of UV radiation, they pass into excited state, and the reverse transition into the ground state is accompanied by emission of visible-range light. Part of the absorbed energy is lost in the nonradiative processes.

1. A CNP sample emits light with wavelength 550 nm upon excitation with 365 nm light. Calculate a) the energy difference between the ground and excited states of the CNP and b) fraction of energy lost in the nonradiative processes.

Intensity of CNP fluorescence is changed upon binding of heavy metal ions, which allows the use of CNP for their sensing and determination. Intensity of the CNP fluorescence ($F$) measured in the presence of different concentrations of mercury(II) is given below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} c_\mathrm{Hg},\ \mathrm{nmol\cdot L^{-1}} & F,\ \text{arb.un.} \\ \hline 0 & 12000 \\ \hline 10 & 11483 \\ \hline 30 & 10573 \\ \hline 60 & 9449 \\ \hline 90 & 8541 \end{array}$$

2. Assuming that the fluorescence intensity follows the Stern–Volmer equation $\dfrac{F(c_\mathrm{Hg}=0)}{F(c_\mathrm{Hg})} = 1 + K_\mathrm{SV}c_\mathrm{Hg}$, calculate the quenching constant $K_\mathrm{SV}$.

3. Calculate the limit of mercury(II) detection using the above method assuming that accuracy of measurement of $F$ is 5%.

In another experiment, it was determined that intensity of the CNP fluorescence was decreased by 40% of the initial value upon addition of an iron(III) salt. In that case, the fluorescence was weakened due to absorption of the exciting light by iron(III) ions, not due to their interaction with CNP.

4. Assuming that fluorescence intensity is directly proportional to intensity of the exciting light, and the light absorption by aqua complexes of iron(III) obeys the Beer’s law ($\varepsilon = 2000\,\mathrm{L\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot cm^{-1}}$ at $\lambda = 365\,\mathrm{nm}$), determine the concentration of iron(III) in the solution. Consider that the intensity of the emitted light was measured at direction perpendicular to the exciting light direction and the optical cell was a cylinder with diameter of 2 cm.

To eliminate the influence iron(III), it was bound in a colorless citrate complex. The resulting intensity of fluorescence was 97% of the initial value for CNP in the absence of iron.

5. Calculate the amount of citric acid added to 100 mL of the sample if the solution pH was 3.8 and the stability constant of the complex prevailing under those conditions, Fe(OH)(Citr), is $10^{8.5}$.

6. Calculate the limit of the mercury(II) detection in the presence of iron(III) ions masked with citric acid as described above.

Another possibility to mask iron(III) is its binding into colorless fluoride complex. However, fluoride ions also react with mercury(II) which makes its determination impossible.

7. Write the reaction between fluoride ions and mercury(II) in an aqueous solution.

Reference data: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, $h = 6.63\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}$, $A = \varepsilon lc$

problems.title: [Clerici solution and the metal M]
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 1). [Clerici solution and the metal M]

The silver-white metal $\mathbf{M}$ tarnishes in air, becoming covered with a black film. $\mathbf{M}$ dissolves well in acids, for instance, in formic acid to form $\mathbf{M}$(+1) formate. A solution of a mixture of $\mathbf{M}$(+1) formate and $\mathbf{M}$(+1) malonate was first obtained by the Italian geologist E. Clerici. This liquid has a high density, which is highly dependent on the composition of the solution and temperature. This allowed the solution to be used in mineralogy to determine the density of minerals and separate them. The refractive index of such solution depends almost linearly on the density ($\mathrm{g/cm^3}$): $n = 0.1152\cdot d + 1.2078$.

1. Calculate the density of the Clerici solution if the measured refractive index is $n = 1.6305$. From the minerals hereunder, select those that will float on the surface of such solution: garnet ($3.48\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$), spinel ($3.72\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$), corundum ($4.10\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$), quartz ($2.62\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$), diamond ($3.55\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$), mirabilite ($1.49\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$).

If an ammonium sulfide solution is added to a solution of $\mathbf{M}$(+1) formate, a black precipitate $\mathbf{A}$ will form. In addition to the basic oxidation state +1, compounds can also be obtained in a higher oxidation state, which is unstable. Thus, the oxidation of $\mathbf{M}$(+1) nitrate with chlorine in an alkali results in the formation of dark brown oxide $\mathbf{B}$, which has a centrosymmetric cubic unit cell. The figure shows 1/8 part (octant) of an elementary cell, the center of the cube is separately highlighted - it is also the center of inversion.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-2-7-fig1.png

2. Calculate the gross composition of $\mathbf{B}$, and the number of formula units in one elementary cell.

When $\mathbf{B}$ reacts with a concentrated solution of hydrochloric acid, a yellow-green gas is emitted and a solution is formed, upon dilution of which a white precipitate of salt $\mathbf{C}$ precipitates. Salt $\mathbf{C}$ can be oxidized with chlorine to a higher chloride – $\mathbf{D}$. When a mixture of a concentrated solution of $\mathbf{D}$ and precipitate $\mathbf{C}$ is heated, a chemical reaction occurs. On slow cooling, lemon-yellow crystals of substance $\mathbf{E}$ ($\omega(\mathrm{Cl}) = 20.7\%$) crystalizes from the solution.

3. Identify all unknown substances $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{E}$, and also write down the equations of chemical reactions.

4. Indicate the real composition of $\mathbf{E}$ and write the equation for its electrolytic dissociation in water.

5. Arrange in a row in order of increasing electrical conductivity aqueous solutions of $\mathbf{E}$, NaCl and $\ce{CaCl2}$ of the same concentrations. Assume that the degree of dissociation of all salts is 100%.

An alternative way to obtain $\mathbf{E}$ is the oxidation of $\mathbf{C}$ with ozone in $\ce{POCl3}$. However, if brownish-yellow poisonous gas $\mathbf{F}$ (density is 3.88 at N.C.) is used as an oxidizing agent, $\ce{POCl3}$ also participate in the reaction to form $\mathbf{G}$ ($\omega(\mathrm{P}) = 15.35\%$). The $\mathbf{M}$ cation in $\mathbf{G}$ is in an octahedral environment. $\mathbf{G}$ has a molecular structure, has two optical isomers, and no geometric isomers.

6. Set the composition of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$, write down the reaction equations, and also draw the structure of the $\mathbf{G}$ molecule. It is known that only two elements change their oxidation states in the reaction of obtaining $\mathbf{G}$.

7. Suggest a method for obtaining $\mathbf{F}$ gas.

problems.title: [Pyrophoric iron]
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 2). [Pyrophoric iron]

As it turned out, "pyrophoric iron" is actually not even iron at all. It has been shown that the process of its production includes in several stages. The products composition on each stage depends on the temperature, composition of the gas atmosphere, and etc. In the problem we will consider the processes that occur when dried precipitate $\mathbf{A}$, obtained by mixing aqueous solutions of ferrous sulfate and potassium oxalate, is heated in an evacuated sealed reactor in an atmosphere of its decomposition products. On the first stage (at 170-230 °C) $\mathbf{A}$ loses about 20 % of its mass and converts to $\mathbf{B}$.

1. Write down the equation of the reaction conversion $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{B}$.

On the second stage (at 230-360 °C) $\mathbf{B}$ partially decomposes producing gaseous mixture and substance $\mathbf{C}$ with the mass of about 53.5 % from that of decomposed part of $\mathbf{B}$. At 360-415 °C undecomposed part of $\mathbf{B}$ reacts with one of the components of the gaseous mixture to form a solid binary substance $\mathbf{D}$, whose mass is approximately on 58 % less the mass of decomposed part of $\mathbf{B}$.

2. Establish the formulas of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ and write down the equations of the reactions taking place on the second stage.

At the third stage (415–535 °C) partial decomposition of $\mathbf{D}$ leads to elementary substances. Above 535 °C substance $\mathbf{C}$ transforms into the final pyrophoric product $\mathbf{E}$.

3. Write down the equations of the reactions taking place in the third stage.

The solid final product has the NaCl structure and a non-stoichiometric composition. The mass fraction of oxygen in one of the investigated samples of $\mathbf{E}$ is equal to 23.36 %, and its density is equal to $5.70\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

4. Establish the possible formulas of the investigated non-stoichiometric $\mathbf{E}$.

5. Establish the formula of the investigated sample $\mathbf{E}$, if according to X-ray data unit cell parameter is equal to 0.4307 nm.

problems.title: [Metal M in an uncharacteristic oxidation state]
problems.problem:
Problem 9 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 3). [Metal M in an uncharacteristic oxidation state]

The compounds of metal $\mathbf{M}$ in uncharacteristic oxidation state (ox. st. = $+\mathbf{n}$) are the strong oxidants, oxidizing even $\ce{H2O}$ in an acidic media: $\mathbf{M}^{\mathbf{n}+} + (\mathbf{n}-2)\bar{e} = \mathbf{M}^{(\mathbf{n}-1)+}$ $\quad E_1^0 = 1.52\,\mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 4\bar{e} = 2\mathrm{H_2O}$ $\quad E_2^0 = 1.23\,\mathrm{V}$.

In high-spin complexes $\mathbf{M}^{\mathbf{n}+}$ ($\mu = [2S(2S + 2)]^{1/2} = 4.90\,\mu_\mathrm{B}$, where S – total spin) O–donor ligands (L), including $\ce{O^{2-}}$, stabilize $\mathbf{M}^{\mathbf{n}+}$. Thus, when alkali is added to the $\mathbf{M}^{(\mathbf{n}-1)+}$ solution, 4.45 g of a slightly pinkish precipitate first forms, which eventually loses 0.45 g of $\ce{H2O}$ and turns into 4.40 g of a brown precipitate containing the stabilizing group $\mathbf{M}$O and $\mathbf{M}^{+\mathbf{n}}$.

1. Calculate $\mathbf{n}$, the number of unpaired electrons at $\mathbf{M}^{\mathbf{n}+}$ and give two possible variants of valence electrons at $\mathbf{M}$. Decoding metal $\mathbf{M}$.

2. Estimate difference of logarithms of formation constants $\beta_x$ ($\mathbf{M}^{\mathbf{n}+} + x\mathrm{L}^- = \mathbf{M}\mathrm{L}_x^{(\mathrm{n}-x)+}$) and $\beta_y$ ($\mathrm{M}^{(\mathbf{n}-1)+} + x\mathrm{L}^- = \mathbf{M}\mathrm{L}_x^{(\mathbf{n}-x-1)+}$), sufficient to prevent oxidation $\mathbf{M}\mathrm{L}_x^{(\mathrm{n}-x)+} + \mathrm{H_2O}$.

Bridging O,O–donor $\ce{CH3COO-}$ forms polynuclear complexes with formula $\mathbf{M}_\mathbf{a}\mathrm{O}_\mathbf{b}$ and stabilize uncharacteristic oxidation state (ox. st.), including mixed. In 1987 Vincent obtained a brown solution from solution $\mathbf{M}(\mathrm{CH_3COO})_{\mathbf{n}-1}\cdot4\mathrm{H_2O}$ (7.35 g) in mixture of $\ce{C2H5OH}$, pyridine (Py) and $\ce{CH3COOH}$ by under the action of $(\mathrm{Bu_4N})\mathbf{M}\mathrm{O_4}$, then using $\ce{NaClO4}$ solution he isolated brown crystals of $\mathbf{A}\mathrm{ClO_4}$ (yield 60 %). When evaporating the solution of $\mathbf{A}\mathrm{ClO_4}$ in $\ce{CH3CN}$ he isolated black crystals $\mathbf{B}$ (3.01 g, yield 65 %). Compositions of carboxylates $\mathbf{A}^+$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are the same, the whole $\mathbf{M}$ is in $\mathbf{M}_\mathbf{a}\mathrm{O}_\mathbf{b}$, and $\nu_{\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}} = 2\nu_\mathbf{M} = 2\nu_\mathrm{Py}$. In $\mathbf{M}_\mathbf{a}\mathrm{O}_\mathbf{b}$ all angles are close to 120º, and the bond distances $l_{\mathbf{M}\text{–}\mathrm{O}}$ are equal to 1.83 Å in $\mathbf{A}^+$; 1.82 Å and 2.15 Å in $\mathbf{B}$.

3. Calculate $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, decoding $\mathbf{A}^+$ and $\mathbf{B}$ and specify ox. st. of $\mathbf{M}$ in them. Write down ionic equation of formation of $\mathbf{A}^+$ in brown solution. Draw structure of $\mathbf{M}_\mathbf{a}\mathrm{O}_\mathbf{b}$ in complex $\mathbf{B}$.

When produced crystals dissolve in $\ce{CH3CN}$, then acting by bipyridine (bipy) the whole Py in them is equimolarly replaced by bipy and a day later from a solution $\mathbf{A}\mathrm{ClO_4}$ red crystals of $\mathbf{D}\mathrm{ClO_4}$ isolated, and dark-red crystals $\mathbf{E}$ isolated from solution $\mathbf{B}$, both have group $\mathbf{M}_\mathbf{d}\mathrm{O}_{2\mathbf{b}}$ in composition.

4. Decoding formula $\mathbf{D}^+$ (19.4 % mass. $\mathbf{M}$; 7.41 % N; 22.6 % O) and $\mathbf{E}$ (20.5 % mass. $\mathbf{M}$; 7.82 % N ; 20.9 % O). Define ox. st. of $\mathbf{M}$ in them.

5. Draw structure of fragment $\mathbf{M}_\mathbf{d}\mathrm{O}_{2\mathbf{b}}$, if both in $\mathbf{D}^+$, and in $\mathbf{E}$ it is based on a polygon with $l_{\mathbf{M}\text{–}\mathrm{O}} = 1.88$ Å and angles $\mathbf{M}$O$\mathbf{M}$ 97º and O$\mathbf{M}$O 83º. In $\mathbf{E}$ planar fragment $\mathbf{M}_\mathbf{d}\mathrm{O}_{2\mathbf{b}}$ has bonds with $l_{\mathbf{M}\text{–}\mathrm{O}} = 2.10$ Å, included in angles O…O$\mathbf{M}$ 180º, and in $\mathbf{D}^+$ non-planar fragment $\mathbf{M}_\mathbf{d}\mathrm{O}_{2\mathbf{b}}$ included in angles O…O$\mathbf{M}$ 130º. $\mathbf{E}$ has inversion center, but not $\mathbf{D}^+$.

problems.title: [Metabolism of the element X in marine microorganisms]
problems.problem:
Problem 10 (Life sciences and polymers section, problem 1). [Metabolism of the element X in marine microorganisms]

Compounds containing an element $\mathbf{X}$ are toxic for mammals. Still, these can be involved into metabolic processes in a number of marine microorganisms. An acid $\mathbf{H_3A}$ is the major $\mathbf{X}$ containing substance in sea water.

1. Deduce the prevailing form of $\mathbf{H_3A}$ ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1} = 2.22$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2} = 6.98$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a3} = 11.53$) in sea water at pH~8. Prove by calculations.

In cells, $\mathbf{H_3A}$ undergoes transformation involving seven successive enzymatic reactions finally leading to the formation of the substance $\mathbf{B}$ (62.42% of $\mathbf{X}$ by mass). After each step, the oxidation state (OS) of the sole atom of $\mathbf{X}$ present in the metabolite changes (either increases or decreases) be two, i.e. $|\Delta\mathrm{OS}_\mathbf{X}| = 2$. The total sum of OS values of $\mathbf{X}$ in all the compounds within the $\mathbf{H_3A}\rightarrow\mathbf{B}$ pathway (including the starting and final ones) equals 32.

2. Deduce all theoretically possible OS values of $\mathbf{X}$ in $\mathbf{H_3A}$. Note that any of deduced values must be found in three (beside $\mathbf{H_3A}$) metabolites.

3. Based on the above information, decide in which group(s) of the Periodic table of elements one can find $\mathbf{X}$, if odd OS values are characteristic of it.

Organic acids $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are neighboring intermediates of the $\mathbf{H_3A}\rightarrow\mathbf{B}$ pathway. The information about $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ is given in the table.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Compound} & \text{Mass fraction of } \mathbf{X}\text{, \%} & \text{Molar fraction of } \mathbf{X}\text{, \%} \\ \hline \mathbf{C} & 61.41 & 9.09 \\ \hline \mathbf{D} & 54.29 & 8.33 \end{array}$$

4. Deduce the structures of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$.

The number of the involved enzymes is significantly lower than that of reactions within the $\mathbf{H_3A}\rightarrow\mathbf{B}$ pathway.

5. Draw the $\mathbf{H_3A}\rightarrow\mathbf{B}$ pathway, giving the structures of all the compounds.

The $\mathbf{H_3A}$ acid enters the intracellular space of marine microorganisms via the transmembrane channel, which is mainly responsible for the transport of a vitally important compound $\mathbf{E}$ from the sea water.

6. Propose the molecular formula of $\mathbf{E}$.

An $\mathbf{X}$ containing drug $\mathbf{Y}$ used to cure tsetse-fly disease has been developed in early 20th century. The one-step process affording $\mathbf{Y}$ was based on the reaction of the compound $\mathbf{Z}$ ($\mathrm{C_6H_6O_6N}\mathbf{X}$) with sodium dithionite. $\mathbf{Z}$ is a polysubstituted benzene. Numerical locants of each substituent in the benzene ring of $\mathbf{Z}$ were multiplied by the atomic number of the element, atom of which is directly linked to the carbon atom of the benzene ring. The total sum of the products equals 86.

7. A) What atoms can be involved in bond formation with the C atoms of the benzene ring;

B) Prove that $\mathbf{Z}$ contains the C-N and/or C-$\mathbf{X}$ bonds. Note that this question is independent of the answers to the previous ones.

8. Deduce the structure of $\mathbf{Z}$, if it contains the C-$\mathbf{X}$ bond.

It was commonly agreed that $\mathbf{Y}$ has the structure with the molecular weight of 366 g/mol ($\mathbf{Y_1}$). However, recent mass spectrometry studies that it is not completely true: the peaks of the protonated molecule ($[\mathbf{Y}+\mathrm{H}]^+$) prevailing in the spectrum have $m/z$ of 550 ($\mathbf{Y_2}$) and 916 ($\mathbf{Y_3}$)

9. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{Y_1}$-$\mathbf{Y_3}$, if in each of these the atoms of $\mathbf{X}$ are equivalent.

problems.title: [Bacterial biodegradation leading to a banned compound X]
problems.problem:
Problem 11 (Life sciences and polymers section, problem 2). [Bacterial biodegradation leading to a banned compound X]

The carcinogenic compound $\mathbf{X}$ is the final product of biodegradation of hundreds of substances used by man, including those affording better results of athletes. In June 2021, the International Ski and Snowboard Federation as well as International Biathlon Union imposed a ban on any products containing $\mathbf{X}$.

Bacterial biodegradation of an organic compound $\mathbf{A}$ by P. oleovorans affording $\mathbf{X}$ is shown on the Scheme. The numerical designation for the substances of this class as well as the molecular masses rounded to integer (g/mol, after the comma) are given next to the metabolite symbols. All the reactions in the Scheme are catalyzed by enzymes; each of the unbranched compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{G}$ contain no more than 15 carbon atoms.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-2-11-fig1.png

1. For the $\mathbf{A}\rightarrow\mathbf{C}$ transformation, propose two sets of interconverting functional groups (fragments of the molecules), if the changes of the molecular masses within $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{C}$ are only due to biotransformation of these groups.

$\mathbf{E}$ is the only substrate of the enzyme catalyzing the $\mathbf{E}\rightarrow\mathbf{F}$ step, the other product (beside $\mathbf{F}$), being a gaseous (under normal conditions) substance.

2. Determine the molar fraction of carbon (in % with the accuracy to integer) in $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, and $\mathbf{F}$, if it is one and the same for all the three compounds.

3. It is possible to unambiguously calculate the degree of unsaturation of $\mathbf{F}$ (by contrast to that of $\mathbf{D}$) based on the above information. Perform the calculation.

In each of the $\mathbf{C}\rightarrow\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{D}\rightarrow\mathbf{E}$ transformations, the number of atoms of only two elements ($\mathbf{El_1}$ and $\mathbf{El_2}$) is changed. $\mathbf{D}$ is composed of atoms of four elements.

4. Decipher $\mathbf{El_1}$ and $\mathbf{El_2}$, if $A_\mathrm{r}(\mathbf{El_1}) > A_\mathrm{r}(\mathbf{El_2})$. Prove by calculations.

5. Determine the molecular formulae of $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{F}$.

One can disclose the principles behind the system of numerical designations of the compounds of this class based on the analysis of the molecular formulae of $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{F}$ (8:2, 7:3, and 7:2).

6. Demonstrate the principles by writing the designation of any structural isomer of $\mathbf{A}$.

The oxidation of $\mathbf{G}$ leading to $\mathbf{X}$ is catalyzed by several successively acting enzymes.

7. Draw all possible structures of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{D}$-$\mathbf{G}$, and $\mathbf{X}$ (without stereochemical details).

8. Choose the statements explaining the reasons for using the $\mathbf{X}$ derivatives (mostly esters) at skiing competitions and why their use should be prohibited:

The reason for using $\mathbf{X}$

• The ingestion of the $\mathbf{X}$ derivatives contributes to an enhanced endurance of athletes in cyclic sports including cross-country skiing (doping)
• The ingestion of the $\mathbf{X}$ derivatives contributes to a lowered arm tremor in biathlon shooting and skate skiing (doping)
• The $\mathbf{X}$ derivatives are used as ski waxes
• The $\mathbf{X}$ derivatives are used to prepare a ski-track profile

The reason for banning $\mathbf{X}$

• $\mathbf{X}$ is not subjected to biodegradation due to its structural distinction, thus being accumulated in water and soil and penetrating in mammals with food
• $\mathbf{X}$ being subjected to bacterial biodegradation in soil produces a colorless gas (at STP) toxic for mammals
• $\mathbf{X}$ being subjected to bacterial biodegradation in soil produces a colored gas (at STP) toxic for mammals
• Penetrating in atmosphere, $\mathbf{X}$ contributes to ozone depletion as a part of the Earth stratosphere

problems.title: [Unusual amino acids from lysine in Streptomyces cattleya]
problems.problem:
Problem 12 (Life sciences and polymers section, problem 3). [Unusual amino acids from lysine in Streptomyces cattleya]

A novel metabolic pathway affording unusual α-amino acids $\mathbf{4}$ and $\mathbf{7}$ in Streptomyces cattleya was reported in Nature in 2019. The scheme leading to these substances from the canonical amino acid lysine (Lys, see structure below) is shown hereunder:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-2-12-fig1.png

The bacterial genome contains a cluster of genes (besA-besE) encoding the enzymes of the pathway. To determine the enzyme sequence, the researchers designed bacterial lines with knockout genes (ΔbesA-ΔbesE) by deleting a single gene of the cluster in each line (denoted by Δ). This led to the following metabolic changes in the lines lacking specific enzymes. The relative quantities (0 to 10) of $\mathbf{2}$-$\mathbf{7}$ found in each line are given hereunder.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c} & \mathbf{2} & \mathbf{3} & \mathbf{4} & \mathbf{5} & \mathbf{6} & \mathbf{7} \\ \hline \Delta\mathit{besA} & 0 & 0 & 10 & 4 & 4 & 10 \\ \hline \Delta\mathit{besB} & 0 & 10 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \hline \Delta\mathit{besC} & 10 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \hline \Delta\mathit{besD} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \hline \Delta\mathit{besE} & 0 & 0 & 8 & 10 & 0 & 0 \end{array}$$

1. Decipher the sequence of action of the enzymes besA-besE.

2. Choose one correct statement concerning the metabolic pathway:

• 1. The reaction catalyzed by the enzyme besA can also be catalyzed by non-specific γ-glutamyl transpeptidases
• 2. The relative content of a metabolite equal to 0 indicates that the rates of its formation and consumption are equal
• 3. Accumulation of the metabolites $\mathbf{4}$ and $\mathbf{5}$ in the ΔbesA line suggests that besA uses both metabolites as its substrate
