• 4. Addition of a solution of the metabolite $\mathbf{2}$ to the ΔbesD line will result in a stable increase in the relative content of $\mathbf{2}$

The detailed scheme (all steps are chemical equations) affording $\mathbf{4}$ and $\mathbf{7}$ is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-2-12-fig2.png

The mass spectrum (A) and $^1$H NMR spectrum (B) were recorded to identify $\mathbf{2}$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-2-12-fig3.png

3. Determine $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{2}$. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{2}$.

4. Calculate (in % to the nearest integer) the ratio of intensities referring to the peaks of the protonated molecule ($[\mathbf{2}+\mathrm{H}]^+$) with m/z of 181 and 183.

5. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{3}$-$\mathbf{7}$.

While studying the $\mathbf{2}\rightarrow\mathbf{3}$ reaction, the substrate concentration was found to start decreasing before introduction of the enzyme. It turned out that $\mathbf{2}$ is capable of non-enzymatic cyclization via nucleophilic substitution giving lactone $\mathbf{8}$ and lactam $\mathbf{9}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-2-12-fig4.png

6. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{8}$-$\mathbf{10}$.

The ammonia solution of acetoacetone was used to detect the formaldehyde produced in the transformation of $\mathbf{2}$ to $\mathbf{3}$. The solution taken in the molar ratio of 2:1 to formaldehyde, it affords a symmetric heterocyclic fluorescent product $\mathbf{Y}$ ($\ce{C11H15NO2}$) via a number of condensation:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2023-2-12-fig5.png

7. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{11}$, $\mathbf{12}$, and $\mathbf{Y}$.

problems.title: [Extraction-photometric determination of mercury]
problems.problem:
Problem 13 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 1). [Extraction-photometric determination of mercury]

For the extraction-photometric determination of the concentration of mercury in an aqueous solution, a certain amount of a mercury(II) salt and 1 mL of 0.5 M potassium bromide are added to a separating funnel, some acid is added, and the aqueous phase is brought to 10 mL with water (solution $\mathbf{1}$). Then, 10 mL of 0.001 M toluene solution of tri-n-octylammonium methyl orangeate was added followed by shaking. After phase separation (extract $\mathbf{2}$, aqueous solution $\mathbf{3}$), the concentration of mercury in solution $\mathbf{1}$ is determined by the light absorption of methyl orange released into aqueous phase $\mathbf{3}$ after adding 1 mL of 1 M NaOH.

1. Write down the equation for the ion-exchange extraction reaction. Designate the tri-n-octylammonium cation as $\mathrm{R_3NH^+}$, the methyl orange anion as $\mathrm{MO^-}$; consider that mercury is extracted in the form of a singly charged tribromide complex. Indicate the phase in which the compound is located in the subscript: $_\mathrm{(o)}$, $_\mathrm{(aq)}$.

2. KBr is added in a large excess to prevent an undesired reaction; write its equation.

3. Mercury is determined by the light absorption of the red or the yellow form of methyl orange? Which of the substances mentioned in the task indicates this?

4. If a preparation of tri-n-octylammonium methyl orangeate contains an admixture of free tri-n-octylammonium, then the result of mercury determination will be: a) still correct, b) overestimated, c) underestimated. Write the equation for the reaction(s) involving tri-n-octylamine ($\mathrm{R_3N}$).

5. Copper(II) is extracted by 10% with the same reagent $\mathrm{R_3NH^+MO^-}$ in the form of anion $\ce{CuBr3-}$. What absolute error in the determined concentration of mercury in solution $\mathbf{1}$ should be introduced by the presence of $1\cdot10^{-5}$ M copper in it?

6. To experimentally determine the error introduced by the presence of copper, organic extract $\mathbf{2}$ was shaken with 10 mL of a 0.05 M KBr solution and the concentration of copper in the resulting aqueous solution $\mathbf{4}$ was determined by another method, obtaining a value of $2.0\cdot10^{-6}$ M. Assume that the distribution of copper between the phases depends only on the concentration of ammonium salt in the organic phase, which does not change.

a) Write the equation for the process that occurs when extract $\mathbf{2}$ is washed.

b) What was the concentration of copper in solution $\mathbf{1}$?

Assume that all extraction equilibria are established quickly.

7. In tasks 1–6, you should have neglected the side process, which is now proposed to be taken into account: $\mathrm{R_3NH^+MO^-_{(o)} + Br^-_{(aq)} = R_3NH^+Br^-_{(o)} + MO^-_{(aq)}}$

What should be the equilibrium constant of this reaction $K_1$ so that the error in the determination of $5\cdot10^{-6}$ M mercury in the aqueous phase would not exceed 5%? Consider that the extraction of mercury proceeds completely, copper(II) and free $\mathrm{R_3N}$ are absent, and trioctylammonium bromide is formed only by the indicated reaction.

problems.title: [Iodatometric determination of tin in bronze-plating electrolytes]
problems.problem:
Problem 14 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 2). [Iodatometric determination of tin in bronze-plating electrolytes]

For applying bronze coatings, electrolytes containing tin(II and IV) and copper(II) salts, hydrochloric acid, and some additives described below are used. The concentration of Sn(II) in these solutions is determined by iodatometric titration.

1. At the beginning of titration with iodate, the solution turns brown. Write down the equation for this reaction.

2. By the end of titration, all the iodine has converted to iodine monochloride and the solution becomes light green.

a) Write the final equation for the tin(II) titration reaction.

b) Which substance(s) determine(s) the yellow-green color of solution at the titration end point?

3. The components of the electrolyte would enter some undesirable reactions with each other if tin were not bound into an oxalate complex. Write down:

a) the undesired reaction and

b) the complexation reaction if a doubly charged oxalate complex is formed. Oxalate is not oxidized with iodate under these conditions.

c) When oxalic acid is added to a weakly acidic electrolyte, not only the tin oxalate complex is formed, but also a blue precipitate, soluble in a large excess of oxalate. Write down the equations for the formation and dissolution of this precipitate.

4. To determine tin(IV), it is reduced to tin(II) with aluminum granules and titrated as described above.

a) Due to the side reaction in which aluminum enters, it is required to introduce its excess. Write down the side reaction.

b) In parallel with the reduction of Sn(IV) contained in the electrolyte by aluminum, a soluble copper-containing product $\mathbf{P}$ is formed. Write down the equation for this reaction (copper is in excess).

c) How can the formation of product $\mathbf{P}$ be experimentally detected by a chemical method? Write down one reaction equation.

d) Product $\mathbf{P}$ will interfere with the determination of tin(II) by the titrimetric method. Confirm this by writing down the equation for the reaction involving product $\mathbf{P}$.

e) Which of the reactions that you should have written above can be used as the basis for a method for eliminating the interfering effect of copper(II) on the determination of tin(IV) due to the formation of product $\mathbf{P}$? Write it down.

5. Calculate the concentrations of tin(II) and tin(IV) in the electrolyte, if 7.2 mL of a 0.0500 M potassium iodate solution was used to titrate 10.00 mL of the electrolyte without reduction, and the same volume of iodate was used to titrate a 5.00 mL aliquot after reduction with aluminum. (If any precipitates formed, they were separated before titration.)

problems.title: [Acid–base and dimerization equilibria of a yellow anion]
problems.problem:
Problem 15 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 3). [Acid–base and dimerization equilibria of a yellow anion]

The salt $\ce{Na2}\mathbf{X}$ is well soluble in water and forms yellow solutions. When acid is added to such a solution, the color changes to orange. The original yellow color can be returned by adding an alkali. It is assumed that the transition in an acidic medium is carried out according to the following mechanism:

$$\mathbf{X}^{2-} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftarrows \mathbf{Y}^- \ (K_1) \qquad 2\mathbf{Y}^- \rightleftarrows \mathbf{Z}^{2-} + \mathrm{H_2O}\ (K_2)$$

1. Give the structural formulas of anions $\mathbf{X}^{2-}$, $\mathbf{Y}^-$, and $\mathbf{Z}^{2-}$.

2. Write the total reaction equation for the transition of $\mathbf{X}^{2-}$ into $\mathbf{Z}^{2-}$. Express the corresponding equilibrium constant $K_3$ in terms of the equilibrium constants of the individual steps $K_1$ and $K_2$.

3. Does the mole fraction of $\mathbf{X}^{2-}$, $\mathbf{Y}^-$, and $\mathbf{Z}^{2-}$ species at a certain pH value depend on the initial concentration ($c_0$) of $\ce{Na2}\mathbf{X}$? Confirm your answer by: a) expressing the equilibrium concentration of $\mathbf{Y}^-$ ($[\mathbf{Y}^-]$) in terms of $c_0$, $[\ce{H+}]$ and equilibrium constants; b) getting the expression for the mole fraction of $\mathbf{Y}^-$ in terms of $[\mathbf{Y}^-]$.

For the spectrophotometric determination of $K_3$, the transmittance ($T = 10^{-A}\cdot100\%$, $A$ – absorbance) was measured for the solutions of $1.50\cdot10^{-4}$ M $\ce{Na2}\mathbf{X}$ at various pH values and wavelengths 352 ($\lambda_1$) and 373 nm ($\lambda_2$) in cuvettes with an optical path length $l = 1\,\mathrm{cm}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{pH} & T_1,\ \% & T_2,\ \% \\ \hline 1.0 & 59.7 & 68.1 \\ \hline 6.0 & 49.3 & 41.9 \\ \hline 11 & 32.3 & 15.9 \end{array}$$

4. Calculate the molar extinction coefficients ($\varepsilon_\lambda = A/(lc)$, $c$ – molar concentration) for $\mathbf{X}^{2-}$ and $\mathbf{Z}^{2-}$ at 352 и 373 nm. Specify the units. As an approximation in solving this question, assume that the concentration and absorbance due to the intermediate species $\mathbf{Y}^-$ are negligible.

5. Calculate the equilibrium constants $K_1$, $K_2$, and $K_3$.

Hint: You can use the intermediate results in question 5 to check the expression you got in question 3.

problems.title: [The acid HX and its derivatives]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [The acid HX and its derivatives]

Organic derivatives of inorganic acids usually become known much later than the corresponding inorganic salts, but there are some exceptions. Thus, in 1956, Huisgen and Ugi obtained the compound PhX ($\mathbf{A}$), the structure of which was unambiguously proven 27 years later by single crystal X-ray diffraction analysis. On the contrary, the studies of the acid HX and its inorganic derivatives were carried out only by quantum chemical methods until the beginning of the 21st century. Thus, in 2001, the existence of the $\ce{FeX2}$ molecule ($\mathbf{B}$) was predicted with the binding energy of the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\ce{2X^-}$ ions forming it only slightly lower than that of the ions in the isoelectronic molecule $\ce{FeY2}$ ($\mathbf{C}$), discovered already in 1951. The light-orange compound $\mathbf{C}$ with the melting point of $173\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the boiling point of $249\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is stable when heated to about $450\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, soluble in organic solvents, including benzene, and insoluble in water. It laid the foundation of a new field of chemistry, which was further included in both inorganic and organic chemistry textbooks.

A derivative of $\mathbf{A}$ was later obtained according to the Huisgen and Ugi procedure from 4-methoxyaniline using NaQ salt. When this new compound was oxidized with ceric(IV) ammonium nitrate (CAN) at $-40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in the presence of zinc nitrate, the formation of a mixed salt $\ce{Zn(X)NO3}$ ($\mathbf{D}$) was observed. When kept at $-20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, this salt decomposes releasing a gas and forming another salt, $\ce{Zn(Q)NO3}$ ($\mathbf{E}$), containing the same elements as $\mathbf{D}$, including 38.59% zinc.

The compound $\mathbf{F}$, an isomer of $\mathbf{B}$, was obtained in 1999. $\mathbf{F}$ is isoelectronic to another known iron compound $\mathbf{G}$, a light-yellow liquid immiscible with cold water. $\mathbf{F}$ dissolves in ethanol, benzene, acetic acid and is used mainly to obtain high-purity iron powder. According to calculations, $\mathbf{F}$ is by $260\,\mathrm{kcal/mol}$ more stable than $\mathbf{B}$, still the binding energy of the components in it does not exceed $33.7\,\mathrm{kcal/mol}$.

In 2017, a stable salt $\mathbf{H}$ was obtained by oxidation of another aryl-X type compound with meta-chloroperbenzoic acid in the presence of iron bis(glycinate). After purification by column chromatography, $\mathbf{H}$ was characterized by single crystal X-ray diffraction analysis. It turned out that this salt has a complex composition: it contains X anions, chloride ion, ammonium and hydronium ($\ce{H3O+}$) cations, whereas the content of hydrogen, nitrogen and chlorine in $\mathbf{H}$ is 4.31%, 81.42% and 6.06%, respectively. Starting from this salt, other salts of the acid HX with a variety of cations are obtained by a cation metathesis reaction.

1. Write down molecular formulas of HX, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{E}$; draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{C}$.

2. Write down equations of the reactions used by Huisgen and Ugi to synthesize PhX.

3. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$.

4. Calculate the molecular formula of $\mathbf{H}$.

problems.title: [Cembrene]
problems.problem:
Problem 2. [Cembrene]

Crystals of an optically active terpene hydrocarbon further referred to as “cembrene” ($\mathbf{I}$) were isolated from Pinus albicaulis (Whitebark Pine) in 1951. This hydrocarbon was the first natural compound, the molecule of which was found to contain a carbocycle of an unusual size. All terpenes are usually considered as polymerization products of the hydrocarbon $\mathbf{II}$. Terpenes are subdivided into monoterpenes ($n = 2$), sesquiterpenes ($n = 3$), diterpenes ($n = 4$), triterpenes ($n = 6$) and polyterpenes depending on the number of units ($n$) of $\mathbf{II}$. One of the industrial syntheses of $\mathbf{II}$ is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-1-2-fig1.png

1. Determine the structures of $\mathrm{C}_X\mathrm{H}_Y$, $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{C}$, and $\mathbf{II}$, if $\mathrm{C}_X\mathrm{H}_Y$ gives a precipitate with an ammonia solution of silver oxide, while the carbonyl compound $\mathbf{A}$ does not react with it.

2. Choose the catalyst for the first step from the list: a) $\ce{Al2O3}$; b) $\ce{H2SO4}$; c) $\ce{(C2H5)3N}$; d) $[(i\text{-}\ce{C3H7})_2\mathrm{N}]\mathrm{Li}$; e) $\ce{KOH}$.

The structure of cembrene was elucidated in 1962. According to the mass spectrum data, the molecular weight of $\mathbf{I}$ is 272 a.m.u. 16.32 g of $\mathbf{I}$ can completely add $2764\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{H2}$ ($50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $2.3\,\mathrm{atm}$) in the presence of Pd/C.

3. Determine the molecular formula of $\mathbf{I}$. Which class of terpenes (monoterpene, sesquiterpene, diterpene, triterpene, polyterpene) does it belong to?

4. Calculate the number of rings ($n_\text{ring}$) and double bonds ($n_{\ce{C=C}}$) in the molecule of $\mathbf{I}$.

The reduction of $\mathbf{I}$ under the action of $\ce{Li/NH3}$ leads to the formation of dihydrocembrene ($\mathbf{III}$). The $^1$H NMR spectra of trans-4-octene and $\mathbf{III}$ are shown below.

5. In the trans-4-octene structure, label the groups $\mathbf{a}$ – $\mathbf{d}$ that give the corresponding signals in the spectrum. Calculate the total number of hydrogen atoms at the double ($n_{\text{H-}sp^2}$) and single ($n_{\text{H-}sp^3}$) C-C bonds in the molecule of $\mathbf{III}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-1-2-fig2.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-1-2-fig3.png

$^1$H NMR spectrum of trans-4-octene.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-1-2-fig4.png

$^1$H NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{III}$.

Ozonolysis of $\mathbf{III}$ with subsequent treatment with $\ce{H2O2}$ gave an equimolar mixture of 2-isopropyl-5-oxohexanoic acid, 2-methylpentanedioic acid and a thermally stable bifunctional compound $\mathbf{X}$; no other carbon-containing products were found.

6. Calculate the molecular formula of $\mathbf{X}$ and determine its structure.

7. Determine the ring size in cembrene.

problems.title: [Osmolytes of deep-sea organisms]
problems.problem:
Problem 3. [Osmolytes of deep-sea organisms]

Don't worry about your problems with math. Believe me, mine are much more serious.
Albert Einstein

The inhabitants of the border regions of the biosphere ought to adapt evolutionarily to extremely strict living conditions. This fact explains that they are usually referred to as extremophiles. In particular, barophiles (for example, some species of fish) are adapted to life under conditions of huge hydrostatic pressure of the ocean depths, which typically causes a disruption in the structure of proteins. In order to minimize the effect of such a press, barophiles produce special low-molecular organic oxygen-containing substances – osmolytes (for example, glycerol or glycine), which stabilize the structure of proteins due to the formation of hydrogen bonds.

The compound $\mathbf{X}$, a major osmolyte in deep-sea organisms, has the carbon to nitrogen mass ratio of 2.57:1. The number of atoms of any of the four elements in the molecule $\mathbf{X}$ can be represented as a power of three ($3^m$, where $m$ is an integer).

1. Prove by giving an appropriate mathematical expression (equation) that the molecular weight of any $\mathbf{X}$ with the formula matching the condition given above is always an odd number (provided that $A_r$ are rounded to the nearest integer).

$\mathbf{X}$ is degraded enzymatically according to the reaction equation:

$$\mathbf{X} \rightarrow \mathbf{X1} + \mathbf{X2}.$$

$\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{X2}$ are gaseous substances under standard conditions ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $1\,\mathrm{atm}$), toxic to humans. The densities of the substances strictly relate as 3:2, when using the atomic masses of the elements rounded to the nearest integer.

2. Determine the molecular formulas of $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{X2}$, keeping in mind that the integrality of the molecular weights is the key idea behind the solution. Show your calculations.

3. Determine the structure of $\mathbf{X}$ if all the carbon atoms in it are equivalent.

Available as a laboratory reagent, white crystalline substance $\mathbf{Y}$ ($M = 111\,\mathrm{g/mol}$), also has osmolyte properties and is used primarily in the study of protein folding to reduce the denaturing effect of urea. $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are identical according to the following: elemental composition (1), mass ratio of carbon and nitrogen (2), equivalence of carbon atoms (3).

4. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{Y}$, paying attention to the angles between the bonds.

The compound $\mathbf{Z}$ is another osmolyte in marine organisms. The functioning of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ is due to a similar structural motif. It is known that the number of hydrogen atoms ($N_\mathrm{H} \le 10$) in the molecule of $\mathbf{Z}$ is the product of the numbers (different from each other) of all other atoms (for example, for an arbitrary substance $\mathrm{C}_a\mathrm{H}_b\mathrm{O}_c\mathrm{N}_d$: $b = a \cdot c \cdot d$ with $a \ne c \ne d$).

$\mathbf{Z}$ is degraded enzymatically according to the reaction equation:

$$\mathbf{Z} \rightarrow \mathbf{Z1} + \ce{CH2=CH-COOH}.$$

5. For a theoretical structural formula of $\mathbf{Z}$, devoid of formal intramolecular charges on the atoms, prove by giving the corresponding molecular formula that of the four elements forming it, only one exhibits an odd valence (denote the unknown element $\mathbf{E}$). Indicate which coefficients in the formula support the proof.

$\mathbf{Z1}$ is non-enzymatically oxidized by molecular oxygen dissolved in sea water to a single product, $\mathbf{Z2}$ ($M = 78\,\mathrm{g/mol}$). The molecule of $\mathbf{Z2}$ contains one type of atom of each element.

6. Determine the molecular and structural formulas of $\mathbf{Z}$, $\mathbf{Z1}$ и $\mathbf{Z2}$. Prove by calculations.

problems.title: [The glyoxylate cycle]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [The glyoxylate cycle]

Metabolism is a paradoxical concept of sustaining life. Although enzymes are incredibly complex in their structure and function, most of substrates, intermediates and products are deceptively simple.

Some species can still grow and develop despite the lack of carbohydrates produced due to photosynthesis or obtained as nutrients. Such organisms can utilize C-2 compounds (molecules containing 2 carbon atoms) as growth substrates. In 1957, Krebs and Kronberg made seminal discovery of a pathway based on glyoxylate (Fig. 1) that solves this problem in plants, prokaryotes, and archaea.

In aqueous solutions, glyoxylic acid exists as a monohydrate (Fig. 2). Spectral analysis suggests an equilibrium with the symmetrical hemiacetal $\mathbf{X}$, formed when the monohydrate reacts with a non-hydrated glyoxylate in a 1:1 molar ratio.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-1-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Glyoxylate cycle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-1-4-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Monohydrate formation.

1. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{X}$.

2. Decipher the scheme in Fig. 1 if it is known that all metabolites within the cycle are composed of the same three elements and that the elemental composition in the table refers to the species found under physiological conditions at pH 7.4. Note that all the metabolites are acyclic products, whereas $\mathbf{A4}$ has E-Z isomers.

3. Write down the balanced net equation of the glyoxylate cycle. If needed, show the coenzyme A residue as –SCoA.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Metabolite} & \text{Overall charge (absolute value)} & \omega(\mathrm{C})\ (\%) \\ \hline \mathbf{A1} & 2 & 36.37 \\ \mathbf{A2} & 2 & 36.94 \\ \mathbf{A3} & 3 & 38.11 \\ \mathbf{A4} & 3 & 42.12 \\ \mathbf{A5} & 3 & 38.11 \\ \mathbf{A6} & 2 & 41.39 \end{array}$$

In 1959, Harold Kronberg, Kreb’s student, discovered that glyoxylate is biosynthesized from C-2 precursors $\mathbf{X1}$, $\mathbf{X2}$ and $\mathbf{X3}$.

4. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{X1}$, $\mathbf{X2}$ and $\mathbf{X3}$, considering the information in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} M\ \text{of the form prevailing at pH 7.4 (g/mol)} & n(\ce{CO2})/n(\ce{H2O})\ \text{from complete combustion of solid X(N)} & \text{Overall charge in an aqueous solution (absolute value)} \\ \hline \mathbf{X3} = \mathbf{X1}\ \text{(rounded to the integer)} & 1\ (\mathbf{X1}) & 1\ (\mathbf{X1}) \\ \mathbf{X2} - \mathbf{X1} = 13 & 2\ (\mathbf{X2}) & 2\ (\mathbf{X2}) \\ & 4/5\ (\mathbf{X3}) & 0\ (\mathbf{X3}) \end{array}$$

The following reaction sequence is found in some plants: $\mathbf{X1} \rightarrow \text{glyoxylate} \rightarrow \mathbf{X3}$.

5. From the list (amidase, oxidase, reductase, transamidase), choose the correct enzymes that are responsible for the $\mathbf{X1} \rightarrow \text{glyoxylate}$ and $\text{glyoxylate} \rightarrow \mathbf{X3}$ transformations.

Mammalian cells can also produce glyoxylate and pyruvate in mitochondria from the non-canonical amino acid 4-hydroxyproline, found as a residue in collagen (Fig. 3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-1-4-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Biosynthesis of glyoxylate from 4-hydroxyproline.

6. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{B1}$, $\mathbf{B2}$, and $\mathbf{B3}$. Note that the last step is catalyzed by aldolase.

7. Propose the scheme of a pathway leading from pyruvate to glyoxylate in organism.

problems.title: [Solubility of nanoparticles and Ostwald ripening]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Solubility of nanoparticles and Ostwald ripening]

The dependence of solubility of a solid substance $c$ on its particle size $r$ obeys the Gibbs–Freundlich–Ostwald equation:

$$c(r) = c_0\, e^{\frac{2\sigma V_\mathrm{m}}{rRT}}$$

($c_0$, $\sigma$, and $V_\mathrm{m}$ are the solubility of the macroscopic phase, specific surface energy, and molar volume of the substance, respectively; $R$ is the universal gas constant; $T$ is the absolute temperature). For a poorly soluble halide $\mathbf{X}$, the solubility of the nanoparticles with $r = 100\,\mathrm{nm}$ is by 9.3% higher compared to the macrophase at the temperature of $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\sigma = 450\,\mathrm{mJ/m^2}$, and density $d = 3.18\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

1. Calculate the molar volume of the halide $\mathbf{X}$. If you failed to determine $V_\mathrm{m}$, use $V_\mathrm{m} = 2.95\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^3/mol}$ in further calculations.

2. Calculate the molar mass and determine the formula of the halide $\mathbf{X}$.

The dependence of solubility on the particle size is behind the Ostwald ripening of precipitates. Since the solubility is increased with the decrease in the particle size, a solution saturated with respect to smaller particles is supersaturated with respect to the larger ones. This leads to gradual transfer of the matter from the smaller particles to the larger ones and, hence, overall increase in the particle size of the precipitate.

3. A specimen of the precipitate of $\mathbf{X}$ contains particles with the size of 40, 60, and 80 nm (10 g of each fraction). Calculate the average size of the particles in the specimen. Hereafter consider that the particles are cubic, their size $r$ corresponding to the edge length of the cube.

4. Calculate the solubility of each fraction if the solubility product of the macrophase is $K_\mathrm{sp} = 3\cdot10^{-11}$.

5. Calculate the average particle size in the precipitate once its Ostwald ripening is complete. Consider that ripening is possible if the solubility of the smaller (dissolving) particles exceeds $10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$, and the difference in the solubilities of the dissolving and growing particles exceeds 5%. Take that the rate of the particles growth is proportional to their initial surface area throughout the entire ripening process.

problems.title: [The salt X and the gases C and D]
problems.problem:
Problem 6. [The salt X and the gases C and D]

At $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the salt $\mathbf{X}$ exists as colorless crystals readily soluble in water. Heating the mixture of $\mathbf{X}$ with either an excess of $\mathbf{A}$ (solid at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $w(\mathrm{O}) = 43\%$ by mass) or an excess of $\mathbf{B}$ (solid at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $w(\mathrm{O}) = 65\%$ by mass) can be used as laboratory methods for obtaining small quantities of gaseous (at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$) binary substances $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$, respectively. $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are readily soluble in water.

If an equimolar amount of $\mathbf{D}$ is introduced into a sealed reactor filled with $\mathbf{C}$ at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$, then the pressure in the reactor decreases to almost zero. The osmotic pressure of the solution prepared from $677\,\mathrm{mg}$ $\mathbf{B}$ and $15.3\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is approximately equal to $1075\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

A saturated (at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) aqueous solution of $\mathbf{D}$ remains practically colorless when stored in air. To determine the concentration of $\mathbf{D}$ in such a solution, an aliquot of $1.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ was titrated with a pre-standardized $\ce{NaOH}$ solution. $26.13\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the alkali solution was consumed. To standardize the alkali solution, the hydrochloric acid was prepared as follows. A $10.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of the $\ce{HCl}$ solution saturated at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (41.8% by mass, density $1.202\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) was placed in a $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask and brought to the mark with water. $10.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the prepared hydrochloric acid was consumed to standardize a $10.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of the alkali solution.

1. Determine the composition and give the formulas of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{X}$. Support by calculations.

2. Write the equations of all the reactions described.

3. Propose a laboratory method for obtaining $\mathbf{D}$ different from that described in the task.

4. A heated concentrated aqueous solution of $\mathbf{X}$ reacts with magnesium. Write the equation of this reaction.

problems.title: [Intermolecular interactions]
problems.problem:
Problem 7. [Intermolecular interactions]

Interactions between molecules, atoms and ions are referred to as intermolecular. These are much weaker than the forces of covalent and ionic interactions, but their play a very important role. The energy ($E_1$) of the interaction of two atoms at the distance between the centers of which equals $R$ can be calculated using the equation:

$$E_1 = b\exp(-aR) - \frac{d}{R^6}.$$

The first term in this equation is responsible for repulsion which leads to an increase in the energy of the system, whereas the second one is responsible for the attraction between instantly induced dipoles which leads to a decrease in the energy of the system. Repulsion predominates at short distances, while attraction prevails at larger ones. Constants $a$, $b$ and $d$ depend on the electronic structure of the particles. The values of these constants (in atomic units, a.u.) for some pairs of atoms obtained from experimental data are given below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \text{He–He} & \text{He–Ne} & \text{He–Ar} & \text{He–Kr} & \text{He–Xe} \\ \hline a & 2.10 & 2.27 & 2.01 & 1.85 & 1.83 \\ b & 6.55 & 33.0 & 47.9 & 26.1 & 42.4 \\ d & 2.39 & 4.65 & 15.5 & 21.85 & 33.95 \end{array}$$

When doing calculations, you should use the value of $R$ in atomic units (a.u.). Potential energy is also obtained in a.u. A negative value of $E_1$ means that the energy of the system at this distance is by the value equal to the absolute value of $E_1$ less than the energy at an infinite distance between particles.

1. Calculate $E_1$ for the system of two He atoms for the distances $R$ equal to 5.00 a.u. and 7.00 a.u.

2. Using the method of successive approximations, estimate the maximum value by which the energy of the system of two He atoms can decrease due to intermolecular interaction.

If the interacting particles are charged, then the Coulomb interaction additionally arises between them, the potential energy of which ($E_2$, in a.u.) can be calculated using the formula:

$$E_2 = \frac{q_1 q_2}{R},$$

where $q_1$ and $q_2$ are the charges of particles in a.u. (1 a.u. of charge is equal to the absolute value of the electron charge), $R$ is the distance in a.u.

3. Let us consider the LiF molecule with a 100% ionic bond. The distance between the centers of the nuclei is $152\,\mathrm{pm}$. Calculate the energy of dissociation of the LiF molecule into ions:

$$\ce{LiF(g) = Li^+(g) + F^-(g)}.$$

Note: Isoelectronic particles have the same constants in the equation for $E_1$.

(If you failed to calculate the dissociation energy of LiF, then take it as $20.0\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$ in further calculations).

4. The ionization energy of the lithium atom is $5.39\,\mathrm{eV}$, and the electron affinity energy of the fluorine atom is $3.45\,\mathrm{eV}$. Calculate the molar bond energy of LiF.

Additional reference materials: 1 a.u. of length = $52.9\,\mathrm{pm}$; 1 a.u. of energy = $27.21\,\mathrm{eV}$.

problems.title: [Mass spectrometry of air]
problems.problem:
Problem 8. [Mass spectrometry of air]

Mass spectrometry is one of the most important methods of analytical chemistry, which allows us to determine the composition and structure of unknown substances. In this problem, you will analyze the results of two independent experiments.

Experiment 1. The mass spectrum of dried air with encoded signals $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{L}$ is given below. The mass spectrum shows the dependence of the signal intensity (Ion count) on the $m/z$ value ($m$ is the molecular mass of the particle, $z$ is the charge of the particle, the cation in this problem). All signals $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{L}$ are formed by five main components of air: $\ce{N2}$, $\ce{O2}$, $\ce{Ar}$, $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{H2O}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-1-8-fig1.png

1. For each signal $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{L}$, give the corresponding particle(s) with the particle charge and mass numbers of the elements.

Experiment 2. The composition of a sample can be estimated from the ratio of signal intensities ($I$) in a mass spectrum. In the experiment, five tests were performed in air in a closed system: 1) 4 human inhalations–exhalations; 2) photosynthesis of a plant (1 day); 3) rusting of iron (30 min); 4) combustion of octane (5 min); 5) decomposition of hydrogen peroxide under the action of baker’s yeast (5 min).

2. Give the reaction equations occurring in the described tests.

The air at the end of each test was then analyzed by mass spectrometry. The results of the experiment are summarized in the table:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{Sample} & I(\ce{O2})/I(\ce{N2}) & I(\ce{O2})/I(\ce{Ar}) & I(\ce{CO2})/I(\ce{Ar}) & I(\ce{H2O})/I(\ce{Ar}) \\ \hline \text{Air (initial)} & 0.214 & 14.4 & 0.23 & 3.2 \\ \text{Sample }\mathbf{I} & 0.179 & 12.1 & 0.35 & 3.6 \\ \text{Sample }\mathbf{II} & 1.97 & 130 & 2.9 & 5.1 \\ \text{Sample }\mathbf{III} & 0.181 & 11.6 & 12.2 & 3.7 \\ \text{Sample }\mathbf{IV} & 0.226 & 16.1 & 0 & 3.7 \\ \text{Sample }\mathbf{V} & 0.054 & 3.3 & 35 & 5.35 \end{array}$$

3. Calculate the content (mol.%) of all components in the initial air.

4. Assign the samples $\mathbf{I}$–$\mathbf{V}$ to the five tests performed. Confirm your answer with calculations or by comparing the numerical values you used.

5. Provide a reaction equation that can explain the increased $\ce{CO2}$ content in the sample $\mathbf{II}$.

problems.title: [Rotational-vibrational spectra of diatomic molecules]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (Physical chemistry section, problem 1). [Rotational-vibrational spectra of diatomic molecules]

Diatomic are the simplest molecules. Accordingly, they have been investigated in detail both theoretically and experimentally. Rotational-vibrational spectroscopy is among the most important methods for studying diatomic molecules. The “Harmonic oscillator – rigid rotator” approximation is a basic model for the description of the vibrational-rotational spectra. Within this model, the types of intermolecular motion under discussion are independent, whereas their energy levels are as follows:

$$E_\mathrm{vib} = \omega_e\left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right), \qquad E_\mathrm{rot} = B_e J(J+1),$$

where $\omega_e = h\nu$ is the vibrational constant, $\nu$ is the frequency of vibrations, $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ is the vibrational quantum number, $B_e = h^2/(8\pi^2\mu r_e^2)$ is the rotational constant, $\mu = m_\mathrm{A}m_\mathrm{B}/(m_\mathrm{A} + m_\mathrm{B})$ is the reduced mass of the molecule, $r_e$ is the equilibrium internuclear distance, $J = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ is the rotational quantum number. Only $(n, J) \rightarrow (n \pm 1, J \pm 1)$ transitions are allowed.

For the HF molecule, the energy of transition from the ground vibrational, ground rotational level to the first vibrational, first rotational level equals $\Delta E(0, 0 \rightarrow 1, 1) = 4180.23\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$; the energy of transition from the ground vibrational, first rotational level to the first vibrational, ground rotational level is $\Delta E(0, 1 \rightarrow 1, 0) = 4096.41\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

1. Calculate $\omega_e$ and $B_e$ in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

2. Calculate $\nu$ in Hz and $r_e$ in Å.

The model of anharmonic oscillator allows a more precise description of the molecular vibrations. In this model, the energy of the $n$th vibrational level equals:

$$E_\mathrm{vib} = \omega_e\left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right) - \omega_e x_e\left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2,$$

where $\omega_e x_e$ is the anharmonicity constant. Decrease in the distance between the neighboring levels ($n$ and $n + 1$) is a specific feature of the model. This leads to the equality of energies $E_\mathrm{vib}(n)$ and $E_\mathrm{vib}(n + 1)$ for a definite $n_\mathrm{max}$, which is due to the absence of the vibrational levels for $n > n_\mathrm{max}$, since the molecule dissociates into atoms above this level.

3. Express $n_\mathrm{max}$ in terms of $\omega_e$ and $\omega_e x_e$.

4. Express the dissociation energy in terms of $\omega_e$ and $\omega_e x_e$.

Beside this, the rotational-vibrational interaction can occur, due to which the rotational constant $B_e$ depends on vibrational state $n$:

$$E_\mathrm{rot} = B_n J(J+1), \qquad B_n = B_e - \alpha_e\left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right),$$

where $\alpha_e$ is the constant of the rotational-vibrational interaction.

5. From the following options, select those, which correctly explain why $B_n$ depends on $n$:
the kinetic energy of rotation of the molecule increases with an increase of $n$;
the average bond length in the molecule changes with an increase of $n$;
due to the repulsion of the atoms, the molecule is rather stretched than compressed during oscillations;
due to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the bond length permanently changes.

Methylidyne CH is the smallest molecule, which can be notionally named organic. Though the radical its extremely unstable, it was detected spectroscopically in the so-called CH-stars. Also, it is involved in the Fischer–Tropsch process. Spectral properties of CH are well studied. The energies ($\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) of some rotational-vibrational transitions are given below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & n = 0 \rightarrow n = 1 & n = 1 \rightarrow n = 2 \\ \hline J = 0 \rightarrow J = 1 & 2759.77 & 2632.66 \\ J = 1 \rightarrow J = 2 & 2785.97 & 2657.79 \end{array}$$

6. Using the data in the table, calculate $\omega_e$, $\omega_e x_e$, $B_e$, and $\alpha_e$ in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

7. Using the expression derived in i. 4, calculate the dissociation energy of the C−H bond in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. If you failed to answer i. 4, use the approximate formula $E \approx \omega_e^2/(4\omega_e x_e)$.

8. Calculate the length of the C−H bond in Å.

Reference materials:

Masses of isotopes (a.m.u.): $m(\mathrm{F}) = 18.9984$, $m(\mathrm{C}) = 12.0000$, $m(\mathrm{H}) = 1.0078$.

Conversion of reciprocal centimeters to joules: $E(\mathrm{J}) = 100hcE(\mathrm{cm^{-1}})$.

$h = 6.626\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}$ is the Planck constant, $c = 2.998\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is the speed of light, $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.022\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$ is the Avogadro’s number.

problems.title: [Ligand field theory and magnetic susceptibility]
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (Physical chemistry section, problem 2). [Ligand field theory and magnetic susceptibility]

Despite its simplicity, the Ligand Field Theory (LFT) satisfactorily explains most of the magnetic and spectral properties of complex compounds of transition elements. Ligands are considered as a source of an electrostatic field with certain symmetry, acting on the electronic system of the central ion. The field shifts the energy levels (terms) of the free ion and splits them. The magnitude and nature of splitting depend on the field strength of the ligands and their location.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-2-fig1.png

Figure 1

Fig. 1 shows the shape of the five $d$-orbitals of a free atom or ion and the arrangement of ligands in an octahedral environment. The three orbitals in the top row are geometrically equivalent. The two orbitals in the bottom row are also equivalent to each other, despite their different appearance.

1. What is the degeneracy factor ($g$) of the energy level of a free ion with a single $d$-electron over the closed shells?

2. Draw a diagram of the level splitting of the central ion in the octahedral complex $\ce{[Ti(H2O)6]^{3+}}$. For split levels, give Mulliken notation based on the symbols for irreducible representations of group theory.

In an octahedral field, the levels are split in the proportion 3 : 2 (relative to the “center of gravity”, i.e. the energy of an ion placed in a spherical shell with the charge equal to the sum of the ligand charges). Let us denote the energy interval between split levels as $\Delta_o$, and the pairing energy of electrons in one orbital as $P$.

3. Distribute electrons onto the energy levels for the low-spin (LS) and high-spin (HS) the states of the complex with the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ion. Indicate the total spin $S$ of the complex and the type of magnetism (paramagnetic/diamagnetic).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-2-fig2.png

4. Find the relationship between $\Delta_o$ and $P$, at which the energies of the LS and HS states of the octahedral complex formed by the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ion are the same.

For the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ion $P = 17600\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and for the complexes $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^{2+}}$ and $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^{4-}}$ $\Delta_o = 10400\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and $33000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, respectively.

5. Which one is high-spin and which one is low-spin?

Fig. 2 shows the dependence of the term energy of the $\ce{Ni^{2+}}$ ion in an octahedral field on the strength of the ligands. For $\ce{[Ni(NH3)6]^{2+}}$ $\Delta_o = 10800\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-2-fig3.png

Figure 2

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-2-fig4.png

Figure 3

6. How many bands are there in the absorption spectrum associated with the $d$–$d$ transitions from the ground electronic state of this complex (choose the correct answer: 3, 6 or 9)? Predict the frequencies ($\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) of the absorption band maxima.

The magnetic susceptibility of a unit volume of a substance $\chi_\mathrm{V}$ (a dimensionless quantity) can be measured by the Gouy method following the apparent change in the mass of the sample in a non-uniform magnetic field (Fig. 3). The magnetic force acting on the sample is:

$$F = \tfrac{1}{2}\chi_\mathrm{V} H^2 \sigma\ \mathrm{dyn}, \qquad (1)$$

where $H$ is the field strength (Gauss, Gs) at the level of the ampoule bottom, $\sigma$ is the ampoule cross section area ($\mathrm{cm^2}$).

The empiric formula for calculating the specific susceptibility (per 1 g of substance) of Mohr’s salt $\ce{(NH4)2Fe(SO4)2*6H2O}$ is:

$$\chi_\mathrm{S} = \frac{9.5}{T+1}\cdot10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm^3/g}, \qquad (2)$$

where $T$ is the temperature in Kelvins. The salt crystals have a cubic structure with the lattice parameter $a = 1.2318\,\mathrm{nm}$, the unit cell contains $Z = 4$ formula units. The salt is placed in a cylindrical ampoule with the diameter $d = 1.4\,\mathrm{cm}$. At $H = 5000\,\mathrm{Gs}$, $\Delta m = 0.868\,\mathrm{g}$.

7. Determine the density $\rho$ ($\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) of the Mohr’s salt crystals and calculate $\chi_\mathrm{S}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assuming that the sample is tightly packed in the ampoule, calculate the $\chi_\mathrm{V}$ of Mohr’s salt.

On the other hand, the molar susceptibility can be expressed as

$$\chi_\mathrm{M} = \frac{N_\mathrm{A}\mu_\mathrm{eff}^2}{3k_\mathrm{B}T}\ \mathrm{cm^3\cdot mol^{-1}}, \qquad (3)$$

where $N_\mathrm{A}$ is the Avogadro’s number, $k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant, $\mu_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective magnetic moment of the central ion in Bohr magnetons $\mu_\mathrm{B} = 0.917\cdot10^{-20}\,\mathrm{erg/Gs}$.

8. Find $\chi_\mathrm{M}$ and determine $\mu_\mathrm{eff}$ of Mohr’s salt in Bohr magnetons at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Expression (3) does not account for the constantly present diamagnetism reducing the susceptibility. The magnetic moment, which is due only to the spin of the central ion, is given as (in Bohr magnetons):

$$\mu_S = 2\sqrt{S(S+1)} = \sqrt{n(n+2)}, \qquad (4)$$

where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

9. Assuming that the magnetic moment of Mohr's salt is determined only by the spin of the $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ion, use the expression (4) to estimate whether this complex is low-spin or high-spin.

Reference materials:

The degeneracy of an energy level is the number of different states corresponding to the given level.

In question 6, in the symbols of the terms of the free ion (on the left) and the split terms (on the right), only the superscripts (multiplicities) are important. The latter are equal to $2S + 1$, where $S$ is the total spin of the $d$-shell of the ion.

Acceleration of free fall near the earth's surface $g = 981\,\mathrm{cm/s^2}$; 1 N (Newton) = $10^5$ dyn, 1 J (Joule) = $10^7$ erg; $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.022\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$; $k_\mathrm{B} = 1.38\cdot10^{-16}\,\mathrm{erg/K}$; 1 a.m.u. = $1.66\cdot10^{-24}\,\mathrm{g}$.

problems.title: [Activation of hydrogen by metal cations]
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (Physical chemistry section, problem 3). [Activation of hydrogen by metal cations]

In $\ce{H2}$ + oxidant (Ox) reactions, metal cations are able to activate $\ce{H2}$ in a solution because of homo- or heterolytic cleavage of the H−H bond, whereas [Ox] is not included in the kinetic equation.

1. Illustrate both types of the H−H bond cleavage using Lewis formulas.

2. Derive the equation and calculate the enthalpies of the transitions $\ce{H2(aq) = 2H(aq)}$ and $\ce{H2(aq) = H^+(aq) + H^-(aq)}$, if the enthalpies of hydration are (kJ/mol): −1088 ($\ce{H+}$); −452 ($\ce{H-}$); −9 ($\ce{H2}$); −13 (H), and standard enthalpies of formation are (kJ/mol): 1536 ($\ce{H+}$); 140 ($\ce{H-}$); 0 ($\ce{H2}$); 218 (H).

Calvin showed that $\ce{Cu+}$ salts with organic anions catalyze the $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ reduction with dissolved $\ce{H2}$, which dissociates homolytically according to the hereunder mechanism, the dissociation being the rate-limiting step:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{2Cu+ + H2 <=> (Cu^{+}*H)2} & (k_1;\ k_{-1}), \\ \ce{(Cu^{+}H)2 + 2Cu^{2+} -> 4Cu+ + 2H+} & (k_2). \end{array}$$

3. Derive the kinetic equation for the reaction.

Halpern and Peters showed that in the absence of $\ce{Cu+}$ activation of $\ce{H2}$ by $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ cation in $\ce{HClO4}$ solution leads to the reaction order change from 2 to 3 with increasing $[\ce{H+}]$ according to the mechanism:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{Cu^{2+} + H2 <=> Cu^{+}H + H+} & (k_3;\ k_{-3}), \\ \ce{CuH+ + Cu^{2+} -> 2Cu+ + H+} & (k_4), \\ \ce{2Cu+} + \text{Cr(VI) substrate} \rightarrow \text{Cr(III) products} + \ce{2Cu^{2+}} & (k_\mathrm{ox},\ \text{fast}). \end{array}$$

4. Derive the kinetic equation for the reaction and give the condition under which the change in the reaction order is possible.

A similar equation but with a more complex expression for the reaction rate was obtained by Halpern when studying the kinetics of Cr(VI) reduction with activation of $\ce{H2}$ by the $\ce{Ag+}$ cation:

$$d[\ce{H2}]/d\tau = k[\ce{Ag+}]^2[\ce{H2}] + k_5[\ce{Ag+}]^2[\ce{H2}]/([\ce{Ag+}] + k_{-5}/k_6[\ce{H+}]).$$

5. Indicate whether this rate equation corresponds to homo- or heterolytic dissociation of $\ce{H2}$. Suggest the reaction mechanism and equation for $k_\mathrm{obs}$, if a binuclear intermediate is formed at the second step.

For the reaction at $27\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $[\ce{Ag+}] = 1\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ in the $\ce{HClO4}$ medium, Halpern obtained the data given in the table and the equation: $k = 6.8\cdot10^7\cdot e^{-14666/RT}$ ($R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}$).

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{pH} & 1 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 8 & 10 \\ \hline k_\mathrm{obs}\cdot10^5,\ \mathrm{L/(mol\cdot s)} & 1.995 & 11.31 & 87.01 & 436.7 & 739.9 & 801.2 & 801.9 \end{array}$$

6. Draw the $k_\mathrm{obs} = f(\mathrm{pH})$ plot and explain its S-shape, indicating the assumptions that must be made.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-3-fig1.png

7. Specify the coordinates, which will allow rectilinear function for the data given in the table. Show how to calculate $k_5$ and $a = k_{-5}/k_6$ from it.

8. Calculate $k$, $k_5$ and $a = k_{-5}/k_6$, using the data for pH = 4 and pH = 5.

problems.title: [Optical chemical dosimeter for nitrogen dioxide]
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 1). [Optical chemical dosimeter for nitrogen dioxide]

Monitoring the concentration of nitrogen oxides in the air of industrial premises is an important task for nitrogen industry enterprises. Development of optical chemical dosimeters that show excess concentrations of nitrogen oxides is one of approaches towards solving this problem. Determination of nitrogen dioxide concentration often involves disproportionation according to the reaction 1 ($\ce{NO2}$ dimerization is neglected due to low concentrations):

$$\ce{2NO2_{(g)} + H2O = NO2^-_{(aq)} + NO3^-_{(aq)} + 2H^+_{(aq)}} \qquad (1)$$

Colorimetric determination of the resulting nitrite can be achieved using the diazotization reaction with subsequent azo coupling.

1. Write down the equation for the reaction of 4-nitroaniline (4-NA) with nitrite ion in an acidic medium affording the 4-nitrophenyldiazonium salt (reaction 2).

The resulting diazonium salt enters an azo coupling reaction with chromotropic acid Chr (see the fig.), that reacts at one of the ortho (with respect to the OH group) positions to form the dye “Acid Red 176”.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-4-fig1.png

2. Write down the equation for the azo coupling (reaction 3) and the structure of the resulting dye.

3. Write down the expressions in accordance with the law of mass action (assume that the assay system contains a buffer medium and do not include the $\ce{H+}$ concentration in the expressions):
a) for the rate $v_1$ of the formation of nitrite ion by reaction 1, rate constant $k_1 = 1\cdot10^5\,\mathrm{L/(mol\cdot s)}$;
b) for the rate $v_2$ of the formation of 4-nitrophenyldiazonium according to reaction 2, the rate constant $k_2 = 1.0\,\mathrm{L/(mol\cdot s)}$;
c) for the rate $v_3$ of the formation of Acid Red according to reaction 3, rate constant $k_3 = 1\cdot10^2\,\mathrm{L/(mol\cdot s)}$.

4. Assume that all the reactions occur on an indicator paper in a film of adsorbed water with the total volume of $50\,\mathrm{\mu L}$, the concentrations of 4-nitroaniline and chromotropic acid in which are 0.1 M each.
a) Calculate the rate of nitrite formation in such aqueous solution by reaction 1 if the concentration of $\ce{NO2}$ in air corresponds to the maximum permissible concentration (MPC) equal to $5\,\mathrm{mg/m^3}$.
b) At what time will the rate of nitrite consumption by reaction 2 become equal to that of its formation by reaction 1? Take the concentration of 4-nitroaniline equal to 0.1 M.
c) What is the rate of formation of Acid Red (P) at a reaction time much higher than the value you found in i. b?
d) Draw qualitatively the dependences of the concentrations of the diazonium salt and Acid Red in the indicator paper on time at reaction times much higher than the value you found in i. b.
e) The color of the indicator paper becomes noticeable when it contains Acid Red in the amount of $5\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{mol}$. What is the time of the color appearance after introducing the paper into the atmosphere of $\ce{NO2}$ with the concentration equal to the MPC?

5. a) Assume that if conducting an infinite number of experiments with concentrations of nitrogen oxides equal to the MPC, the signal (color) is observed in 90% of the experiments. Two similar experiments were carried out at the concentration equal to the MPC. What is the probability that nitrogen oxides will be detected (“Yes, the concentration of nitrogen oxides has reached the MPC”)? In the case of one positive and one negative result, the answer will be uncertain.
b) How many parallel experiments must be carried out in order to judge that the MPC is exceeded with at least 95% probability?

problems.title: [1-Hydroxyimidazoles: tautomerism and extraction]
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 2). [1-Hydroxyimidazoles: tautomerism and extraction]

On May 8, 1980, the World Health Organization declared the complete liquidation of smallpox, therefore, the universal vaccination of the population was stopped. For this reason, the number of people susceptible to this infection increases every year. In previously immunized populations, immunity against smallpox viruses weakens by half every ten years, so the number of human-to-human infections, such as monkeypox virus, is increasing. 1-Hydroxyimidazole derivatives inhibit the smallpox virus and at the same time have low cytotoxicity. The new 1-hydroxyimidazole derivatives were prepared according to the following scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-5-fig1.png

1. Determine the structures of $\mathbf{X}$–$\mathbf{P}$, if $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ are isomers and $\mathbf{P}$ is a zwitter ion.

$\mathbf{X}$ is in a tautomer equilibrium with $\mathbf{A}$ in aqueous solution. The equilibrium constant of tautomerism is $K_\mathrm{AX} = \frac{[\mathrm{X}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = 0.09$.

2. Determine the molar fraction of $\mathbf{X}$ (%) in the aqueous solution after equilibrium has been established.

3. Determine the structure of $\mathbf{A}$.

Twice the volume of aniline was added to the aqueous solution of $\mathbf{A}$, and the mixture was shaken. The equilibrium of tautomerism in the organic phase is shifted toward $\mathbf{X}$, as can be decided from the value of the equilibrium constant $K_\mathrm{A_1X_1} = \frac{[\mathrm{X_1}]}{[\mathrm{A_1}]}$, which is 25 times higher than the tautomerism constant for the aqueous solution.

4. Determine the total yield of $\mathbf{X}$ (%) if isolation of this compound from the organic phase is being done after establishing the extraction and tautomerism equilibria; take $K_\mathrm{AA_1} = \frac{[\mathrm{A_1}]}{[\mathrm{A}]} = 1$.

By adding hexane ($\ce{C6H14}$), which is immiscible with water and aniline, a three-phase system can be obtained and described by the following equilibria:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-5-fig2.png

5. Determine the unknown equilibrium constants (write them for the “left-to-right” and “top-to-bottom” transitions).

6. Determine the total yield of $\mathbf{X}$ (%) that can be isolated from the organic phases, if 1 M aqueous solution of $\mathbf{A}$ is extracted with equal volumes of aniline and hexane added simultaneously ($V^\mathrm{aq} = V_1^\mathrm{org} = V_2^\mathrm{org} = 1\,\mathrm{L}$).

7. One volume of an aqueous solution of $\mathbf{X}$ was contacted with different volumes of other solvents and shaken (experiments a–d). Arrange the experiments in the increasing order of the yield of $\mathbf{X}$ when isolated from the organic phase(s).
a) Equal volume of aniline and hexane.
b) Equal volume of aniline.
c) Twice the volume of hexane.
d) Twice the volume of aniline.

problems.title: [Blood alcohol content]
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (Analytical chemistry section, problem 3). [Blood alcohol content]

Alcohol, depending on its content in the human body, leads to various negative effects. Blood alcohol content (BAC) is usually calculated as the mass of ethanol (g) in a unit volume of blood (L) or expressed as a percentage (BAC of 1% corresponds to 1 g of ethanol in 100 mL of blood). The Widmark formula can be used to estimate BAC (in g/L) from the amount of alcohol consumed:

$$\mathrm{BAC} = \frac{a}{V_\mathrm{d}} - \beta t = \frac{a}{m\cdot k_\mathrm{d}} - \beta t,$$

where $a$ is the mass of ethanol consumed (g); $V_\mathrm{d}$ is the volume of ethanol distribution in the body (L); $m$ is the mass of a person (kg); $k_\mathrm{d}$ is the Widmark distribution coefficient, which is equal to 0.71 and $0.58\,\mathrm{L/kg}$ for males and females, respectively; $\beta$ is the rate of ethanol elimination, averaging $0.15\,\mathrm{g/(L\cdot h)}$; $t$ is the time since alcohol consumption (h).

1. Calculate how many times the lethal dose of ethanol for a female weighing 60 kg is less than that for a male weighing 80 kg. Consider that the effect of alcohol is determined only by its concentration in the blood, regardless of gender.

The vast majority of countries have BAC limits for drivers. The maximum allowed BAC ranges from 0 (total ban) to 0.08%, e.g. in China the BAC limit is 0.02%.

2. Calculate the maximum volume $V_\mathrm{max}$ (mL) of the Chinese alcoholic beverage Huangjiu ("yellow wine") with the ethanol content ($\varphi$) of 10 vol.% that can be drunk by a male weighing 80 kg 30 min before driving. The density of pure ethanol ($\rho$) is $0.789\,\mathrm{g/mL}$.

Note! Despite acceptable BAC values other than 0 (which is due to metabolic peculiarities in different people), drinking alcohol before driving is extremely unsafe!

The determination of BAC can be carried out using a variety of analytical methods. For quick analysis, such as when checking drivers on the road, breathalyzers are used to determine the amount of ethanol in one’s breath. One of the first breathalyzers was developed by R.F. Borkenstein. Exhaled air was passed through a solution of $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ in the presence of $\ce{H2SO4}$ and small amounts of $\ce{AgNO3}$. The intensity of the color change from orange to blue-green was used to conclude the degree of intoxication of the person being tested.

3. Write down the reaction equation that underlies the Borkenstein breathalyzer.

To find the amount of reacted $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ and thus ethanol in the sample, it is possible to use the spectrophotometric method. The table summarizes the results of absorbance ($A$) measurements from testing people with different levels of BAC. Measurements were made at a wavelength at which absorbance by the reaction products can be neglected. The volume of solution in the breathalyzer is 3.0 mL and the volume of exhaled air is 1.0 L. Assume that 1 mL of blood contains on average the same amount of ethanol as 2100 mL of exhaled air.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{BAC} & 0.000\% & 0.030\% & 0.060\% & 0.100\% & 0.150\% \\ \hline A & 0.898 & 0.640 & 0.382 & 0.150 & 0.150 \end{array}$$

4. Calculate the maximum $\mathrm{BAC_{max}}$ value (%) that can be numerically determined with this breathalyzer.

5. Calculate the concentration $c(\ce{K2Cr2O7})_0$ (mM) in the stock solution. Assume that the volume of the solution in the breathalyzer does not change when passing the analyzed breath.

In hospitals, an enzymatic assay (EA) is often used to determine BAC. For this, the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) is added to blood serum, resulting in the oxidation of ethanol with the coenzyme $\ce{NAD+}$. The BAC can be calculated by measuring the absorbance of the solution.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-6-fig1.png

6. Write down the equation of the reaction occurring during the EA of ethanol in blood serum.

7. Using the given UV absorption spectrum of $\ce{NAD+}$ and NADH, give the value of wavelength $\lambda$ (nm) that is optimal for measuring the absorbance for BAC calculation.

When analyzing samples with a complex matrix, such as blood serum, the method of standard additions is used. For this purpose, known amounts of the determined substance are introduced into the analyzed sample, and the EA of the resulting solutions is carried out. As a result of such analysis, the following calibration dependence of absorbance ($A$) on the concentration of added ethanol ($c_\mathrm{add}$, $\mathrm{\mu M}$) was obtained: $A = 6.20\cdot10^{-3}\cdot c_\mathrm{add} + 0.155$. Calibration solutions were prepared by adding the calculated amounts of the standard ethanol solution to the $100\,\mathrm{\mu L}$ aliquots of blood serum followed by dilution with the physiological solution to 1.00 mL.

8. Calculate the concentration of ethanol $c(\mathrm{EtOH})$ ($\mathrm{\mu M}$) in the analyzed blood serum.

problems.title: [A drug for bone metastases]
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (Life sciences and polymers section, problem 1). [A drug for bone metastases]

A drug based on the compound $\mathbf{X}$ ($M = 696\,\mathrm{g/mol}$) is used to reduce pain in patients with malignant neoplasms complicated by tumor metastasis to the bones.

$\mathbf{X}$ is obtained from the organic acid $\mathbf{Y}$, the non-ionized form of which has 3 types of H atoms, 2 types of each of C and O atoms, and 1 type of N atoms.

It is known that the fraction of protons ($p$, elementary particles) belonging to the carbon atoms from the number of protons of all atoms in the molecule of $\mathbf{Y}$ is 15.93%. Similar fractions for hydrogen and nitrogen atoms in $\mathbf{Y}$ are 8.85% and 6.19%, respectively. Assume that the molecule of $\mathbf{Y}$ is formed exclusively by atoms of the most common isotopes in nature of each of the five elements.

1. From the four elements mentioned above, select those for which the ratio of mass fractions and that of the sums of protons of all identical atoms in the molecule of $\mathbf{Y}$ numerically coincide pairwise [in other words, the equality $\omega(\mathrm{El}_1) : \omega(\mathrm{El}_2) = N_p(\mathrm{El}_1) : N_p(\mathrm{El}_2)$ is true].

The total number of atoms of the five elements that form the non-ionized form of $\mathbf{Y}$ is 44.

2. Find the total number of protons of all atoms in the molecule of $\mathbf{Y}$. Prove by calculations.

3. Find the molecular formula of $\mathbf{Y}$. Prove by calculations.

It is known that $\mathbf{Y}$ can be obtained by prolonged heating of ethylenediamine, formaldehyde and inorganic acid $\mathbf{A}$ in a strongly acidic medium.

4. Find the structure of $\mathbf{Y}$.

$\mathbf{X}$ is a neutral double salt containing, among other things, the cation of an alkali metal (represented by the most abundant isotope) and the anion of the acid $\mathbf{Y}$. The total number of atoms of all elements forming $\mathbf{X}$ is 42, and the total number of protons is 335

5. Deduce the structure of $\mathbf{X}$.

When a sealed ampoule containing an aqueous solution of $\mathbf{X}$ is left standing for a long time, the compound $\mathbf{Z}$ ($M = 696\,\mathrm{g/mol}$) is formed, which does not undergo further transformations. The reaction behind this process determines the therapeutic effect of the drug.

6. Deduce the structure of $\mathbf{Z}$.

7. Write down the equation for the reaction underlying the mechanism of action of the pharmaceutical based on $\mathbf{X}$.

8. Write down the equation for the reaction explaining how $\mathbf{X}$ predominantly accumulates in bone tissue.

9. Select the most rational way in clinical practice (peroral, intravenous, rectal or by inhalation) for administering the drug based on $\mathbf{X}$ into the human body.

Problem 8 (Life sciences and polymers section, problem 2). [DNA-cross-linked polymer hydrogels]

The interaction of complementary nucleobases (A–T and G–C) leads to the formation of reversible noncovalent crosslinks (double-helix fragments of DNA) between the chains of the polymer $\mathbf{P1}$. This polymer was synthesized via AIBN-initiated radical copolymerization and then modified with oligonucleotide fragment $\mathbf{ODN}$, which allowed transformation of an aqueous solution of the linear polymer into insoluble cross-linked gel by tuning the external conditions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-8-fig1.png

$\mathbf{ODN}$, a 20-unit oligonucleotide containing terminal n-dodecylamine moiety, was prepared via the synthesis on solid substrate $\mathbf{SS}$ bearing surface −COCl groups. In the structures of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{NB}$ stands for a nucleobase (A, C, G, T).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-8-fig2.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-8-fig3.png

1. $\mathbf{P}$ consists of two types of repeat units. A sample of $\mathbf{P}$ (mass of 2.00 g) was treated with 10.00 mL of NaOH (0.100 mol/L), and then excess of alkali was titrated with 1.60 mL of HCl (0.400 mol/L). Draw the structures of the repeat units in $\mathbf{P}$ and determine the molar fraction of the units containing the succinimide group.

2. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{SS1}$–$\mathbf{SS4}$ formed after one cycle of steps 3–5. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{ODN}$ and denote the 3'- and 5'-ends of the oligonucleotide part of the molecules. Use the $\mathbf{SS}$ and $\mathbf{NB}$ notation in the structures.

3. Complete the partially deciphered nucleotide sequence of $\mathbf{ODN}$ to obtain the sequence affording the most efficient pairing with the $\mathbf{ODN}$ fragment of another polymer chain. Calculate the molar mass of $\mathbf{ODN}$. If you have failed to determine the sequence of $\mathbf{ODN}$, consider its composition to be $\mathrm{A_4C_{10}T_6}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-8-fig4.png

4. The interaction of $\mathbf{P}$ with $\mathbf{ODN}$ is accompanied by hydrolysis of the succinimide units, conversion of the latter being complete. Draw the structures of the repeat units in $\mathbf{P1}$ and calculate the molar fraction of the $\mathbf{ODN}$-modified units to the hydrolyzed units in the product if the mass fraction of phosphorus in $\mathbf{P1}$ is 2.19% (consider the acidic groups to be in the protonated state).

5. Determine the lowest average molar mass of $\mathbf{P1}$, macromolecules of which can be converted into a gel (completely cross-linked into a joint structure). Consider the complementary pairing of $\mathbf{ODN}$ to be quantitative.

6. Give the range of acidity of the aqueous solution within which $\mathbf{P1}$ can form insoluble hydrogel via complementary pairing of the $\mathbf{ODN}$ fragments. Point at the pH value, at which the non-porous hydrogel of $\mathbf{P1}$ being at equilibrium with the aqueous medium absorbs the largest amount of water.

Hydrogels formed via self-assembly of DNA macromolecules avoiding the use of additional reagents are of special interest.

7. The structure of the DNA sample $\mathbf{Q}$ is formed via repetition of the 5'−CACAGTCGCGTTAGGTAAACGAAT−3' fragment. Suggest a sequence of the DNA molecule capable (upon interaction with two fragments of $\mathbf{Q}$) of formation of an element of three-dimensional network with three DNA chains meeting at each node of it. There are no single-strand parts in the formed network, and the length of the linker between the macromolecules $\mathbf{Q}$ is 12 base pairs. Complete the scheme of the formation of the network element containing molecules of $\mathbf{Q}$ (already drawn as lines) and the molecule(s) suggested by you (complete the drawing). Assign the 3'- and 5'-ends of all chains.
