problems.title: "Dark-cell" tumor
problems.problem:
Problem 9 (Life sciences and polymers section, problem 3). "Dark-cell" tumor

Pheochromocytoma (PCC) is a hormone-producing tumor causing periodic acute increase in blood pressure, phenoxybenzamine being the drug of choice for its reduction. It can block irreversibly the receptors covalently binding to a cysteine residue according to $\mathrm{S_N1}$ mechanism (see the hereunder scheme, $\mathbf{I}$ is the most stable intermediate):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-9-fig1.png

1. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{I}$ and the product of its interaction with the receptor.

The interaction of the hormone (L) produced by PCC with the receptor (R) can be described by a dynamic equilibrium with the dissociation constant $K_\mathrm{d}$.

$$\ce{L + R <=>[][$K_\mathrm{d}$] LR} \qquad (1)$$

2. Derive the dependence of the fraction ($\theta$) of the receptor bound to the hormone on the hormone concentration for scheme (1).

In some cases, more than one equivalent of a hormone can bind to its receptor:

$$\ce{$n$L + R <=>[][$K_\mathrm{d}$] L_{$n$}R} \qquad (2)$$

Then the dependence of the fraction of the receptor bound to the hormone ($\theta$) on the hormone concentration is described by the Hill equation.

3. Derive the Hill equation.

4. Derive the linear form of the Hill equation.

The Hill equation can be used to describe the dose–effect relationship (the dependence of the effect of the receptor stimulation on the hormone concentration).

5. Choose the graph of the dose–effect relationship describing the effect of phenoxybenzamine (the bold line corresponds to the graph before the drug administration).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-9-fig2.png

6. What is the hormone concentration that corresponds to the half-maximal effect of the receptor stimulation?

Diagnostics of PCC begins with the laboratory analysis of the concentration of $\mathbf{M1}$ and $\mathbf{M2}$ (products of enzymatic breakdown of hormones) in urine. $\mathbf{M1}$ and $\mathbf{M2}$ are formed as a result of the reaction catalyzed by the enzyme COMT as shown in scheme (3). The final metabolite $\mathbf{B}$ is an intermediate in the organic synthesis of a well-known confectionery flavoring (part of this synthesis is shown framed).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-9-fig3.png

Addition of iron(III) chloride to the $\mathbf{R\text{-}H}$ solution results in an emerald-green coloration. When reacted with iron(III) chloride, the isomers $\mathbf{R'\text{-}H}$ and $\mathbf{R''\text{-}H}$ are colored dark purple and brown, respectively. The mass fraction of oxygen $\omega(\mathrm{O})$ in $\mathbf{M1}$ is by 1.0767 times higher than that in $\mathbf{M2}$.

7. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{R\text{-}H}$, $\mathbf{R'\text{-}H}$, and $\mathbf{R''\text{-}H}$.

8. From the options given below, choose the compound which is most suitable as $\mathbf{X}$. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{Y}$ corresponding to your choice of $\mathbf{X}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-9-fig4.png

9. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{M1}$, and $\mathbf{M2}$.

The content of $\mathbf{M1}$ and $\mathbf{M2}$ in urine is assayed by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS). The sample is first subjected to chromatography and the separated substances are analyzed in the multiple reaction monitoring mode. This method involves ionization of the initial metabolite and isolation of a single ion, which is further split into several new ions. Only one of these is subjected to further analysis. For example, in the case of $\mathbf{M1}$ the $[\mathbf{M1} + \ce{H+} - \ce{H2O}]$ ion is first isolated, and only the $[\mathbf{M1} + \ce{H+} - \ce{H2O} - \ce{CH3OH}]$ ion obtained after splitting is further analyzed. Finally, the intensity of the chromatogram peaks is used to determine the concentration of $\mathbf{M1}$.

10. Draw the structures of the $[\mathbf{M1} + \ce{H+} - \ce{H2O}]$ and $[\mathbf{M1} + \ce{H+} - \ce{H2O} - \ce{CH3OH}]$ ions.

problems.title: [Superconductors]
problems.problem:
Problem 10 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 1). [Superconductors]

The phenomenon of superconductivity was discovered in 1911. Superconductors are substances with electrical resistance dropping down to zero below a certain critical temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$. The transition to the superconducting ($s$) state from the normal ($n$) one is possible for many metals, alloys, intermetallic compounds, some hydrides, mixed oxides and other compounds. In Figure 1, the temperature dependences of the resistivity ($\rho$) of substances with semiconductor and metallic conductivity are shown, as well as of those having a transition to the superconducting state.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-10-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

1. Indicate the type of conductivity for each of the dependences 1, 2, and 3 (semiconductor, metal or superconductor).

There are superconductors of two types (I and II). The magnetic field destroys superconductivity of all superconductors, when the value of critical strength ($H_\mathrm{c}$) is reached. The temperature dependence of $H_\mathrm{c}$ for type I superconductors is described by the formula: $H_\mathrm{c} = H_\mathrm{c0}\cdot\left(1 - \frac{T^2}{T_\mathrm{c}^2}\right)$, where $H_\mathrm{c0}$ is the value of critical strength at $T = 0\,\mathrm{K}$.

Mercury with $T_\mathrm{c} = 4.156\,\mathrm{K}$ was the first metal for which superconductivity was discovered. The vast majority of metals having the transition to the superconducting state are classified as type I superconductors.

2. Calculate the value of critical strength $H_\mathrm{c}$ for mercury at the temperature $T = 3.00\,\mathrm{K}$, if $H_\mathrm{c0} = 3.2627\,\mathrm{kA/m}$.

In 1950, samples of different isotopes of mercury were shown to have different $T_\mathrm{c}$ values. This dependence of $T_\mathrm{c}$ on the molar mass of an isotope is referred to as the isotopic effect; for many superconductors the dependence can be written as $T_\mathrm{c} \sim \mathrm{const}/M^\zeta$. The parameter $\zeta$ varies for different superconductors. $M$ is the molar mass of an isotope or element with an account for the isotopic distribution.

3. Calculate the value of the parameter $\zeta$ for mercury, if $T_\mathrm{c} = 4.177\,\mathrm{K}$ for the monoisotopic sample $\ce{^{198}Hg}$ ($M = 197.97\,\mathrm{g/mol}$).

4. Using the data presented in the table for stable isotopes, determine the range, in which the $T_\mathrm{c}$ values can vary for monoisotopic samples of mercury.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} M,\ \mathrm{g/mol} & 195.97 & 197.97 & 198.97 & 199.97 & 200.97 & 201.97 & 203.97 \\ \hline A & 196 & 198 & 199 & 200 & 201 & 202 & 204 \end{array}$$

Phase transitions for the type I superconductors between the $n$ and $s$ states are classified as the first-order phase transitions but one point, at which the phase transition is of the second order. During the transition to the superconducting state, the changes in specific entropy ($S$) and specific heat capacity ($C$) are described by the formulas:

$$\Delta S = S_s - S_n = \frac{H_\mathrm{c}}{4\pi}\left(\frac{\partial H_\mathrm{c}}{\partial T}\right)_P, \qquad \Delta C = C_s - C_n = \frac{H_\mathrm{c0}^2 T}{\pi T_\mathrm{c}^2}\left(3\frac{T^2}{T_\mathrm{c}^2} - 1\right).$$

5. At what temperature (other than the absolute zero) is the $n \rightarrow s$ transition for mercury classified as the second-order phase transition, characterized by the absence of an entropy jump?

6. Calculate at what temperature (other than absolute zero) the heat capacities of the $s$ and $n$ states of Hg are equal.

One of the first intermetallic compounds with superconducting properties was discovered in 1929. This binary compound $\mathbf{X}$ had a low value of $T_\mathrm{c} = 1.8\,\mathrm{K}$, but it was of interest, since none of its components was a superconductor in the form of a simple substance.

7. Determine the composition of $\mathbf{X}$, if it is known that heating in air and subsequent interaction of the products with concentrated hydrochloric acid leads to the formation of a solution of a compound containing the metal $\mathbf{A}$ and a precipitate of the colored metal $\mathbf{B}$, the mass of which accounts to 65.34% of that of $\mathbf{X}$. When an excess of cesium iodide is added to the solution, an orange precipitate of a complex salt is formed, in which the mass fraction of the cation $\mathbf{A}$ is $w(\mathbf{A}) = 24.60\%$, and the mole fraction $x(\mathbf{A}) = 16.67\%$. Write the equations of the mentioned reactions.

Metals and intermetallic compounds have low $T_\mathrm{c}$ values. It became possible to obtain compounds with $T_\mathrm{c}$ close to room temperatures in the 21st century. The discovery of superconductivity at 260 K in hydrogen-rich compounds such as $\ce{LaH10}$ has intensified the search for superconductivity among both well-known and new hydrides. At high pressures, decomposition of $\mathbf{T1}$, which is stable under normal conditions, affords the compound $\mathbf{T2}$ and a simple substance. $\mathbf{T2}$ is stable at pressures up to 37 GPa. An increase in pressure above 110 GPa leads to the formation of $\mathbf{T3}$ with $T_\mathrm{c} \approx 203\,\mathrm{K}$, which has the same quantitative composition as $\mathbf{T2}$. The unit cells of $\mathbf{T2}$ and $\mathbf{T3}$ are shown in Figures 2 and 3, respectively. The unit cell parameter of $\mathbf{T3}$ is $0.2984\,\mathrm{nm}$, $d = 4.388\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-10-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-10-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

8. Determine quantitative composition of $\mathbf{T3}$ and $\mathbf{T1}$.

9. Indicate the molecular structural fragments that are present in the $\mathbf{T2}$ structure. Write down the formula for $\mathbf{T2}$ representing these structural fragments. Write the reaction for obtaining $\mathbf{T2}$ from $\mathbf{T1}$.

problems.title: [Intermetallic compounds of the metal Y]
problems.problem:
Problem 11 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 2). [Intermetallic compounds of the metal Y]

The metal $\mathbf{Y}$, when alloyed with cesium, forms an intermetallic compound $\mathbf{M}$ (the molar fraction of cesium $x(\mathrm{Cs}) = 8/19$). All the $\mathbf{Y}$ atoms form clusters with the cesium atoms located between them in the structure of $\mathbf{M}$. Despite the large number of $\mathbf{Y}$ atoms forming the cluster, a trigonal prism $\mathbf{Y}_6$ with an equilateral triangle at the base is the structural basis. Other $\mathbf{Y}$ atoms are located at a distance of 2.68 Å or 2.64 Å to the nearest $\mathbf{Y}$ atoms of the trigonal prism. In this case, the cluster has the same symmetry as a trigonal prism.

1. Determine the quantitative composition of $\mathbf{M}$. Draw the cluster fragment of $\mathbf{Y}$ atoms in its structure.

Elements $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{Z}$ are found in another intermetallic compound $\mathbf{N}$. A sample of $\mathbf{N}$ weighing 42.60 g ($d = 6.864\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$) was completely dissolved in concentrated nitric acid. An excess of concentrated sodium hydroxide solution was added to the obtained solution, as a result of which a mixture of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ precipitated and the solution $\mathbf{C1}$ was formed. The precipitates were separated, kept in air for a long time, and then an excess of dilute sulfuric acid solution was added. A part of the precipitate dissolved to form a solution of the compound $\mathbf{D}$. The undissolved brown precipitate weighing 8.545 g was isolated and slowly heated to $120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. As a result, the substance $\mathbf{E}$ formed (with the mass loss 23.67 wt.%). $\mathbf{E}$ exhibits the properties of both an oxidizing agent and a reducing agent. When $\mathbf{E}$ is fused with sodium peroxide, a green substance $\mathbf{G}$ is formed, which is unstable in water. When $\mathbf{E}$ reacts with concentrated hydrochloric acid, a gas is released and a complex compound $\mathbf{H}$ is formed, the effective magnetic moment of which is $\mu_\mathrm{eff} = 4.9\,\mu_\mathrm{B}$. Metallic zinc was added to the solution of $\mathbf{D}$, which led to the formation of a white precipitate $\mathbf{F}$ containing the element $\mathbf{X}$. If sulfuric acid is added dropwise to the $\mathbf{C1}$ solution, a white precipitate first forms, which is readily dissolved in an acid excess, forming the $\mathbf{C2}$ solution. The metal $\mathbf{Y}$ can be obtained by electrolysis of the $\mathbf{C2}$ solution. When $\mathbf{Y}$ reacts with $\ce{HgCl2}$, a binary chloride $\mathbf{I}$ is formed ($\omega(\mathrm{Cl}) = 50.4\%$).

2. Identify $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{I}$ and write down the reaction equations.

3. Indicate the oxidation states of the elements in $\mathbf{I}$.

4. For $\mathbf{H}$, choose the correct energy diagram in the Answer Sheet, label the atomic orbitals and place the electrons of the central atom on them.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-11-fig1.png

The figure shows the projections of the $\mathbf{N}$ unit cell on the $ab$, $bc$ and $ac$ planes. It is known that the $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ atoms are in the same position, and their ratio can be different, which leads to the formation of the $\mathbf{XY}_{\mathbf{a}-\delta}\mathbf{Z}_{\delta}$ solid solution.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-11-fig2.png

5. Determine the exact composition of $\mathbf{N}$ used in the experiments.

6. Determine the range of existence of the solid solution ($\delta_\mathrm{min}$ and $\delta_\mathrm{max}$) of the $\mathbf{XY}_{\mathbf{a}-\delta}\mathbf{Z}_{\delta}$ intermetallic compound, if its density varies within the range of $6.847$–$7.118\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Consider the unit cell parameters to be constant for all the solid solution compositions.

problems.title: [Hydrogen cations, hydride anions and dihydrogen complexes]
problems.problem:
Problem 12 (Inorganic chemistry section, problem 3). [Hydrogen cations, hydride anions and dihydrogen complexes]

For a long time, hydrogen was believed to form the $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{H-}$ ions in gaseous phase, and the $\ce{H2+}$ particle under gas discharge at low pressure. Later, the molecular cation $\ce{H3+}$ was discovered in gas discharges (Thomson) and in the atmosphere of hydrogen planets (Mac Nab). Relatively recently, it was shown that the $\ce{H2}$ molecules can attach to $\ce{H3+}$ to form $\ce{H5+}$, $\ce{H7+}$, and $\ce{H9+}$.

1. Draw the structure of the $\ce{H3+}$ cation, if the hydrogen atoms are equidistant from each other. Draw the overlap of the $s$-orbitals of the atoms and choose what type of bond is formed in the $\ce{H3+}$ cation. Draw the structures of the cations $\ce{H5+}$, $\ce{H7+}$ and $\ce{H9+}$, in which 3 atoms form right triangle in the mirror symmetry plane, while other atoms are in the planes perpendicular to the latter and containing the medians of the triangle.

In an aqueous solution, the existence of bound $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{H-}$ as parts of compounds is possible.

2. Write the reactions that describe the behavior of unbound $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{H-}$ in an aqueous solution. By calculating $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$ of the reaction $\ce{H2O + H- -> }\ldots$ ($E^\circ_{\ce{H2/H-}} = -2.23\,\mathrm{V}$; $E^\circ_{\ce{H2O/H2}} = -0.83\,\mathrm{V}$) prove that the existence of an unbound $\ce{H-}$ in the solution is impossible.

The $\ce{H-}$ anion, which is unstable in solution, is stabilized in complexes with the formation of a M−H bond. Like $\ce{H+}$, it most often has the CN = 1. At the same time, it turned out that in hydrides $\ce{H-}$ can form bridges and have the CN up to 6.

3. Draw the structures of $\mathrm{HM}_n$ fragments in the complexes: $\ce{[(CO)5WHW(CO)5]+}$ (angle MHM < 180°); $\ce{[HRh3(C5H5)4]}$ (angle close to 109.5°); $\ce{[HCo6(CO)15]-}$ (angles of 90 and 180°).

Hydrides are often obtained by an oxidative addition reaction, which occurs with the oxidation of the M complex: cis-$\ce{[MClCO(PPh3)2]} + n\ce{H2} = \mathbf{A}$, Ph = $\ce{C6H5}$. In the mechanism of oxidative addition, an intermediate formation precedes that of the hydride $\mathbf{A}$. This is accompanied by the appearance of the band $\nu \sim 1500\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in the IR spectrum of the hydride $\mathbf{A}$ (in $\ce{H2}$ $\nu = 4160\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$), whereas the $r_\mathrm{H-H}$ distance changes from 0.074 nm in $\ce{H2}$ to ~0.170 nm in the hydride.

4. Decipher M, if $\omega_\mathrm{Cl} = 4.53\%$, and $\omega_\mathrm{H} = 4.13\%$ in $\mathbf{A}$. Give the formula of $\mathbf{A}$, the number of electrons around M, and the oxidation state of M in the original complex and in $\mathbf{A}$. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{A}$.

The researchers failed to synthesize the intermediate of the oxidative addition reaction until 1980, when Kubas managed to stop the reaction at the step of the intermediate formation. After passing hydrogen ($p = 1\,\mathrm{atm}$) for 20 min through a dark purple solution in toluene containing 4.1442 g of trans-$\ce{[M'(CO)3(PCy3)2]}$, Cy = $\ce{C6H11}$, he isolated 3.74 g of the yellow crystals $\mathbf{B}$ containing the ligand L (the reaction yield was of about 90%). The band appears at $\nu = 2690\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in the IR spectrum of the complex $\mathbf{B}$; the bond length $r_\mathrm{H-H} = 0.084\,\mathrm{nm}$ and $\omega_\mathrm{M'} = 22.13\%$ in $\mathbf{B}$.

5. Decipher M’ and $\mathbf{B}$. Draw its spatial structure.

It is rarely possible to stop the reaction at the intermediate step. Even if it looks like so, a mixture of the intermediate and hydride is usually formed, because their thermodynamic characteristics are close. Thus, Luo and Harbtree obtained a product as a result of the treatment of $\ce{[ReCl3(CO)(PMe2Ph)3]}$ with $\ce{LiAlH4}$ in ether at 193.2 K. Addition of $\ce{HBF4*OEt2}$ in $\ce{CD2Cl2}$ at 193.2 K to the product leads to an equilibrium mixture of $\mathbf{D}^+$ and $\mathbf{E}^+$ cations. For equilibrium $\mathbf{D}^+ \rightleftarrows \mathbf{E}^+$, the enthalpy $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ is $-4.6\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, and the entropy $\Delta_\mathrm{r}S^\circ$ is $-10\,\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}$.

6. Determine the formulas of $\mathbf{D}^+$ and $\mathbf{E}^+$, if there are two $r_\mathrm{H-H}$ distances (0.087 and 0.180 nm) in the structure of $\mathbf{E}^+$ and only one $r_\mathrm{H-H}$ distance (0.176 nm) in that of $\mathbf{D}^+$.

7. Calculate the equilibrium constant and the composition of the equilibrium mixture $\chi$ in mol%.

Analysis of the synthesized compounds showed that different ligands in the complex can contribute to the formation of either the intermediate or hydride.

8. Give the MO diagram for the ligand L and calculate the bond multiplicity in it. Indicate with an arrow the possible direction of the electron transfer between $\pi_d$-orbitals of M and molecular orbitals of L.

problems.title: [Total synthesis of untenone A and plakevulin A]
problems.problem:
Problem 13 (Organic chemistry section, problem 1). [Total synthesis of untenone A and plakevulin A]

In 2022, K.B. Sharpless became the second scientist in the history who has received two Nobel Prizes in chemistry. The first prize was awarded for the discovery of the enantioselective epoxidation of alkenes, which has preparative significance in the synthesis of various organic compounds. As an example of the use of this reaction, the total synthesis of the natural products untenone A and plakevulin A isolated from marine sponges and exhibiting inhibitory activity against mammalian DNA polymerases is given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-13-fig1.png

Grubbs = Grubbs catalyst

1. Give the structures of $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{M}$ and untenone A, taking into account stereochemistry. Note that Dowex 50W-8 is a strongly acidic cation-exchange resin in the $\ce{H+}$ form. After all reactions with organometallic reagents, the reaction mixture was treated with water before isolation.

In addition to the basic reaction scheme that leads to the desired products, the authors attempted to synthesize untenone A and plakevulin A using a different sequence of steps. However, it did not lead to success.

2. Which reagents (I, II, and III) could be used by the authors? Under what reaction conditions (IV) it could be possible to try obtaining plakevulin A from untenone A in one step?

3. Determine the absolute configuration of the stereocenters in plakevulin A.

problems.title: Short but bright life of intermediates
problems.problem:
Problem 14 (Organic chemistry section, problem 2). Short but bright life of intermediates

The higher is the energy of a particle, the higher is its reactivity. Usually, it is impossible to isolate high-energy particles in a free form, and they immediately enter into further transformations, so they are often reactive intermediates. Let’s consider three ways to generate the intermediate $\mathbf{A}$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-14-fig1.png

1. Write down the structures of $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{A}$.

$\mathbf{A}$ rapidly interacts with various reagents:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-14-fig2.png

problems.title: Nucleophilic substitution
problems.problem:
Problem 15 (Organic chemistry section, problem 3). Nucleophilic substitution

The properties of atoms, molecules, and ions in solutions are very different from those in the solid state or gas phase. The solvent can change the direction of the reaction, whereas the rates of the same reaction in different solvents can differ by the factor of millions. Reactions in which charges arise in the transition state or charges already present in the reagents are concentrated in a smaller space are accelerated with increasing polarity of the solvent. If the ionic charges of the reactants are neutralized in the transition state or distributed over a larger space, the reactions slow down as the polarity of the solvent increases. Let us consider the effect of a solvent polarity on the progress of nucleophilic substitution reactions.

1. Match the solvents (Solv: $\ce{H2O}$, $\ce{CH3OH}$, $\ce{C2H5OH}$, $\ce{HCOOH}$) with the relative rate (1, 9, 12200, 335000) of solvolysis of tert-butyl chloride:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-15-fig1.png

2. For the nucleophilic substitution reactions below, indicate the mechanism ($\mathrm{S_N1}$/$\mathrm{S_N2}$), the change in charge distribution in the transition state (charge neutralization/separation/distribution), and the effect of increasing solvent polarity on the reaction rate (acceleration/deceleration).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-15-fig2.png

The hydroxyl group is a very poor nucleofuge, since in most cases its replacement is thermodynamically unfavorable. However, several approaches have been proposed for $\mathrm{S_N2}$ processes in alcohols, the Mitsunobu reaction being among the most regio- and stereoselective:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-15-fig3.png

3. Write the products of reactions 7)–10) taking into account the stereochemistry of the Mitsunobu reaction. Indicate which reactions are regioselective and which are stereoselective.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-15-fig4.png

Note that the stereocenter configuration has not changed in $\mathbf{A2}$; $\mathbf{A3}$ has three triplets (1H, 3H, 3H), two quadruplets (2H, 2H), and a quintet (2H) in the $^1$H NMR spectrum; there are no singlets in $\mathbf{A4}$, compared to the signals of the starting substances. All reagents in reactions 7)–10) are taken in equimolar quantities.

The Mitsunobu reaction is effectively used in the synthesis of various biologically active compounds. Thus, in the synthesis of the tumor cell inhibitor (−)-Spongidepsin, the Mitsunobu reaction was applied for the convergent assembly of two fragments of the target molecule:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-15-fig5.png

Grubbs catalyst – Ru-based alkene metathesis catalyst
DMP – Dess-Martin periodinane

4. Determine the structures of $\mathbf{B}$–$\mathbf{L}$. Use the following information: characteristic absorption frequencies of functional groups in IR spectra: (−CHO) = $1740\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$; (C=O) = $1720\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$; (lactone) = $1770\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

5. Determine the absolute configurations of the stereocenters 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in (–)-Spongidepsin.

Organocatalytic process in which phosphorus compounds are used in catalytic quantities due to their participation in the cycle is an alternative option for nucleophilic substitution of the hydroxyl group in alcohols. The mechanism of catalysis, each step of which can be described as a nucleophilic substitution, is presented in the scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2024-2-15-fig6.png

6. Suggest the structures of $\ce{[cat1]+}$ and $\ce{[cat2]+}$, if there is no signal of the OH group in the $^1$H NMR spectrum of $\ce{[cat1]+}$, but there is a signal of OH group in that of $\ce{[cat2]+}$. Indicate the position of the isotopic label after the second cycle.

problems.title: [Geometric isomerism of alkenes]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [Geometric isomerism of alkenes]

The geometric isomerism of alkenes ($\pi$-diastereomerism) is among the key concepts of modern stereochemistry. To designate the geometric isomers, both the cis/trans and Z/E nomenclatures are used. The former is based on the relative arrangement of identical substituents with respect to the $\ce{C=C}$ bond, while the latter takes into account the positions of the groups with higher priority (according to the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority rules).

I-1.1 (1 pt) The chlorocyclodecane framework is provided in the Answer Sheet. Insert the $\ce{C=C}$ bond at the appropriate position of the framework to obtain: a) ($Z$)-1-chlorocyclodecene; b) ($E$)-1-chlorocyclodecene; c) ($Z$)-5-chlorocyclodecene; d) ($E$)-5-chlorocyclodecene.

In synthetic practice, it is important to have a procedure, which allows interconverting $\pi$-diastereomers. One such approach (Method 1) is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-1-1-fig1.png

I-1.2 (1.5 pt) Draw the structures of cis-$\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, trans-$\mathbf{I}$, and the zwitterionic intermediate [$\mathbf{int1}$]. Starting alkene cis-$\mathbf{I}$ exhibits three signals with an intensity ratio of $1 : 2 : 3$ in the $^1$H NMR spectrum.

To convert one diastereomer into another, unsaturated hydrocarbons can be heated in the presence of catalytic amounts of iodine (Method 2). For example, if $6.48\,\mathrm{g}$ of cis-$\mathbf{II}$ ($\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_m$; $n$ and $m$ are even) is dissolved in xylene (boiling point $138\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), a small amount of $\ce{I2}$ is added, and the mixture is refluxed for several hours, then $0.0356\,\mathrm{mol}$ of trans-$\mathbf{II}$ can be isolated from the mixture upon reaching the equilibrium.

I-1.3 (3.5 pt) For the equilibrium cis-$\mathbf{II} \rightleftarrows$ trans-$\mathbf{II}$ ($\Delta_r G = -15.5\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$), calculate the equilibrium constant $K$ and the mole fractions of cis-$\mathbf{II}$ and trans-$\mathbf{II}$ in the equilibrium mixture. Determine $M_\mathrm{r}(\mathbf{II})$ and deduce the molecular (MF) and structural (SF) formulae of the substances. Provide your calculations. Draw the structure of the radical intermediate [$\mathbf{int2}$] that explains the catalytic action of $\ce{I2}$.

I-1.4 (0.5 pt) Propose Method 3 for converting cis-$\mathbf{I}$ into trans-$\mathbf{I}$ in three steps, if it is known that excess $\ce{KOH}$, alcohol, and heat is used at one of the steps. If you failed to decipher $\mathbf{I}$ in question I-1.2, use any cis- and trans-isomers of hydrocarbons.

In 1977, compounds containing overlapping trans-substituted $\ce{C=C}$ bonds, “betweenanenes” (from the English “between”), were described. One of the syntheses of a betweenanene is given below. The numbers inside the molecule (12 and $n$ in the scheme) indicate the number of carbon atoms in each ring.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-1-1-fig2.png

I-1.5 (1 pt) Determine $n$ and draw the structures of the dialdehyde cis-$\mathbf{III}$ and compounds cis-$\mathbf{IV}$ and cis-$\mathbf{V}$.

Alkenes that contain both donor and acceptor substituents can exhibit a low barrier to rotation about the $\ce{C=C}$ bond, while the bond length increases significantly. $\mathbf{VII}$ is an example of such a compound:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-1-1-fig3.png

I-1.6 (2 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{VI}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{VII}$.

I-1.7 (0.5 pt) Using structural formulae, demonstrate why the barrier to rotation about the $\ce{C=C}$ bond is relatively low in $\mathbf{VII}$ and why its length is much greater than that in ethylene.

problems.title: [Wöhler’s compound]
problems.problem:
Problem 2. [Wöhler’s compound]

The beginning of organic chemistry as a science can be dated to 1828, when Friedrich Wöhler first synthesized the organic compound $\mathbf{A}$ (20.00 wt% carbon, 46.65 wt% nitrogen, and 26.64 wt% oxygen) under laboratory conditions. Remarkably, it was obtained from an inorganic substance that is an isomer of $\mathbf{A}$. Today, $\mathbf{A}$ is a multi-ton industrial product, widely used in agriculture as the mineral fertilizer richest in nitrogen.

I-2.1 (0.5 pt) Provide the structure of $\mathbf{A}$.

I-2.2 (0.5 pt) Provide the structure of the compound from which $\mathbf{A}$ was first synthesized.

I-2.3 (0.5 pt) $\mathbf{A}$ is currently produced on industrial scale via a two-step process. Provide the chemical equations of the reactions involved.

$\mathbf{A}$ exhibits basic properties and reacts with acids.

I-2.4 (1 pt) Arrange $\mathbf{A}$, ammonia ($\ce{NH3}$), and hydrazine ($\ce{N2H4}$) in the order of increasing their base strength in aqueous solution.

When $\mathbf{A}$ reacts with concentrated nitric acid, compound $\mathbf{B}$ is formed (34.14 wt% of nitrogen).

I-2.5 (1 pt) Determine the formula of $\mathbf{B}$. Provide your calculations.

$\mathbf{B}$ decomposes upon heating: the composition of the products significantly depends on the temperature. In one study, it was found that, with heating at $450\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the components of air are not involved in the decomposition of $\mathbf{B}$. Mass spectrometry revealed that there were $0.78\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\ce{NH3}$, $0.49\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\ce{HNO3}$, $0.22\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\ce{CO2}$, and $0.69\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\ce{H2O}$ in the decomposition products of $1\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathbf{B}$. After passing all the decomposition products of $1\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathbf{B}$ through a column containing solid $\ce{NaOH}$, the residual (unabsorbed) gaseous mixture contained three binary compounds and had a mass of $36.37\,\mathrm{g}$ and a volume of $34.12\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ (at $20.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100.0\,\mathrm{kPa}$).

I-2.6 (3 pt) Which compounds are present in the unabsorbed gaseous residue obtained after passing the decomposition products of $\mathbf{B}$ through a column with a solid base? Calculate the volume fractions of these substances, given that, according to quantitative analysis, $w(\mathrm{N}) = 66.26\%$ in the residue, and that it changes color upon exposure to air. Provide your calculations.

In the described experiment, substance $\mathbf{C}$ was detected in the decomposition products of $\mathbf{B}$ in addition to the listed above compounds. Under other experimental conditions (at a lower temperature), compounds $\mathbf{D1}$–$\mathbf{D4}$ were detected among the decomposition products of $\mathbf{B}$. $\mathbf{D1}$–$\mathbf{D4}$ each have a more complex structure than that of $\mathbf{C}$.

I-2.7 (2 pt) Determine the formula of $\mathbf{C}$ and provide the structures of its isomers. Show your calculations.

I-2.8 (0.5 pt) Which of the isomers of $\mathbf{C}$ is present in the decomposition products of $\mathbf{B}$?

I-2.9 (1 pt) Provide the structural formula of at least one of the compounds $\mathbf{D1}$–$\mathbf{D4}$ that are formed during the decomposition of $\mathbf{B}$ at a lower temperature.

problems.title: [Five liquids from herbaceous plants]
problems.problem:
Problem 3. [Five liquids from herbaceous plants]

A highly fascinating class of organic non-heterocyclic compounds is produced by some herbaceous plants. This class includes five compounds ($\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$), which are liquids at standard temperature and pressure and serve as the five starting members of the corresponding homologous series.

To determine their composition, equimolar amounts of each of $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$ were taken. Half of the mass of each compound was burnt in an excess of oxygen, with the combustion products (gaseous at $150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $1\,\mathrm{atm}$) being completely absorbed by aqueous solutions of calcium hydroxide (identical in composition and mass) taken in deliberate excess, which resulted in the formation of white precipitates (Experiment No. 1). The other halves of compounds were subjected to a similar experiment except that the combustion products were first passed through phosphorus(V) oxide, which led to a decrease in their volume (Experiment No. 2). The results of the experiments are presented in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Compound} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Mass of precipitate, g}\\ \text{(in both Experiments No. 1 and No. 2)}\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Difference in masses of the supernatant solutions for } \mathbf{X}_{i+1} \text{ and } \mathbf{X}_i,\\ {[m_\mathrm{s}(\mathbf{X}_{i+1}) - m_\mathrm{s}(\mathbf{X}_i)]}\text{, g (in both Experiments No. 1 and No. 2)}\end{array} \\ \hline \mathbf{X1} & 108.2 & - \\ \hline \mathbf{X2} & 126.2 & 8.4 \\ \hline \mathbf{X3} & 144.2 & 8.4 \\ \hline \mathbf{X4} & 162.2 & 8.4 \\ \hline \mathbf{X5} & 180.2 & 8.4 \end{array}$$

It is known that the molecules $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$ do not contain any halogen atoms or oxygen.

I-3.1 (1 pt) Using only mathematical and chemical equations, provide a general proof that the sums of all the coefficients in the reaction equations of complete combustion of compounds $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$ are five consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression.

I-3.2 (1.5 pt) The data in the table are sufficient to unambiguously determine the ratio of the number of atoms of one (and only one!) element ($\mathbf{E}$) in the molecules of compounds $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$, as $N_\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{X1}) : N_\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{X2}) : N_\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{X3}) : N_\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{X4}) : N_\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{X5})$. Determine this ratio, showing your calculations.

Let’s indulge in a bit of imagination: assume that the precipitates in each experiment represent individual compounds and that $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$ are not homologs; moreover, disregard the specific mass difference value given in the table ($8.4\,\mathrm{g}$). All other information provided above must be taken into account!

I-3.3 (2.5 pt) Draw the hypothetical structures of $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$, using the ratio obtained in your answer to the previous question.

In reality, the precipitates obtained in the experiment are mixtures.

I-3.4 (1.5 pt) Determine the molar ratio of the components of the precipitate ($N$) in Experiment No. 1 for $\mathbf{X1}$. Show your calculations.

It is known that in the molecule of at least one of the compounds $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$ the sum of the numbers of atoms of two certain elements equals 12, and in at least one of other compounds, the sum of the numbers of atoms of two certain elements equals 16. The pairs of elements need not be identical.

I-3.5 (1 pt) Determine the molecular formulae of $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$.

I-3.6 (2.5 pt) Propose all possible finally determined structural formulae for $\mathbf{X1}$–$\mathbf{X5}$, if, according to NMR spectroscopy data, each of the five compounds contains three types of hydrogen atoms and three types of carbon atoms.

problems.title: [A binary explosive]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [A binary explosive]

Binary explosive compound $\mathbf{X}$ consists of atoms of elements $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ from the same group of the periodic table. $\mathbf{X}$ contains 8.77 wt% of $\mathbf{A}$. The synthesis of $\mathbf{X}$ is shown in the scheme below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-1-4-fig1.png

I-4.1 (1 pt) Determine elements $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. Show your calculations.

I-4.2 (2.25 pt) a) Write the equations of the reactions in the scheme. b) Write the formulae of $\mathbf{P}$–$\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{X}$ reflecting their structure (spatial structure is not required).

The oxygen balance $\Omega$ of an explosive compound is the mass of oxygen involved in the reaction of its complete combustion, relative to the mass of an explosive compound. If combustion of the compound requires oxygen, the value of $\Omega$ is considered negative; if decomposition of the compound leads to the evolution of oxygen, $\Omega > 0$. Specific (relative to the compound mass) heat evolved during the explosion linearly depends on the oxygen balance of the explosive compound.

I-4.3 (1.25 pt) Calculate $\Omega$ (%) for a) trinitroglycerin, b) tetryl ($N$-methyl-$N$,2,4,6-tetranitroaniline), and c) compound $\mathbf{X}$.

I-4.4 (1 pt) Specific heat of explosion $Q$ of trinitroglycerin and tetryl equals 6228 and $4340\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, respectively. Calculate specific heat of explosion of $\mathbf{X}$ (kJ/kg).

I-4.5 (1 pt) Calculate the enthalpy of formation of $\mathbf{X}$ (kJ/mol). The enthalpies of formation of the combustion products of elementary substances of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are $-746$ and $0\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ (per $1\,\mathrm{mol}$ of atoms of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$), respectively. If you failed to determine either the composition of $\mathbf{X}$ and/or its heat of explosion, use $\mathbf{A}_2\mathbf{B}_3$ as the formula and $Q = 5000\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$.

I-4.6 (3 pt) Using the data provided in the problem, estimate the minimum pressure (Pa) developed in a 10-L closed vessel containing oxygen (pressure $10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}$), $100\,\mathrm{g}$ of ice, and $35\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathbf{X}$ at temperature $-10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, upon explosion of $\mathbf{X}$. Consider the heat capacities of ice ($2.0\,\mathrm{J/(g{\cdot}K)}$), liquid water ($4.2\,\mathrm{J/(g{\cdot}K)}$), and gaseous compounds ($12.5\,\mathrm{J/(mol{\cdot}K)}$) independent of temperature; the heat of melting for ice is $332\,\mathrm{J/g}$; the heat of evaporation for water is $2256\,\mathrm{J/g}$. The volume of any condensed phase and heat capacity of condensed products of explosion of $\mathbf{X}$ can be neglected.

I-4.7 (0.5 pt) Write the equation of a chemical reaction occurring in the system described in I-4.6. Accounting for this reaction would improve the estimate of the developed pressure.

problems.title: [Salts of two diprotic acids]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Salts of two diprotic acids]

Inorganic salts $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, and $\mathbf{D}$ are white substances. $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are formed from diprotic acid $\mathrm{H_2}\mathbf{X}$, while $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are formed from diprotic acid $\mathrm{H_2}\mathbf{Y}$. The following experiments were carried out to determine the composition of the salts and the acidity constants of the acids:

1) All the salts give a yellow color in the flame test.

2) $\mathbf{A}$ reacts with both $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$. In both cases a colorless and odorless gas is released.

3) Barium chloride solution reacts with both $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, forming a white precipitate in both cases.

4) Calcium chloride solution does not react with $\mathbf{C}$, but reacts with $\mathbf{D}$, forming a white precipitate.

5) The pH values of $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ solutions of the salts are:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{Solution} & \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} & \mathbf{C} & \mathbf{D} \\ \hline \text{pH} & 1.57 & 7.52 & 8.34 & 11.65 \end{array}$$

6) When the solutions are diluted by the factor of 10, only the pH of the solution of $\mathbf{C}$ remains nearly unchanged.

I-5.1 (2 pt) Write the formulae of the salts $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{D}$.

I-5.2 (1 pt) Write the equations of the five reactions mentioned above.

I-5.3 (4 pt) Determine the acidity constants $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a,1}(\mathrm{H_2}\mathbf{X})$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a,2}(\mathrm{H_2}\mathbf{X})$, $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a,1}(\mathrm{H_2}\mathbf{Y})$ and $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a,2}(\mathrm{H_2}\mathbf{Y})$. If any of the acidity constants cannot be reliably determined from the given data, place a dash (–) in the corresponding box in the Answer Sheet.

I-5.4 (1 pt) Calculate the pH of a $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ solution of the diprotic acid $\mathrm{H_2}\mathbf{Z}$ with the acidity constants $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a,1}(\mathrm{H_2}\mathbf{Z}) = -3.0$ and $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a,2}(\mathrm{H_2}\mathbf{Z}) = 1.0$.

An acid $\mathbf{E}$ is monoprotic ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = 3.17$), but can also form salts with a hydrogen-containing anion. When $120\,\mathrm{mg}$ of $\mathbf{E}$ reacts with $68\,\mathrm{mg}$ of $\ce{NH3}$ ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{b} = 4.79$), an equimolar mixture of salts $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ is formed. $\mathbf{G}$ contains 8.83% hydrogen by mass.

I-5.5 (1.5 pt) Determine the composition of the acid $\mathbf{E}$ and the salts $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ and write their formulae.

I-5.6 (0.5 pt) Calculate the pH of the solution obtained by mixing equal volumes of $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ solutions of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\ce{NH3}$.

problems.title: [The Looking-Glass Olympiad: element X]
problems.problem:
Problem 6. [The Looking-Glass Olympiad: element X]

After her adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass, Alice became fascinated with chemistry and even took part in the Looking-Glass Mendeleev Olympiad. The Olympiad in Looking-Glass-land is organized somewhat differently from the one in which you participate. At the second exam, each problem should include questions from as many branches of chemistry as possible, but each problem is devoted to a single element. In the Looking-Glass Olympiad, the participants compose the problems while the Jury members solve them. We invite you to try your hand as a Jury member of the Looking-Glass Olympiad by solving the problem composed by Alice about element $\mathbf{X}$.

Inorganic Chemistry

The elementary substance composed of $\mathbf{X}$ is obtained from the waste of copper production: compound $\mathbf{A}$ is subjected to calcination, during which substance $\mathbf{B}$ is formed. By reaction of $\mathbf{B}$ with alkali, substance $\mathbf{C}$ is obtained. Pure $\mathbf{X}$ is produced by the reduction of $\mathbf{C}$ with $\ce{SO2}$. A feature of $\mathbf{X}$ is its tendency to form $\mathbf{X}{-}\mathbf{X}$ bonds, for example, in compounds $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{I}$, as well as in cyclic polycations, such as in $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{H}$. The ionic compound $\mathbf{G}$ is obtained in liquid $\ce{SO2}$ from a mixture of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{X}$ taken in a molar ratio of $1 : 6$, in the presence of $\ce{AlCl3}$. When $\mathbf{G}$ is washed with a large amount of $\ce{SO2}$, it disproportionates into $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$; $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ are formed in a molar ratio of $1 : 3$. The synthesis of these compounds, as well as the mass composition of some of them, are shown in the scheme below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-1-6-fig1.png

$\mathbf{A}$: $w_\mathrm{Cu} = 22.91\%$; $w_\mathbf{X} = 56.95\%$;

$\mathbf{D}$: $w_\mathrm{K} = 27.14\%$; $w_\mathbf{X} = 54.81\%$; $w_\mathrm{C} = 8.34\%$; $w_\mathrm{N} = 9.72\%$;

$\mathbf{E}$: $w_\mathbf{X} = 69.02\%$; $w_\mathrm{Cl} = 30.98\%$;

$\mathbf{I}$: $w_\mathrm{Na} = 22.55\%$; $w_\mathbf{X} = 77.45\%$.

I-6.1 (2.5 pt) Using calculations, determine the element $\mathbf{X}$ and the compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{G}$–$\mathbf{I}$.

Organic Chemistry

Heterocyclic aromatic compounds containing $\mathbf{X}$ have found several applications: synthesis of pharmaceuticals, materials for organic transistors, light-emitting diodes, and solar batteries. The scheme below displays the synthesis of the antidepressant $\mathbf{P}$, which contains two atoms of $\mathbf{X}$. One of the $\mathbf{X}$ atoms is part of an aromatic ring, while the other connects two aromatic rings together. In addition, it is known that compound $\mathbf{P}$ does not contain any aliphatic carbon atoms.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-1-6-fig2.png

I-6.2 (2.5 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{L}$–$\mathbf{P}$, given that compound $\mathbf{N}$ contains two atoms of $\mathbf{X}$.

Physical Chemistry

A series of molecules $\mathbf{Y}(N)$, whose structure contains $N$ fused aromatic heterocycles containing $\mathbf{X}$, possess interesting electronic properties leading to their use as organic diodes or transistors. Increasing the number of cycles $N$, as well as introducing various substituents, makes it possible to vary the properties of these molecules.

To describe the $\pi$-electrons of molecules $\mathbf{Y}(N)$, one can use the “particle on an ellipse” model. In this case the electron density of $\mathbf{Y(1)}$ is a circle with radius $r_1$, and the electron densities of all other $\mathbf{Y}(N)$ are ellipses with semiaxes $r_1$ and $r_N$.

I-6.3 (1 pt) It is known that the energy of the transition to the first excited state in molecule $\mathbf{Y(1)}$ is $4.989\,\mathrm{eV}$, and that in molecule $\mathbf{Y(2)}$ is $4.106\,\mathrm{eV}$. Calculate $r_1$ and $r_2$.

I-6.4 (1 pt) Assuming that $r_N$ depends linearly on $N$, estimate for which values of $N$ the transition to the first excited state corresponds to absorption of visible light (380–780 nm).

Note:

Energy of a particle on an ellipse: $E_n = \dfrac{h^2 n^2}{2 m_\mathrm{e} S^2}$, where $n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots$, is the number of the energy level, $h$ is Planck’s constant, $m_\mathrm{e}$ is the electron mass, and $S$ is related to the semiaxes $a$ and $b$ of the ellipse as $S = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{a^2 + b^2}{2}}$.

Biochemistry

The $\alpha$-amino acids $\mathbf{Z2}$ and $\mathbf{Z3}$ containing the element $\mathbf{X}$ can be incorporated into proteins in the process of translation on ribosomes (programmed or erroneous). The difference in the mass fractions of $\mathbf{X}$ in $\mathbf{Z2}$ and $\mathbf{Z3}$ is 6.72%. The scheme of the biosynthesis of $\mathbf{Z2}$ from the proteinogenic amino acid $\mathbf{Z1}$ and the inorganic salt $\mathbf{C}$ is given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-1-6-fig3.png

problems.title: [Polymer A and its monomer]
problems.problem:
Problem 7. [Polymer A and its monomer]

Polymer $\mathbf{A}$ was accidentally discovered in 1938 by chemists working on a project for the DuPont company. They found that gas $\mathbf{B}$, pumped into a pressurized cylinder, kept escaping from the cylinder until instrumental control showed the cylinder to be empty; however, the weight of this “empty” cylinder turned out to be greater than that of a standard empty cylinder. The cylinder was cut open, and a slippery, wax-like material $\mathbf{A}$ was found inside. In 1954, the French engineer Marc Gregoire developed aluminum cookware coated with polymer $\mathbf{A}$, which became so widely used that such cookware can now be seen in nearly every kitchen in every country worldwide. Polymer $\mathbf{A}$ found applications in various branches of human activity.

I-7.1 (1 pt) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{B}$ and the formula of the monomeric unit of polymer $\mathbf{A}$.

Industrial production of $\mathbf{A}$ from $\mathbf{B}$ requires the use of special apparatuses to prevent the local overheating of the mixture, as this may lead to the explosive decomposition of $\mathbf{B}$ with the formation of binary gas $\mathbf{C}$ and elementary substance $\mathbf{D}$. In industry, $\mathbf{B}$ is obtained by the reaction of chloroform with gas $\mathbf{E}$, which forms product $\mathbf{F}$, followed by $\mathbf{F}$ thermolysis. Along with $\mathbf{F}$, compound $\mathbf{G}$ is formed in these conditions. Thermolysis of $\mathbf{G}$ leads to the elimination of $\mathbf{E}$ and formation of $\mathbf{B}$. Gases $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ are used as refrigerants and in the production of electronics; they do not affect the ozone layer but are classified as greenhouse gases. $\mathbf{C}$ has extremely low solubility in water but is soluble in benzene and chloroform, while $\mathbf{G}$ is soluble in both water ($1\,\mathrm{g/L}$) and organic solvents.

I-7.2 (2 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{E}$–$\mathbf{G}$.

$\mathbf{G}$ can be applied in organic synthesis. The first approach is based on its deprotonation in the presence of an electrophile. For example, the compound $\mathbf{H}$ is formed (after neutralization) in the presence of benzophenone, and the compound $\mathbf{I}$ is formed in the presence of trimethylchlorosilane. Organolithium or organomagnesium derivatives formed upon deprotonation of $\mathbf{G}$ are extremely unstable even at $-80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and readily convert into the unstable intermediate $\mathbf{J}$, which reacts readily with various compounds. For example, it forms product $\mathbf{K}$ in the reaction with 1-butene, whereas in the absence of any reaction partners it converts into $\mathbf{B}$.

I-7.3 (2 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{H}$–$\mathbf{K}$.

The intermediate $\mathbf{J}$ may exist in two forms that have different electronic properties and different geometries.

I-7.4 (2 pt) Draw the structures of each form of $\mathbf{J}$. For each form, choose the approximate value for the bond angle. Circle the more stable form.

$\mathbf{I}$ is actively used in organic synthesis. In the presence of tetrabutylammonium fluoride, $\mathbf{I}$ reacts with benzaldehyde to form product $\mathbf{L}$. Upon treatment with dilute acid, $\mathbf{L}$ is converted into compound $\mathbf{M}$. $\mathbf{M}$ can also be obtained in another way: methyl benzoate, $\mathbf{I}$, and $\ce{Bu4NF}$ with subsequent addition of dilute acid give product $\mathbf{N}$; treatment of $\mathbf{N}$ with sodium borohydride gives $\mathbf{M}$.

I-7.5 (1.5 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{L}$–$\mathbf{N}$.

On the other hand, the treatment of $\mathbf{G}$ with potassium tert-butoxide in the presence of silver(I) acetate generated compound $\mathbf{O}$. The reaction of $\mathbf{O}$ with 4-bromobenzonitrile afforded product $\mathbf{P}$. However, the structure of $\mathbf{O}$ could not be determined. Very recently, a paper was published in Organic Letters, in which silver(I) trifluoromethanesulfonate was treated with two equivalents of potassium tert-butoxide; an excess of gas $\mathbf{G}$ was passed through the solution, followed by the addition of tetrabutylammonium bromide (1 eq.). The authors showed that that the resulting salt $\mathbf{Q}$ contained 22.09 wt% silver. $\mathbf{P}$ is also formed when $\mathbf{Q}$ reacts with 4-cyanophenyldiazonium tetrafluoroborate. In contrast, it was previously found that when $\mathbf{G}$ is heated under pressure with sodium tert-butylate in tert-butanol, it is converted into product $\mathbf{R}$, containing 67.20 wt% carbon. $\mathbf{R}$ shows two signals in the $^1$H NMR spectrum and three signals in the $^{13}$C NMR spectrum.

I-7.6 (1.5 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{P}$–$\mathbf{R}$.

problems.title: [A toxic binary compound X]
problems.problem:
Problem 8. [A toxic binary compound X]

“Like dissolves like” — Chemical wisdom

A toxic binary compound $\mathbf{X}$, which exhibits pronounced corrosive properties, is predominantly found in the hydrosphere. Therefore, the sanitary authorities of many countries have set indirect standards for the content of $\mathbf{X}$ in drinking water. Notably, compounds $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$, which are similar to $\mathbf{X}$ in chemical properties and have the same elemental composition, show diametrically opposite abundances in nature and toxicity: the poisonous $\mathbf{Y}$ is found in vanishingly small amounts, whereas the relatively safe $\mathbf{Z}$ is widespread. However, cases of human fatalities associated with the intake of certain quantities of $\mathbf{Z}$ are well-documented.

A single ingestion of a small amount of $\mathbf{X}$ may be practically harmless because its half-life in the human body is about 10 days.

I-8.1 (0.75 pt) Calculate the number of days $t$ after a single ingestion of $\mathbf{X}$ when the amount of this compound in the body would decrease down to 10% of the initial dose. Assume that we are dealing with first-order pharmacokinetics.

$\mathbf{X}$ can be involved in various biochemical processes. For example, in vitro it enzymatically reacts with compound $\mathbf{A}$ to form three products $\mathbf{B1}$, $\mathbf{B2}$, and $\mathbf{B3}$, gaseous at standard temperature and pressure. The ratio of densities of these gases is $2.59 : 1.12 : 1.00$, respectively. The reaction is

$$\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{X} \rightarrow \mathbf{B1} + \mathbf{B2} + \mathbf{B3}$$

The molar masses of $\mathbf{B3}$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $\mathbf{B2}$, and $\mathbf{X}$, when rounded to whole numbers, form consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression.

I-8.2 (5.5 pt) Determine all the unknown substances described above. Where necessary, propose all possible variants of the formulae for the substances. Give your calculations.

I-8.3 (0.75 pt) Based on its physicochemical properties, estimate the solubility of $\mathbf{X}$ in water at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Write the number of the appropriate variant in the Answer Sheet.

$$\begin{array}{c|l|c|l} \text{No.} & \text{solubility} & \text{No.} & \text{solubility} \\ \hline 1 & \text{less than 0.01 g in 100 g of water} & 3 & \text{1 g to 50 g in 100 g of water} \\ \hline 2 & \text{0.01 g to 1 g in 100 g of water} & 4 & \text{unlimited} \end{array}$$

There are also other reactions in which an equimolar mixture of gaseous products is formed, with the same density ratio, as in the reaction of $\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{X}$.

I-8.4 (2 pt) Propose one reaction equation for each of the following two cases: a) both reactants are different from $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{X}$; b) one of the reactants is either $\mathbf{A}$ or $\mathbf{X}$.

I-8.5 (1 pt) Write the reaction equation that initiates (i.e., develops without the involvement of the metal) the corrosion process of aluminum container in which $\mathbf{X}$ is stored at room temperature.

problems.title: [Prebiotic synthesis of cytidine]
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem II-1). [Prebiotic synthesis of cytidine]

Today a hypothetical stage in the origin of life on Earth is recognized: the RNA world, when this biopolymer performed the functions of genetic information storage and catalysis of biochemical processes in the earliest forms of living matter, instead of DNA and proteins in contemporary living things.

For the main nitrogenous bases inherited by extant organisms from the RNA world, a synthesis from prebiotic molecules (PM) has been modeled. These are compounds that, being present in proto-planetary gas-dust clouds, can participate in the formation of key biomonomers on recently formed celestial bodies. However, the probability of forming any significant molecules in outer space is low; therefore, species containing from three to five atoms inclusively are classified as simple PM, while those containing six or more atoms are considered complex.

Both constituent parts of cytidine can be formed from PM: the cytosine moiety from compounds $\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{Y1}$, and the sugar moiety from acyclic compounds $\mathbf{Z1}$ and $\mathbf{Z2}$ (with only the precursors of ribose being complex PM). The synthesis scheme for cytosine, consisting of reaction equations, is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-1-fig1.png

II-1.1 (1.5 pt) Based on general considerations, propose a set of three stable simple PM (each with a molecular mass not exceeding 30 a.m.u.), which together contain five $\pi$-bonds and a total of 11 atoms.

II-1.2 (4 pt) Determine the structural formulae of $\mathbf{X1}$, $\mathbf{X2}$, $\mathbf{Y1}$, and $\mathbf{Y2}$, given that $\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{Y1}$, as non-ionized molecules and contain the same functional group. Note that $M_\mathrm{r}$ of $\mathbf{Y2}$ is the highest among the quartet under consideration. Prove your answer by the calculation or reasoning in commonly accepted chemical language.

II-1.3 (1 pt) Propose a scheme for the prebiotic synthesis of another pyrimidine base, uracil, using only the substances present in the cytosine synthesis scheme. You may use the $\mathbf{X1}$, $\mathbf{X2}$, $\mathbf{Y1}$, and $\mathbf{Y2}$ to denote the respective compounds.

Analysis of an aqueous solution, originally containing $\mathbf{Z1}$ and $\mathbf{Z2}$, shows the presence of four products including D-ribose after storage at room temperature for an extended period. Equation of the reaction of D-ribose synthesis is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-1-fig2.png

Molecular masses (g/mol) of $\mathbf{Z1}$ and $\mathbf{Z2}$, rounded to whole numbers, are composite numbers that can be factored into similar sets of single-digit prime factors, differing only in one position ($k$ in the case of $\mathbf{Z1}$ and $m$ in the case of $\mathbf{Z2}$, where $k < m$).

II-1.4 (1.5 pt) Without revealing the formulae of $\mathbf{Z1}$ and $\mathbf{Z2}$, use mathematical considerations to determine the numerical value of the sum $k + m$. Prove by calculations.

II-1.5 (1.5 pt) Determine the structures of $\mathbf{Z1}$ and $\mathbf{Z2}$ (indicating stereochemistry where necessary), given that they contain identical functional groups.

II-1.6 (2.5 pt) Depict the structures of three products other than D-ribose that are found in the reaction mixture originally containing $\mathbf{Z1}$ and $\mathbf{Z2}$. Encircle those that do not occur in living nature, at least on our planet.

A direct reaction between ribose and cytosine to form cytidine is impossible (primarily due to the delocalization of the lone electron pair on the N1 atom of cytosine). To resolve this contradiction, a mechanism for the synthesis of ribocytidine-2,3-cyclic phosphate involving the same PM in a phosphate buffer solution was proposed. The mechanism is given below as a set of reaction equations):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-1-fig3.png

II-1.7 (3 pt) Depict the structures of $\mathbf{Z3}$–$\mathbf{Z5}$ (without stereochemistry), considering that the number of heterocycles and the number of heteroatoms in them increase stepwise as the numerical index increases.

problems.title: [An aluminium-containing antiulcer drug and the Malaprade reaction]
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (Life Sciences and Polymers section, problem II-2). [An aluminium-containing antiulcer drug and the Malaprade reaction]

The drug $\mathbf{X}$ ($M = 2662.04\,\mathrm{g/mol}$) was used in the early 21st century for the treatment of peptic ulcer disease due to its ability to increase the pH of gastric juice. Substance $\mathbf{A}$ is the starting material for the synthesis of $\mathbf{X}$. In order to identify $\mathbf{A}$, the Malaprade reaction was employed, which is an oxidative cleavage of vicinal diols by metaperiodate ion. The mechanism of this transformation, using ethylene glycol as an example, is shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-2-fig1.png

II-2.1 (1.5 pt) For the compounds provided in the Answer Sheet, write the products of the oxidative cleavage corresponding to the enframed fragments of the starting substrates.

It is known that $\mathbf{A}$ exists in solution as a single chiral isomer, the complete acidic hydrolysis of which produces isomeric compounds $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ in equimolar amounts. An excess of sodium metaperiodate ($0.2139\,\mathrm{g}$) was added to a solution containing $0.1\,\mathrm{mmol}$ of $\mathbf{C}$. The volume of the resulting solution was adjusted to $100.0\,\mathrm{mL}$. An excess of solution of potassium iodide in aqueous sulfuric acid was added to a $10.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquot (reactions 1 and 2), and then the mixture was titrated with a $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution ($c = 0.0500\,\mathrm{M}$) (reaction 3). The titration required $14.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of titrant.

When each of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ is treated with equivalent amount of sodium metaperiodate, mixtures of compounds are formed. Structures of only some of them are given in the scheme below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-2-fig2.png

II-2.2 (1.5 pt) Combine in pairs the products of partial cleavage of $\mathbf{D}$ shown in the above scheme to obtain all theoretically possible products of the original unbranched compounds. How many of these fragments ($N_\mathrm{frag}$) are there?

II-2.3 (1.5 pt) Write the equations of reactions 1–3.

II-2.4 (2.5 pt) Determine the number of carbon atoms ($N$) in $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$; provide the corresponding calculations.

II-2.5 (3 pt) Give the structures of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{C}$, and $\mathbf{D}$.

The synthesis of $\mathbf{X}$ is carried out according to the scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-2-fig3.png

To assess the efficacy of $\mathbf{X}$, the patient’s gastric contents (volume $0.973\,\mathrm{L}$, $\mathrm{pH} = 1.12$) were aspirated. After adding $4.660\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathbf{X}$ to the gastric juice, the pH increased to 2.41. Then, the solution was titrated with $13.2\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a $\ce{KOH}$ solution until the pH reached 4.00. The precipitate formed after titration was burnt in an excess of oxygen. The mass of the remaining aluminum oxide was found equal to $1.366\,\mathrm{g}$. Assume the gastric juice is a solution of hydrochloric acid. Changes in volume upon addition of substance $\mathbf{X}$ can be neglected.

II-2.6 (1 pt) Calculate the ratio of the amount of aluminum atoms to the amount of substance $\mathbf{X}$, $n(\mathrm{Al}) : n(\mathbf{X})$.

II-2.7 (0.75 pt) Calculate the ratio of the amount of basic groups in $\mathbf{X}$ to the amount of substance $\mathbf{X}$, $n(\text{basic}) : n(\mathbf{X})$.

II-2.8 (3.25 pt) Provide the structural formulae of $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{X}$; be sure to depict the structure of the inner coordination sphere of aluminum. If you failed to determine the structure of $\mathbf{A}$, denote this substance here as $\ce{R-OH}$.

Note:

For $\ce{Al(OH)3}$: $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{b1} = 8.08$; $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{b2} = 8.68$; $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{b3} = 8.86$; $K_\mathrm{sp} = 2\cdot10^{-33}$.

Problem 4 (Organic Chemistry section, problem II-4). [Towards dendrochrysanene]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-4-fig1.png

In 2017, Katsuki and co-authors published the first total synthesis of the natural product dendrochrysanene ($\mathbf{X}$), which is found in plants of the orchid family. The structure of $\mathbf{X}$ had already been established earlier using X-ray crystallography, which revealed the presence of a spirolactone core. A similar framework fragment is also present in compound $\mathbf{A}$, which can be obtained via a tandem reaction consisting of oxidative dimerization of 2-naphthol followed by a rearrangement of the carbon framework. Salts such as $\ce{FeCl3*6H2O}$ or $\ce{Cu(NO3)2*3H2O}$ can be used as catalysts for these transformations.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-4-fig2.png

II-4.1 (0.5 pt) Determine the structure of $\mathbf{A}$, if it is characterized by absorption at $1805\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in the IR spectrum, a signal at $175\,\mathrm{ppm}$ in the $^{13}$C NMR spectrum, and a non-symmetrical structure according to $^1$H NMR data.

The researchers’ path to the successful synthesis of $\mathbf{X}$ was not an easy one. You are now invited to decipher two synthetic schemes towards the compounds $\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{X2}$ related to dendrochrysanene.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-4-fig3.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-4-fig4.png

The following signals are observed in the $^1$H NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{C}$ ($400\,\mathrm{MHz}$, $\ce{CDCl3}$): 8.87 (d, $J = 9.2\,\mathrm{Hz}$, 1H), 7.98 (d, $J = 2.8\,\mathrm{Hz}$, 1H), 7.13 (d, $J = 2.8\,\mathrm{Hz}$, 1H), 7.04–7.00 (m, 2H), 6.90 (s, 1H), 4.03 (s, 3H), 3.92 (s, 3H), 1.52 (s, 9H), 1.40 (s, 9H). The mechanism of formation of intermediate $\mathbf{E}$ is similar to the Wittig reaction and proceeds through a four-membered transition state. Compounds $\mathbf{W1}$ and $\mathbf{W2}$, $\mathbf{Y1}$ and $\mathbf{Y2}$ share identical structural fragments and differ only in substituents.

II-4.2 (6 pt) For synthetic scheme “a” determine:

a) structures of $\mathbf{B}$–$\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{W1}$, $\mathbf{Y1}$, and $\mathbf{X1}$;

b) conditions for reactions $\mathbf{I}$–$\mathbf{III}$.

II-4.3 (6.5 pt) For synthetic scheme “b” determine:

a) structures of $\mathbf{E}$–$\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{W2}$, $\mathbf{Y2}$, and $\mathbf{X2}$;

b) conditions for reactions $\mathbf{IV}$ and $\mathbf{V}$.

From $\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{X2}$, Katsuki and his team proposed variants of dendrochrysanene synthesis, as shown in the scheme below. However, only one of the schemes was implemented experimentally.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-4-fig5.png

II-4.4 (1.5 pt) Determine the structures of $\mathbf{X3}$, $\mathbf{X4}$, and $\mathbf{X}$, if $\mathbf{X4}$ and $\mathbf{X}$ differ by one type of substituent ($\mathbf{R1}$, $\mathbf{R2}$, or $\mathbf{R3}$), and $\mathbf{X1}$ and $\mathbf{X}$ share one identical type of substituent ($\mathbf{R1}$, $\mathbf{R2}$, or $\mathbf{R3}$).

II-4.5 (0.5 pt) Hypothesize final step of which scheme (“a” or “b”) could not be carried out by the researchers. Justify your answer by selecting the correct statements.

$$\begin{array}{c|l} \text{a} & \text{Scheme “a” is impossible, since substituent } \mathbf{R1} \text{ does not react with } \mathrm{BBr_3} \\ \hline \text{b} & \text{Scheme “a” is impossible, since substituent } \mathbf{R2} \text{ does not react with } \mathrm{BBr_3} \\ \hline \text{c} & \text{Scheme “b” is impossible, since substituent } \mathbf{R3} \text{ does not react with CuBr/NaOMe} \\ \hline \text{d} & \text{Substituent } \mathbf{R3} \text{ reacts neither with CuBr/NaOMe nor with } \mathrm{BBr_3}\text{, since it is sterically hindered} \\ \hline \text{e} & \text{Substituents } \mathbf{R1} \text{ and } \mathbf{R2} \text{ do not react with } \mathrm{BBr_3} \text{ because of their positions in the aromatic ring} \\ \hline \text{f} & \text{Substituent } \mathbf{R3} \text{ reacts neither with CuBr/NaOMe nor with } \mathrm{BBr_3}\text{, because of its position in the aromatic ring} \\ \hline \text{g} & \text{Scheme “a” is impossible because of many side reactions} \\ \hline \text{h} & \text{Scheme “b” is impossible because of many side reactions} \end{array}$$

problems.title: [Ligands in palladium-catalysed cross-coupling]
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (Organic Chemistry section, problem II-6). [Ligands in palladium-catalysed cross-coupling]

Ligands surrounding the metal play a key role in metal complex catalysis. However, their effect on the course of the reaction is not always as straightforward as it may appear at first glance. Let us consider, as an example, the Pd-catalyzed Stille reaction:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-6-fig1.png

It is known that the rate of this reaction decreases markedly both at excessively high and at excessively low concentrations of triphenylphosphine in the reaction mixture.

II-6.1 (2 pt) Provide the mechanism of the catalytic cycle of the Stille reaction that explains the decrease in the reaction rate at very high concentrations of triphenylphosphine. Encircle the step, the rate of which decreases with an increase in phosphine concentration.

II-6.2 (1 pt) At too low a concentration of triphenylphosphine in the reaction mixture, an elementary substance $\mathbf{Z}$ is formed, which noticeably reduces the reaction rate. Draw the formula of $\mathbf{Z}$.

Oxidative addition is one of the main steps of Pd-catalyzed reactions. Aryl chlorides are much cheaper and more readily available than the corresponding bromides and iodides, thus activation of aryl chlorides is an important challenge in metal complex catalysis. However, the oxidative addition of aryl chlorides to standard triphenylphosphine palladium complexes is hindered due to the high strength of the carbon–chlorine bond; therefore, ligands that render the complex more reactive by creating coordinatively unsaturated species are used to carry out reactions with aryl chlorides.

II-6.3 (1 pt) Which of the given ligands allow for the formation of coordinatively unsaturated complexes capable of undergoing oxidative addition with aryl chlorides?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-6-fig2.png

Oxidative addition is not an elementary step and can proceed via different mechanisms. a) Concerted three-center addition and b) nucleophilic aromatic substitution are the two most frequently encountered mechanisms. To determine which one is operative, one can assess the influence of the electronic effects of substituents in the aryl halide. For a quantitative assessment of the electronic effect of a substituent, it is convenient to use the Hammett constants $\sigma$, calculated from the acidity constants of substituted benzoic acids: $\sigma_\mathrm{X} = \lg\left(\dfrac{K_\mathrm{X}}{K_\mathrm{H}}\right)$, where $\sigma_\mathrm{X}$ is the Hammett constant for substituent X, $K_\mathrm{H}$ is the acidity constant of unsubstituted benzoic acid, and $K_\mathrm{X}$ is the acidity constant of the benzoic acid containing substituent X in the ring.

The figure shows the dependence of the logarithm of the ratio of the rate constants for the oxidative addition of the triphenylphosphine nickel complex to aryl chlorides on the Hammett constant of the substituent in the aryl chloride ($m$ – meta-position, $p$ – para-position, $k$ – rate constant for the reaction with the substituted aryl chloride, $k_0$ – rate constant for the reaction of chlorobenzene).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-6-fig3.png

II-6.4 (1 pt) Match each substituent with the mechanism of oxidative addition to the corresponding aryl chloride. Complete the table in the Answer Sheet.

II-6.5 (0.5 pt) For which substituent is it impossible to unambiguously establish the mechanism of oxidative addition using this method?

Reductive elimination, through which a new carbon–carbon bond is typically formed, is another key step in Pd-catalyzed reactions. In this case, the nature of the ligand can dramatically affect the course of the reaction. For example, the palladium complex $\mathbf{N}$, whose synthesis scheme is shown below, does not undergo reductive elimination even at high temperatures. However, $\mathbf{N}$ is observed to release ethane upon treatment with iodomethane.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-6-fig4.png

II-6.6 (3 pt) Provide the structures of complexes $\mathbf{M}$, $\mathbf{N}$, and $\mathbf{O}$ that reflect their spatial arrangement.

II-6.7 (1.5 pt) a) Provide the mechanism for the formation of ethane in the final stage. b) Encircle “Y” is this reaction is catalytic, encircle “N” is this reaction is not catalytic.

The choice of ligand for the palladium catalyst can influence the reaction pathway. The reaction between butylmagnesium iodide and vinyl iodide may lead to different products depending on the ligand chosen:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-6-fig5.png
