problems.title: [Vibrational partition function and the isotope effect in water ionization]
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (Physical Chemistry section, problem II-7). [Vibrational partition function and the isotope effect in water ionization]

According to the Boltzmann distribution, the probability to find a molecule of an ideal gas in a state with energy $E_n$ is given by the formula

$$\rho(E_n) = \frac{1}{Q}\exp\left(-\frac{E_n}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right),$$

where $k_\mathrm{B} = 1.381\cdot10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}$ is the Boltzmann constant; $Q$ is the molecular partition function (the sum over all states). The expression for $Q$ follows from the normalization constraint (the sum of all probabilities equals one).

II-7.1 (3 pt) Derive the expression for the vibrational partition function $Q_\mathrm{vib}$, assuming that the vibrational energy is measured from the ground (lowest, $n = 0$) state.

At high vibrational frequencies and room temperature, the overwhelming majority of particles is in the ground state ($n = 0$); therefore, the contributions of all other states can be neglected.

II-7.2 (2 pt) At what temperature (K) will 99.9% of all particles be in the zero (ground) vibrational state, if the vibrational frequency is $3000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$?

Knowledge of the partition function allows one to calculate any thermodynamic function of the harmonic oscillator, in particular the Gibbs free energy (per an oscillator):

$$G = G_0 + G_\mathrm{vib} = G_0 - k_\mathrm{B}T\ln Q_\mathrm{vib},$$

where $G_\mathrm{vib}$ is the vibrational contribution to the Gibbs energy, and $G_0$ includes all other contributions, including the constant that defines the energy reference level.

II-7.3 (2 pt) Assuming now that the vibrational energy is measured from the bottom of the oscillator’s potential well, obtain an expression for $G_\mathrm{vib}$ in two cases: a) all vibrational states are taken into account; b) all molecules are in the ground state.

The vibrational contribution to the Gibbs energy explains the isotope effect, that is the change in the equilibrium constant upon isotopic substitution, since the vibrational frequency (and, consequently, the Gibbs energy) changes.

II-7.4 (1 pt) Which types of energy of a gas will change upon isotopic substitution?

a. Electronic

b. Kinetic

c. Rotational

d. Intermolecular interaction

Table 1 lists the ionization constants of light and heavy water at different temperatures.

Table 1.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} T,\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} & 10 & 15 & 20 & 25 & 30 & 35 & 40 & 45 & 50 \\ \hline \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{w}(\ce{H2O}) & 14.53 & 14.34 & 14.17 & 14.00 & 13.83 & 13.68 & 13.54 & 13.40 & 13.27 \\ \hline \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{w}(\ce{D2O}) & 15.50 & 15.30 & 15.12 & 14.95 & 14.78 & 14.63 & 14.48 & 14.33 & 14.20 \end{array}$$

II-7.5 (2 pt) Find the change in enthalpy (J/mol) and entropy (J/(mol·K)) upon the ionization of light and heavy water.

II-7.6 (1 pt) Estimate the neutral pH and pD values for light and heavy water at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

In Table 2 the vibrational frequencies (in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) for various species are given.

Table 2.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \ce{H2O} & \ce{D2O} & \ce{H3O+} & \ce{D3O+} \\ \hline 3755.79 & 2788.05 & 3463.34 & 2606.72 \\ \hline 3656.65 & 2671.46 & 3421.13 & 2582.81 \\ \hline 1594.59 & 1178.33 & 3408.18 & 2466.45 \\ \hline & & 1605.61 & 1184.99 \\ \hline & & 1602.56 & 1183.82 \\ \hline & & 567.04 & 504.46 \end{array}$$

II-7.7 (4 pt) Using the data from Table 2 and the previous parts of the task, estimate the vibrational frequencies ($\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) of the $\ce{OH-}$ and $\ce{OD-}$ ions. If you failed to answer II-7.5, use the following values: for light water $\Delta H = 49210\,\mathrm{J/mol}$ and $\Delta S = -77.15\,\mathrm{J/(mol{\cdot}K)}$; for heavy water $\Delta H = 50790\,\mathrm{J/mol}$ and $\Delta S = -90.07\,\mathrm{J/(mol{\cdot}K)}$.

Notes:

a) Masses of isotopes (a.m.u.): $m(\mathrm{H}) = 1.0078$, $m(\mathrm{D}) = 2.0141$, $m(\mathrm{O}) = 15.9949$.

b) The sum of a geometric progression with ratio $-1 < q < 1$:

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} q^n = \frac{1}{1-q}.$$

c) The energy of the $n$-th level of an oscillator with frequency $\nu$ ($n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$):

$$E_n = h\nu\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right).$$

d) The vibrational frequency of the A−B bond:

$$\nu = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}},$$

where $k$ is the force constant and $\mu = m_\mathrm{A}m_\mathrm{B}/(m_\mathrm{A} + m_\mathrm{B})$ is the reduced mass.

e) $1\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}} = 2.9979\cdot10^{10}\,\mathrm{Hz} = 1.986\cdot10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J}$.

f) If a polyatomic molecule has several types of vibrations, then the contributions from each vibration are summed in the harmonic approximation.

problems.title: [Kinetics of ligand substitution in chelate complexes]
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (Physical Chemistry section, problem II-8). [Kinetics of ligand substitution in chelate complexes]

Dissociation is often the first step in substitution reactions in cyclic complexes. In the case of bidentate ligands, dissociation proceeds stepwise as $\mathrm{M(A_2)}_n \rightleftarrows \mathrm{M(A_2)}_{n-1} + \mathrm{A_2}$ ($k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_n$), is catalyzed by $\ce{H+}$, and the rates of the steps depend on the ligand field stabilization energy (LFSE, with values for the $d$-orbitals shown in the table).

Energy of $d$-orbitals (in $Dq$ units):

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Complex polyhedron} & d_{x^2-y^2} & d_{z^2} & d_{xy} & d_{yz} & d_{zx} \\ \hline \text{Octahedron} & 6.00 & 6.00 & -4.00 & -4.00 & -4.00 \\ \hline \text{Square} & 12.28 & -4.28 & 2.28 & -5.14 & -5.14 \\ \hline \text{Tetrahedron} & -2.67 & -2.67 & 1.78 & 1.78 & 1.78 \end{array}$$

II-8.1 (2 pt) a) Choose the CFT diagram for $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Ni^{2+}}$; b) calculate the LFSE ($Dq$) in $\mathrm{M(A_2)_3}$ and $\mathrm{M(A_2)_2}$; c) write the relationships between LFSE to explain why in the case of $\mathrm{Fe(A_2)_3}$ $k_1 < k_2$, while in the case of $\mathrm{Ni(A_2)_3}$ $k_1 > k_2$.

The dissociation steps are reversible. The reverse reaction ($k_{-1}$) can be prevented by using electrophilic or nucleophilic reagents to accelerate the dissociation (schemes):

$\mathrm{M(A{-}A)} \rightleftarrows [{-}\mathrm{M{-}A{-}A}{-}]$ ($k_1$, $k_{-1}$);

$[{-}\mathrm{M{-}A{-}A}{-}] + \mathbf{B} \rightarrow [\mathrm{B{-}M{-}A{-}A}{-}]$ ($k_2$);

$[\mathrm{B{-}M{-}A{-}A}{-}] \rightarrow \mathrm{MB} + \mathrm{A{-}A}$ ($k_3$)   scheme 1;

$\mathrm{M(A{-}A)} \rightleftarrows [{-}\mathrm{M{-}A{-}A}{-}]$ ($k_1$, $k_{-1}$);

$[{-}\mathrm{M{-}A{-}A}{-}] + \mathbf{D} \rightarrow [{-}\mathrm{M{-}A{-}A{-}D}]$ ($k_2'$);

$[{-}\mathrm{M{-}A{-}A{-}D}] \rightarrow \mathrm{M} + \mathrm{D\,(A{-}A)}$ ($k_3'$)   scheme 2.

II-8.2 (2 pt) Among $\ce{H+}$, $\ce{OH-}$, $\ce{CN-}$, $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$, and $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$, indicate which are a) electrophilic and b) nucleophilic reagents. State which type of reagents (a or b) $\mathbf{B}$ belongs to.

The substitution reactions $\mathrm{MY^{2-}} + \mathrm{Me^{2+}}$ ($\mathrm{Y^{4-}}$ is ethylenediaminetetraacetate) are not always catalyzed by $\ce{H+}$. For example, the reaction $\mathrm{PbY^{2-}} + \ce{Zn^{2+}}$ proceeds via two pathways. The first is catalyzed by an acid and includes the cleavage of the Pb−OCO bond ($k_1$, $k_{-1}$), protonation ($k_2$), and attack by $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ ($k_3$). The second pathway is independent of $[\ce{H+}]$, and its rate is equal to $\dfrac{dc_{\mathrm{ZnY^{2-}}}}{d\tau} = \dfrac{k_4 k_1 c_{\mathrm{PbY^{2-}}} c_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}}}{k_{-1} + k_4 c_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}}}$.

II-8.3 (2 pt) Using the method of stationary approximations, derive the kinetic equation of the first reaction path of the reaction $\mathrm{PbY^{2-}} + \ce{Zn^{2+}}$:

Pb−OCO bond cleavage: $\mathrm{PbY^{2-}} \rightleftarrows \mathrm{(PbY{-})^{2-}}$ ($k_1$, $k_{-1}$);

protonation: $\mathrm{(PbY{-})^{2-}} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow \mathrm{(PbY{-}H)^{-}}$ ($k_2$);

attack by $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$: $\mathrm{(PbY{-}H)^{-}} + \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnY^{2-}} + \mathrm{Pb^{2+}} + \mathrm{H^+}$ ($k_3$).

II-8.4 (2 pt) Propose a mechanism for the other pathway.

For $\mathrm{NiY^{2-}} + \ce{Zn^{2+}}$ ($\ce{Cu^{2+}}$) in the pH range 3–6 at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the data were obtained for the observed rate constant $k_\mathrm{obs}$, (L/(mol·s)) as a function of pH: $1.56\cdot10^{-6}$ (3.00); $2.23\cdot10^{-6}$ (4.00); $2.40\cdot10^{-6}$ (5.00). An associative mechanism with the rate equation $\dfrac{dc_{\mathrm{ZnY^{2-}}}}{d\tau} = (k_5[\mathrm{NiY^{2-}}] + k_6[\mathrm{NiHY^{-}}])c_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}}$ was proposed, which adequately explains the pH dependence of the rate.

II-8.5 (2 pt) a) Derive the equation for calculating and b) calculate the dissociation constant ($K_\mathrm{a}$) for $\mathrm{NiHY^{-}} \rightleftarrows \mathrm{NiY^{2-}} + \mathrm{H^+}$, if the formation constants for the complexes $\mathrm{NiY^{2-}}$ ($\beta_1 = 4.2\cdot10^{18}$) and $\mathrm{NiHY^{-}}$ ($\beta_2 = 3.6\cdot10^{11}$), as well as the dissociation constant of the ligand $\mathrm{HY^{3-}}$ ($K_4 = 5.5\cdot10^{-11}$), are known.

II-8.6 (2 pt) Derive the equation for $k_\mathrm{obs}$ that depends solely on $K_\mathrm{a}$ and $[\ce{H+}]$, and calculate $k_5$ and $k_6$.

The intermediate is formed only in the pathway with $k_5$, in which first an associate is formed reversibly ($K$), and then the reaction product is formed ($k$). It turned out that for the reaction of $\mathrm{NiY^{2-}}$ with $\mathrm{Me^{2+}}$, the relationship between $K$ and $k_5$ is linear: $\lg k_5 = -12.35 + 1.01\cdot\lg K$.

II-8.7 (3 pt) Derive the kinetic equation, and calculate $K$ and $k$.

problems.title: [Size effects in gold nanoparticles and nanofilms]
problems.problem:
Problem 9 (Physical Chemistry section, problem II-9). [Size effects in gold nanoparticles and nanofilms]

Chemical and physical properties of substances can depend significantly on the size of a sample. A decrease in the melting temperature has been observed for nanocrystals of Ag, Al, Au, Bi, Cu, Ga, In, Pb, and Sn. From a thermodynamic point of view, the transition from the solid to the liquid state with increasing temperature begins with the appearance of a thin liquid layer on the surface of a nanoparticle while its core remains solid. This phenomenon is caused by the surface tension at the solid phase/liquid interface, which alters the energy of the system. For spherical and cylindrical nanoparticles, the Gibbs energy is higher than that of the macrophase due to the excess surface pressure ($p$):

$$G_\mathrm{solid} = G_\mathrm{solid}^{\infty} + pV_\mathrm{m}$$

The excess pressure for spherical ($p_1$) and cylindrical ($p_2$) particles of radius $r$ can be calculated using Laplace's equation:

$$p_1 = \frac{2\sigma}{r}, \qquad\qquad p_2 = \frac{\sigma}{r},$$

Here, $\sigma$ is the surface tension at the solid phase/liquid phase interface.

II-9.1 (1 pt) Calculate the excess pressure (atm) at the specified interface at the melting temperature for a) a gold wire with the diameter of $0.5\,\mathrm{mm}$; b) gold nanoparticles with the diameter of $15\,\mathrm{nm}$. The surface tension of gold is $3\,\mathrm{mN/cm}$.

The dependence of the melting temperature of gold nanoparticles on the radius $r$ can be described by the Gibbs–Thomson equation:

$$T_\mathrm{melt} = T_\mathrm{melt}^{\infty}(1 - a/r),$$

where $T_\mathrm{melt}^{\infty}$ is the melting temperature of the macrophase, and $a$ is a parameter that depends on $V_\mathrm{m}$, $\sigma$, and $\Delta H_\mathrm{melt}$ and is equal to $4.88\cdot10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$. Equilibrium between the two phases at constant pressure and temperature is achieved when the molar Gibbs energies of the substance in these phases are equal. For example, at a melting temperature

$$G_\mathrm{solid}(T_\mathrm{melt}) = G_\mathrm{liq}(T_\mathrm{melt}), \qquad\qquad \Delta S_\mathrm{melt} = \Delta H_\mathrm{melt}/T_\mathrm{melt}^{\infty}.$$

II-9.2 (3 pt) Determine the density of gold ($\mathrm{kg/m^3}$), if $\Delta H_\mathrm{melt}^\mathrm{Au} = 12.55\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. Hint: derive the equation for the dependence of the melting temperature on the radius of the nanoparticles (the Gibbs–Thomson equation) and obtain an expression for the parameter $a$.

The melting temperatures of gold as nanoparticles with a radius of $6.5\,\mathrm{nm}$ and as the macrophase differ by $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

II-9.3 (1.5 pt) Determine the standard entropy of melting of gold (J/(mol·K)).

II-9.4 (1.5 pt) Calculate the standard electrode potential (V) of the $\ce{AuI2-}$/Au pair at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, given that $E^0_{\mathrm{Au^+/Au}} = 1.69\,\mathrm{V}$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{AuI_2^-}} = 5.6\cdot10^{18}$.

II-9.5 (3 pt) Write the ionic equation for the dissolution reaction of a gold nanowire with the diameter of $10\,\mathrm{nm}$ in a solution of $\ce{KI3}$ (1 M) + $\ce{KI}$ (1 M) and calculate its equilibrium constant at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The surface tension at the solid phase/water interface for gold is $0.55\,\mathrm{N/m}$, $E^0_{\mathrm{I_2/2I^-}} = 0.536\,\mathrm{V}$, $\beta_{\mathrm{I_3^-}} \approx 1$. If you failed to determine the density of gold in II-9.2, assume it to be $19000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

The electrical conductivity of nanofilms drops significantly with decreasing their thickness. The presence of lattice defects arising from an increased surface-to-volume ratio is one of the factors for the increase in the resistance. The classical theory of size effects in the electrical conductivity of thin films is known as the Fuchs–Sondheimer model. For the resistivity of a thin film with thickness $d$ and an electron mean free path $l$, the following empirical equation has been obtained:

$$\rho = \rho_0\cdot\left(1 + \frac{3l}{8d}\right).$$

The electron mean free path can be estimated by the formula:

$$l = k\cdot\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{8\pi}}\cdot\frac{h}{e^2\cdot\sqrt[3]{n^2}}\cdot\sigma_0,$$

where $\sigma_0$ is the electrical conductivity of the macrophase (in $1/(\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m})$), $e$ is the electron charge ($1.602\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$), $n$ is the concentration of conduction electrons ($1/\mathrm{m^3}$), $h$ is Planck’s constant ($6.626\cdot10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}$), and $k$ is a proportionality factor ($8.69\cdot10^{5}$).

Below are the values of the electrical conductivity of gold nanofilms of various thicknesses:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \sigma,\ 1/(\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}) & 36.10 & 39.82 & 41.35 & 42.24 & 44.15 & 44.85 \\ \hline d,\ \mathrm{nm} & 40 & 60 & 80 & 100 & 140 & 180 \end{array}$$

II-9.6 (3 pt) Calculate the resistivity of the macrophase $\rho_0$ (in $\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$) and the electron mean free path in gold (in nm).

II-9.7 (2 pt) Calculate the number of conduction electrons ($N_\mathrm{e}$) per gold atom in the thin film. If you failed to determine the resistivity of macrophase $\rho_0$ and the electron mean free path $l$, assume them as $0.0182\,\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$ and $40\,\mathrm{nm}$, respectively, for further calculations.

problems.title: [150 years of the Division of Inorganic Chemistry at Moscow State University]
problems.problem:
Problem 10 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem II-10). [150 years of the Division of Inorganic Chemistry at Moscow State University]

In 2025, the Division of Inorganic Chemistry at the Chemistry Department, Lomonosov Moscow State University celebrates its 150th anniversary. Let us consider several outstanding works done by the Division researchers.

The distinguished academician I.A. Kablukov was one of the first heads of the Division (1917–1926); some of his works were devoted to the theory of solutions. He investigated the electrical conductivity of electrolyte solutions in non-aqueous media and introduced the concept of ion solvation.

II-10.1 (1 pt) Arrange the following solutions in order of increasing their molar electrical conductivity: 0.01 M $\ce{NaCl}$ in water, 0.01 M $\ce{NaCl}$ in ethanol, 0.01 M $\ce{[PdCl2(NH3)2]}$ in water, 0.01 M $\ce{CaCl2}$ in water, 0.01 M $\ce{H2SO4}$ in water.

Academician V.I. Spitsyn, the head of the Division (1942–1988), is the founder of the chemistry of rare and trace elements in Russia. Spitsyn’s works made a background for production of metal $\mathbf{M1}$ from the binary mineral $\mathbf{A}$, which has a layered structure with van der Waals interactions between the layers only. Each layer consists of trigonal prisms joined along common edges, with an $\mathbf{M1}$ atom located at the center of each prism. The figure shows a top view over such a layer.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-10-fig1.png

II-10.2 (0.5 pt) Determine the ratio of atoms in $\mathbf{A}$.

The technology of obtaining $\mathbf{M1}$ involves calcination of mineral $\mathbf{A}$ (which contains 60 wt% of $\mathbf{M1}$) in oxygen to produce oxide $\mathbf{B}$. To purify the oxide, $\mathbf{B}$ is dissolved in ammonia to yield the crystalline product $\mathbf{C}$; $\mathbf{C}$ reverts to $\mathbf{B}$ upon thermal decomposition. Reduction of $\mathbf{B}$ with hydrogen at heating is the final production step.

II-10.3 (3.5 pt) a) Decipher $\mathbf{M1}$ and write the formulae of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$; b) write the equations of the described reactions.

The works of academician A.V. Novoselova dated back to the 1930s–40s were devoted to the chemistry of rare metals and their compounds. She made a significant contribution to the study of the rare light metal $\mathbf{M2}$, which does not react with water or steam but readily dissolves in a concentrated ammonium fluoride solution due to the formation of a stable water-soluble fluoride complex $\mathbf{X1}$. $\mathbf{M2}$ is in tetrahedral environment of fluoride ions in the structure of $\mathbf{X1}$. The problem of synthesizing the high-melting orthosilicate of $\mathbf{M2}$ from oxides was resolved by conducting the reaction under a gas-transport regime. The substance $\mathbf{X2}$, a sodium analog of $\mathbf{X1}$, was used as a transport agent. The formation of two main gaseous components $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$, from which the orthosilicate is produced, was proved by mass-spectrometry of this gas-transport reaction. The mass numbers of $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ are 89 and 82, respectively.

II-10.4 (2.5 pt) a) Determine $\mathbf{M2}$, $\mathbf{X1}$, $\mathbf{X2}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{Z}$; b) write the equations for the dissolution of $\mathbf{M2}$ in $\ce{NH4F}$ and the synthesis of the orthosilicate from $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$.

II-10.5 (0.5 pt) What is the structure of $\mathbf{Z}$ in the gas phase?

a) tetrahedron; b) trigonal planar; c) disphenoid; d) T-shape; e) octahedron; f) angular

The study of high-temperature superconductors is among the most important research directions at the Division since late 1980s. Thus, Corresponding Member of Russian Academy of Sciences E.V. Antipov and Dr. S.N. Putilin described a multi-step synthesis of compound $\mathbf{N}$. Initially, compound $\mathbf{R}$ is obtained by sintering three salts, $\mathbf{S1}$–$\mathbf{S3}$, in a molar ratio of $2 : 1 : 2$ at $925\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in an oxygen atmosphere; these salts contain identical anions. Subsequent sintering of $\mathbf{R}$ with the binary compound $\mathbf{T}$ in equimolar amounts at an oxygen pressure of 18 kbar and $880\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ leads to the formation of $\mathbf{N}$, which has a superconducting critical temperature $T_\mathrm{C} = 104\,\mathrm{K}$. The mass fraction of the heaviest element in $\mathbf{N}$ is 26.97%. The ratio of the mass fractions of the cation and nitrogen in $\mathbf{S1}$ is 4.90. The mass fractions of cations in $\mathbf{S2}$ and $\mathbf{S3}$ are 16.97% and 26.30%, respectively. $\mathbf{T}$ cannot be obtained by the thermal decomposition of a salt containing the same anion as in $\mathbf{S1}$–$\mathbf{S3}$, but it can be prepared by treatment of that salt with an alkali. The mass percentage of the cation in $\mathbf{T}$ is 92.61%.

II-10.6 (4.5 pt) a) Write formulae of $\mathbf{N}$, $\mathbf{S1}$–$\mathbf{S3}$, $\mathbf{R}$, and $\mathbf{T}$; provide your calculations. b) Write the reaction of the formation of $\mathbf{R}$.

One of the most interesting works of recent years is devoted to nano-objects. Professor R.B. Vasiliev’s research group obtained nanosheets and nanoscrolls of cadmium telluride with a sphalerite structure ($a = 6.48\,\text{Å}$). The reaction proceeds between cadmium acetate and tellurium in trioctylphosphine, resulting in cadmium telluride nanosheets in which both surfaces consist solely of cadmium atoms. To stabilize the nanoparticles, each cadmium atom is coordinated by an anion of oleic (cis-9-octadecenoic) acid. A ligand exchange reaction with hexadecanethiol was performed to determine the thickness of the sheets. The mass loss of 4.148% was observed as a result of complete ligand replacement.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-10-fig2.png

II-10.7 (2 pt) a) Write the ligand exchange reaction; b) calculate the thickness $s$ of a single nanosheet (Å).

II-10.8 (0.5 pt) Production of which metals and their compounds:

a) $\mathbf{M1}$, b) $\mathbf{M2}$, c) metal in $\mathbf{T}$, d) cadmium

requires specially strict safety measures to prevent their entry into the human body and the environment, which could lead to an ecological disaster?

problems.title: [An elusive anion X]
problems.problem:
Problem 11 (Inorganic Chemistry section, problem II-11). [An elusive anion X]

For a long time, chemists failed to obtain inorganic salts containing the anion $\mathbf{X}$, an analog of a well-studied anion containing a neighboring element from the same group of the periodic table. The first reports on the synthesis of sodium salt $\mathbf{A}$ with this anion appeared as early as 1894. In this synthesis, the salt $\mathbf{B}$ ($w(\mathrm{Na}) = 41.07\%$) was used as the starting material. $\mathbf{B}$ was obtained by the reaction of sodium with the compound $\mathbf{C}$, a gas (at $20.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $100.0\,\mathrm{kPa}$) with a characteristic odor. The authors assumed that $\mathbf{A}$ was formed as a result of the reaction between $\mathbf{B}$ and CO. In addition to $\mathbf{A}$, water is produced in this reaction, which prevented the isolation of $\mathbf{A}$ from the reaction mixture, since water decomposes $\mathbf{A}$ into the salt $\mathbf{D}$ ($w(\mathrm{Na}) = 33.80\%$) and $\mathbf{C}$. The authors considered the presence of $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ in the reaction products as indirect evidence for the formation of $\mathbf{A}$.

II-11.1 (4 pt) Determine the formulae of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, and $\mathbf{D}$. Give your calculations.

II-11.2 (1 pt) Write equations of the reactions that, according to the authors, occur during the synthesis of $\mathbf{A}$.

It took a very long time before the erroneous views of the authors reported the first synthesis of the salt $\mathbf{A}$ were disproved. Only in 2011 (117 years later!) the reaction between $\mathbf{B}$ and CO was re-investigated using modern analytical methods. It has been found that, instead of $\mathbf{A}$, the salt $\mathbf{E}$ ($w(\mathrm{Na}) = 28.05\%$) is formed, along with trace amounts of the salt $\mathbf{F}$ ($w(\mathrm{Na}) = 27.37\%$).

II-11.3 (2 pt) Write a) the formulae of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$; b) draw structural formulae of their anions. Give your calculations.

The acid $\mathbf{Y}$, which contains the anion $\mathbf{X}$, was more fortunate than $\mathbf{A}$. The isolation of $\mathbf{Y}$ was reported for the first time in 1961. The composition and structure of $\mathbf{Y}$ were confirmed by IR spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, and elemental analysis. Moreover, the compound $\mathbf{G}$ was the sole product of the reaction of $\mathbf{Y}$ with an excess of hydrogen chloride at $-110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, which indirectly confirmed the composition and structure of $\mathbf{Y}$.

II-11.4 (2 pt) Write a) equation of the reaction of $\mathbf{Y}$ with an excess of hydrogen chloride and b) draw the structural formula of $\mathbf{G}$.

In 2004, the first successful two-step synthesis of the salt $\mathbf{H}$ was reported. The salt consists of a tetraphenylphosphonium cation ($\ce{PPh4+}$) and an anion, which is an adduct of $\ce{B(CF3)3}$ and $\mathbf{X}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-11-fig1.png

II-11.5 (3 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{H}$, $\mathbf{H1}$, and $\mathbf{H2}$.

Notably, $\mathbf{H}$ is stable for several days in moist acetonitrile. An attempt to obtain the potassium salt in the exchange reaction between $\mathbf{H}$ and $\ce{K[BPh4]}$ in the presence of moisture was unsuccessful and resulted in the formation of potassium salt $\mathbf{J}$ ($w(\mathrm{K}) = 11.64\%$) with a different anion.

II-11.6 (3 pt) Draw the structure of the anion of salt $\mathbf{J}$.

problems.title: [Chalcogenides of element X]
[An adulterant in dairy products]
problems.problem:
Problem 13 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem II-13). [An adulterant in dairy products]

An organic compound $\mathbf{A}$ is synthesized on an industrial scale and is mainly used in the production of polymer resins. This substance was also at the center of one of the largest food industry scandals that occurred in 2008. Investigations revealed that several manufacturers in one country were adding $\mathbf{A}$ to their dairy products to artificially increase the measured protein content. Unfortunately, this led to urinary system problems of thousands of children.

$\mathbf{A}$ contains three equivalent amino groups. The mass fraction of one of the elements in $\mathbf{A}$ is 66.67%. The mass spectrum of $\mathbf{A}$ (electrospray ionization, positive ion detection mode, $I$ is relative intensity) is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-13-fig1.png

II-13.1 (3 pt) Determine the molecular formula of $\mathbf{A}$ and propose structures for the species corresponding to the $m/z$ 43 and $m/z$ 127 signals.

An analytical laboratory took milk samples containing $\mathbf{A}$ and conducted three analyses. In analysis No 1 based on the Kjeldahl method, a $2.00\,\mathrm{g}$ milk sample was heated with concentrated sulfuric acid. After treatment with a base, a gas $\mathbf{B}$ was released and absorbed by boric acid. The titration of the resulting tetraborate salt required $7.15\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$.

II-13.2 (2 pt) a) Provide the molecular formula of $\mathbf{B}$.
b) Write the equation for its reaction with boric acid.

II-13.3 (2 pt) a) Write the equation for the titration reaction.
b) Calculate the nitrogen mass fraction ($w(\mathrm{N})$, %) in the milk sample analyzed by the Kjeldahl method. If you failed to obtain an answer, use the value of 1.00% in further calculations.

Analysis No 2 was performed using the Sørensen method (formol titration), which allows determining the number of free amino groups ($\ce{R-NH2}$) in a protein. A $20.0\,\mathrm{g}$ milk sample was titrated with $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaOH}$ using phenolphthalein as an indicator until a faint pink color appeared, which required $9.60\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the titrant. Assume that at this point: all organic acids in the milk have been titrated; $\mathbf{A}$ is present in its neutral form; protein amino groups are protonated ($\ce{R-NH3+}$). Then, $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of an aqueous formaldehyde solution (37%, density $1.09\,\mathrm{g/mL}$) was added, allowed to react for a few minutes, and titrated again until a faint pink color appeared. The total $\ce{NaOH}$ volume required for the first and second titrations was $14.15\,\mathrm{mL}$. To account for the neutralization of the formaldehyde solution, a control experiment was performed separately. The titration of $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the formaldehyde solution required $2.35\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaOH}$.

II-13.4 (2 pt) Write the reaction equations that occur: a) upon the addition of formaldehyde; b) during subsequent titration with the base; c) in the control experiment.

A standard milk sample contains $3.20\,\mathrm{g}$ of protein per $100\,\mathrm{g}$ of milk. Free amino groups in proteins account for an average of 4.7% of the total nitrogen content, and the nitrogen mass fraction in protein is on average 15.7%.

II-13.5 (3 pt) a) Calculate the mass fraction of $\mathbf{A}$ ($w(\mathbf{A})$, %) in the analyzed milk.
b) Determine the factor ($x$), by which the protein content in the analyzed milk is lower than the standard value.

Detecting compound $\mathbf{A}$ in various food matrices remains a challenging task requiring the development of cost-efficient and express methods. Fluorescent analysis is one of promising approaches, in which $\mathbf{A}$ binds to a sensor $\mathbf{C}$ via the formation of six hydrogen bonds. $\mathbf{C}$ is synthesized according to the following scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-13-fig2.png

II-13.6 (1 pt) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{C}$.

The analytical laboratory performed analysis No 3 using the fluorescence method. For this, $200\,\mathrm{\mu L}$ of the milk sample was diluted with an organic solvent to a total volume of $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$. Then, $1.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the obtained solution was mixed with $1.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\mathbf{C}$ solution to obtain solution 1. In another $200\,\mathrm{\mu L}$ milk sample, $2.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a $500\,\mathrm{ppm}$ solution of $\mathbf{A}$ (1 ppm corresponds to 1 mg of a substance per 1 L of the solution) was added, followed by dilution to $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$. Then, $1.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the resulting solution was mixed with $1.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\mathbf{C}$ solution to obtain solution 2. The fluorescence intensity of solution 1 was $I_1 = 3.46$ a. u. (arbitrary units), while solution 2 had $I_2 = 4.87$ a. u. The fluorescence intensity of the control solution, i.e., without milk and $\mathbf{A}$, was $I_0 = 2.72$ a. u.

II-13.7 (2 pt) Calculate the concentration of $\mathbf{A}$ ($c(\mathbf{A})$, mg/mL) in the analyzed milk according to the fluorescence method.

problems.title: [Solubility of phosphate minerals]
problems.problem:
Problem 14 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem II-14). [Solubility of phosphate minerals]

Answering all the questions in this problem, provide your calculations.

The necessary physical and chemical conditions for the formation of calcium phosphates occur near the bottom sediments of water reservoirs with high biological productivity. In these relatively shallow areas, phosphorus is bioconcentrated. The biogenic material formed by organisms contains a significant amount of phosphorus and due to shallow depths quickly reaches the bottom with minimal loss of phosphorus. As a result, concentrations of the dissolved mineral phosphorus of up to 5–10 mg/L are registered near the bottom sediments, which is sufficient to form even the most soluble (amorphous) apatite. Phosphate minerals also include monazite ($\ce{CePO4}$) and francolite, a carbonate-rich form of fluorapatite.

The solubility of salts containing anions of weak acids depends on pH. To calculate such solubilities, the protonation of anions of the weak acid must be taken into account, which shifts the dissolution equilibrium towards the products. The values of the mole fractions of anions at different pH values are given at the end of the problem. Ignore the change in pH of water during dissolution, the content of extraneous ions, and the hydrolysis of the cation in all subsequent parts of the problem, if not stated otherwise.

II-14.1 (2 pt) Monazite was discovered in the South Ural Mountains close to the city of Miass. $28.82\,\mathrm{mg}$ of monazite is dissolved in $1\,\mathrm{m^3}$ of pore water with pH 7.46 initially containing $2\,\mathrm{\mu g/L}$ of the inorganic phosphorus. Calculate the solubility product of monazite $K_\mathrm{sp}^\mathrm{monazite}$.

II-14.2 (2 pt) Noting the molar solubility of francolite ($\ce{Ca_{9.54}Na_{0.33}Mg_{0.13}(PO4)_{4.8}(CO3)_{1.4}F_{2.48}}$) by $s$, express the solubility product $K_\mathrm{sp}^\mathrm{francolite}$ in terms of $s$ and the mole fractions of the anions $\alpha_{\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}}$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}}$, and $\alpha_{\mathrm{F^-}}$.

II-14.3 (3 pt) Determine the total concentration (mg/L) of inorganic phosphorus formed by dissolution of francolite $\ce{Ca_{9.54}Na_{0.33}Mg_{0.13}(PO4)_{4.8}(CO3)_{1.4}F_{2.48}}$:

a) in pore waters of Lake Turgoyak (Chelyabinsk region, Russia) with pH 7.46.

b) in acidic waters of the Leviathan mine (California, USA) with pH 3.83.

$K_\mathrm{sp}^\mathrm{francolite} = 10^{-94.7}$.

It is known that isomorphic substitution of $\ce{PO4^{3-}}$ by $\ce{CO3^{2-}}$ because of an increased carbonate alkalinity is accompanied by an increase in the solubility of apatites. For francolites ($\mathrm{Ca_{10}(PO_4)}_{5.83-0.57x}\mathrm{(CO_3)}_x\mathrm{F}_{2.52-0.3x}$), the hereunder linear relationship between $\log_{10}K_\mathrm{sp}$ of francolite and corresponding fluorapatite ($x = 0$) was found:

$$\log_{10}K_\mathrm{sp}^\mathrm{francolite} = \log_{10}K_\mathrm{sp}^\mathrm{fluorapatite} + kx,$$

where $k$ is the proportionality factor.

To study the dependence of francolite solubility on the degree of isomorphic substitution of $\ce{PO4^{3-}}$ by $\ce{CO3^{2-}}$, the composition of mine waters from the Lovozero alkaline massif (Kola Peninsula, Russia) with pH 11.74 was investigated (note that these waters can be considered as a saturated solution over francolites):

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} x & 0.25 & 0.5 & 1 & 1.25 \\ \hline [\ce{Ca^{2+}}],\ \mathrm{M} & 4.60\cdot10^{-7} & 9.05\cdot10^{-7} & 1.72\cdot10^{-6} & 2.75\cdot10^{-6} \end{array}$$

Assume that the $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$, $\ce{PO4^{3-}}$, $\ce{CO3^{2-}}$, and $\ce{F-}$ ions are formed in solution only due to dissolution of francolite.

II-14.4 (6 pt) Determine $K_\mathrm{sp}^\mathrm{fluorapatite}$ and the proportionality factor $k$. If you failed to determine $K_\mathrm{sp}^\mathrm{fluorapatite}$ and $k$, use $10^{-130}$ and 13.0, respectively, in subsequent calculations.

The Leviathan Mine was reported to produce some few million liters of acidic water each year. During spring and fall, precipitation volumes increase significantly, which results in up to 15 million liters of acid mine waters generated annually.

II-14.5 (2 pt) Calculate $K_\mathrm{sp}$ for the francolite $\ce{Ca10(PO4)_{5.4}(CO3)_{0.75}F_{2.3}}$. How many years ($t$) are needed to have 50 tons of this mineral dissolved in the Leviathan mine?

Notes:

a) Mole fractions of anions at different pH values:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Mole fraction} & \text{pH 3.83} & \text{pH 7.46} & \text{pH 11.74} \\ \hline \alpha_{\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}} & 3.56\cdot10^{-12} & 2.34\cdot10^{-5} & 0.41 \\ \hline \alpha_{\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}} & 9.52\cdot10^{-10} & 1.25\cdot10^{-3} & 0.96 \\ \hline \alpha_{\mathrm{F^-}} & 0.817 & 1 & 1 \end{array}$$

b) The mole fraction for the anion: $\alpha_{\mathrm{A}^{n-}} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}^{n-}]}{[\mathrm{A}^{n-}] + \ldots + [\mathrm{H}_n\mathrm{A}]} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}^{n-}]}{c_0^{\mathrm{A}^{n-}}}$

problems.title: [Detection and determination of cyanides]
problems.problem:
Problem 15 (Analytical Chemistry section, problem II-15). [Detection and determination of cyanides]

Hydrocyanic acid $\ce{HCN}$ and its salts (cyanides) are lethal poisons that, when ingested, inhibit the enzyme of the respiratory electron transport chain and lead to cellular hypoxia. The maximum permissible daily dose of $\ce{HCN}$ is $0.6\,\mathrm{mg}$ per $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of human body weight.

Various detection reactions are used to identify cyanide in solutions, such as described in Experiments 1–3:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Experiment} & \text{Procedure} & \text{Observations} \\ \hline 1 & \ce{CN-} + \text{reagent } \mathbf{A}\text{, then reagent } \mathbf{B} & \text{dark blue precipitate} \\ \hline 2 & \ce{CN-} + \text{reagent } \mathbf{C}\text{, then reagent } \mathbf{B} & \text{blood-red coloration of the solution} \\ \hline 3 & \text{reagent } \mathbf{D} + \text{reagent } \mathbf{E}\text{, then } \ce{CN-} & \text{dissolution of black precipitate, release of gas with a pungent odor} \end{array}$$

II-15.1 (5.5 pt) Select the appropriate reagents $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{E}$ from the list below (all proposed reagents are aqueous solutions):

$\ce{NaOH}$, $\ce{HNO3}$(conc.), $\ce{HCl}$, $\ce{FeSO4}$, $\ce{Fe2(SO4)3}$, $\ce{(NH4)2S}$, $\ce{(NH4)2S2}$, $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$, $\ce{KMnO4}$, $\ce{CuSO4}$

Write the ionic equations for the chemical reactions described in a) Experiment 1, b) Experiment 2, and c) Experiment 3.

Cyanogenic substances that form $\ce{HCN}$ upon entering the body are present in the fruits of certain plants. For example, bitter almonds contain the cyanogenic compound amygdalin ($\ce{C20H27NO11}$), which is responsible for their bitterness and characteristic aroma. The average amygdalin content is $44\,\mathrm{g}$ per $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of almonds, and the mass of a single almond kernel is approximately $3.2\,\mathrm{g}$.

II-15.2 (2 pt) Calculate the maximum number of bitter almond kernels ($N$) that a 65 kg person can safely consume in one day. Assume the almond kernels are indivisible.

For the qualitative analysis of cyanogenic substances, the fruit is ground into a powder, placed in a flask with a gas outlet tube, mixed with water and $\ce{NaOH}$, and thoroughly stirred. Then, 1 M $\ce{H2SO4}$ is gradually added to the suspension while passing a stream of air through it. The outlet tube is placed into a solution of $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]SO4}$ containing an excess of $\ce{NH3}$. If cyanides are present in the sample, the blue color of the solution changes to green due to the formation of a neutral complex $\mathbf{G}$, which contains copper ions in different oxidation states and an equal number of $\ce{NH3}$ and $\ce{CN-}$ ligands. The formation of $\mathbf{G}$ requires 5/3 mol of $\ce{CN-}$ per 1 mol of $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$, of which 1/3 mol undergoes a two-electron oxidation to the ion $\mathbf{F}$.

II-15.3 (2 pt) Identify the ion $\mathbf{F}$ and determine the composition of the complex $\mathbf{G}$.

Another source of $\ce{HCN}$, along with dozens of other toxic substances, is smoking. About 10% of the $\ce{HCN}$ released during tobacco combustion passes through the filter and enters the cigarette smoke inhaled by a smoker. The amount of $\ce{HCN}$ in cigarette smoke can be estimated spectrophotometrically. For this, a cigarette is connected to the inlet tube of a gas wash bottle filled with $40.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a 2% $\ce{Na2CO3}$ solution. The outlet tube is connected to a vacuum pump, and the cigarette is lit, causing all the cigarette smoke to pass through the $\ce{Na2CO3}$ solution. A $1.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquot of the resulting solution is mixed with $0.50\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a 0.5% ninhydrin ($\mathbf{X}$) solution and left for 15 min to allow the following reaction to take place, during which the yellow color of the solution changes to red due to the formation of the compound $\mathbf{Y}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-15-fig1.png

The experiment was repeated for two additional cigarettes using fresh $\ce{Na2CO3}$ solutions. The absorbance ($A$) of all three solutions was measured at the maximum absorption wavelength of $\mathbf{Y}$ with a molar extinction coefficient of $\varepsilon = 1.40\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$. The cuvette width was $l = 1\,\mathrm{cm}$. The absorbance values relative to the blank solution for the three aliquots were 0.277, 0.265 and 0.274.

II-15.4 (3 pt) Calculate the total mass of $\ce{HCN}$ ($m(\ce{HCN})_0$, $\mathrm{\mu g}$) released during the combustion of one cigarette.

Addition of 1 M $\ce{NaOH}$ solution to $\mathbf{Y}$ results in the solution color change to blue due to the formation of substance $\mathbf{Z}$. The absorption spectra of $\mathbf{X}$–$\mathbf{Z}$ are given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/imcho-2025-2-15-fig2.png

II-15.5 (2.5 pt) Provide the structure of $\mathbf{Z}$ and match the spectra I–III to $\mathbf{X}$–$\mathbf{Z}$.
